title: Master: daemon lifecycle, pty, child and peer-uid check
description:
`acs _master` process lifecycle (DESIGN §4.2, §4.5).

- Started by the proxy: double-fork, `setsid`, stdio to `/dev/null`; take the
  session creation lock; bind the socket **before** spawning the child;
  report readiness over a pipe (dtach's statusfd) so the proxy never races
  the bind.
- Child: `$SHELL -l` in `$HOME`, or the `-- command...` given; env `TERM`,
  `COLORTERM` from HELLO, `ACS_SESSION=<name>`.
- Reap the child on SIGCHLD, keep its wait status; unlink the socket on exit.
- Every minute re-check the socket path and re-bind if it was removed
  (tmpfiles cleanup).
- On every accepted connection verify the peer uid (`SO_PEERCRED` on Linux,
  `getpeereid` on macOS) and drop foreign uids.
- Instance id: random u64 minted at creation.

Tests: start a master in a temp `ACS_SOCKET_DIR` running `/bin/sh -c`; two
concurrent starts produce one master; child exit status observed; socket
removed on exit and re-bound after deletion.
close_reason: master.rs: spawn() with readiness pipe on fd 3, fork+setsid daemon, creation lock around check+bind, child on pty with setsid/TIOCSCTTY and TERM/COLORTERM/ACS_SESSION, SIGCHLD reaping, socket unlink on exit and re-bind after deletion, peer-uid check; tests: exit status, concurrent starts, rebind, missing session, protocol mismatch

title: Run the session menu and the attach over one ssh connection
description:
Wanted: a plain `acs <host>` makes two ssh connections, one to list sessions for the menu and one for the session, each paying a full TCP + key exchange + auth handshake. Reduce it to a single call to connect faster. The user's `acs -v corello` on v0.6.0 shows `ssh … _proxy --list` followed by `ssh -o ControlMaster=no -o ControlPath=none … _proxy --session main --mode attach-or-create`.

Verified (v0.6.0): src/pick.rs `choose` lists with `list::query(.., Call::Side, ..)`, then the attach dials its own connection. The session call opts out of multiplexing on purpose (DESIGN §3: a reconnect must never wait on a dead multiplexer), so even `ControlMaster auto` + `ControlPersist` cannot share it. Ending a session with 'x' in the menu is a third kind of call, `_proxy --kill <name>` (pick.rs `end`, src/proxy.rs). The second handshake costs a few hundred ms, more through a jump host, and a hardware key needs two touches.

This revisits a recorded decision: DESIGN §4.4 says "reusing one connection for both is not worth a second proxy mode." The implementing PR updates §4.4 (and §3/§4.3/§5.1 as needed) and says why the decision changed: connect latency and the double auth.

Sketch: a picker mode on the session connection, e.g. `_proxy --pick` with the usual transport options. The proxy first sends the session list as frames (the STATUS data `--list` gathers). The client decides on that list exactly as today (none detached: create; else the menu in menu.rs, unchanged). Menu actions travel on the same connection: '.' (refresh with attached sessions), 'x' (end a session, then a fresh list), new. The pick ends with the ordinary HELLO naming the session and mode (and `force` after a confirmed takeover); the proxy then connects to or starts that master and relays as now. Leaving the menu (Esc/exit) closes the connection cleanly.

Unchanged: redials (they know the session and use the plain session call), `acs <host> <name>`, `--new`, `--list`, and the non-tty fallback, which are already a single call. Keep the install path working: a host without acs answers ACS-NEED on the pick call as on any other, so install, then continue. The ACS-READY marker and the dial deadlines (§5.3) apply to the pick phase. Mind the menu's idle time: the connection sits open while the user reads it, with no liveness pings before WELCOME.

Done when `acs -v <host>` with detached sessions shows one ssh invocation from list to attach, 'x' and '.' work without extra ssh calls, the proto/proxy changes have unit tests and an end-to-end test (scripts/e2e_ssh.sh or the in-process tests) covers pick → attach on one connection, and DESIGN/README describe it.
close_reason: Implemented in PR #40 (1dc2233): _proxy --pick runs the session menu, x and the attach over one ssh connection

title: Specify an ssh local port forward on the command line, mirroring ssh -L
description:
User's words: "Make it possible that ssh port forward can be specified on command line, mirroring ssh '-L'".

Today `-L` is rejected outright: the accepted ssh options are exactly `-i -p -J -F -o` (src/cli.rs:162), and any other short option falls through to src/cli.rs:192 and errors with `unknown option -L`.

## It is already possible, badly

`-o` is an unvalidated pass-through — acs never inspects the value — so this works right now:

```sh
acs -o LocalForward="8080 localhost:80" box
```

That matters for scoping: this bead is **not** about making forwarding possible, it is about making it correct and ergonomic. Three reasons it still deserves doing, in order of weight:

**1. The `-o` route is actually wrong, not merely ugly.** `user_opts` is shared by all three `Call` kinds (src/ssh.rs:96-123). `Call::Session` is the user's shell, but `Call::Side` (`acs list <host>`, remote install, the session menu) and `Call::Batch` (`acs list` over every alias, §7.3) build their argv from the same `user_opts`. A `LocalForward` given via `-o` is therefore handed to every one of those ssh processes as well, so several concurrent ssh children try to bind the same local port. ssh's default `ExitOnForwardFailure=no` means each one warns and carries on, so it is noisy and wrong rather than fatal. A real `-L` can be emitted for `Call::Session` only.

**2. No validation.** A malformed `-o LocalForward=` spec is discovered by ssh, per dial, mid-reconnect-loop, as a line of ssh stderr on a terminal acs is otherwise keeping clean.

**3. Ergonomics and muscle memory.** acs replaces `ssh`+`dtach`; `-L` is the spelling people already know, and `-o LocalForward="8080 localhost:80"` requires knowing that the config-file form uses a space where `-L` uses a colon.

## Verified about the code (v0.11.4)

- **The argv is built in exactly one place**, `Transport::argv()` at src/ssh.rs:96-123, layout `<ssh> <fixed opts for the Call> <user_opts…> [-i <key>] -- <destination> <remote command>`. Every call site funnels through it (src/client.rs:357, src/install.rs:210, src/list.rs:61,142, src/pick.rs:54,463).
- **Order is load-bearing.** ssh keeps the *first* value it sees, which is why acs puts its own transport options before the user's (docs/DESIGN.md:876-883). A forward must be emitted with or after `user_opts`, not before.
- **Reconnect needs no work.** `reconnect::run()` (src/reconnect.rs:60-169) clones `ClientArgs` once at :75 and re-dials through the same builder each pass (:76-88 → client.rs:357), so the argv is rebuilt from scratch every dial. A forward stored on `Transport` is re-applied on every reconnect for free.
- **But the forward does drop during a redial.** The old ssh child is dead, so the listening socket is released and rebound. Worth one line in the docs, and it is the argument for `-o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes` being considered — a rebind that loses a race (a stale TIME_WAIT, a second acs on the same port) otherwise leaves a live session with a silently dead forward.
- **No duplicate bead.** Every "forward" hit in src/ is keystroke forwarding (src/keys.rs:62, src/proxy.rs:287); `acs-aps` is ssh *agent* forwarding, a different thing. A grep for LocalForward/tunnel/socks over src/, docs/, README.md and tests/ finds nothing, and all 107 records in .beads/issues.jsonl were checked.

## Implementation sketch

1. src/cli.rs:162 — accept `Short('L')`, repeatable, and validate the `[bind:]port:host:hostport` spec with a real error. USAGE at src/cli.rs:20-51 needs the entry too.
2. src/ssh.rs:51-66 — a new `Transport` field (`local_forwards: Vec<String>`) rather than stuffing `user_opts`, precisely so it can be gated.
3. src/ssh.rs:96-123 — emit `-L <spec>` after `user_opts`, **only when `call == Call::Session`**.
4. Optional, and the reason to look at acs-c9d: a `local_forwards` list setting, global and per alias, mirroring `local_networks` exactly (Config field config.rs:129, `Option` field on Alias config.rs:99, `KEYS` :166, `ALIAS_KEYS` :199, a type const beside `NETWORKS` :211, a `*_for(alias)` accessor like :509, and a branch in config_cmd::typed at config_cmd.rs:93). Per-alias is the natural home for "this host always needs its database forwarded". `acs-mbd` (identity file per alias) is the precedent for a per-alias ssh-affecting setting.
5. Docs: docs/DESIGN.md §3 (:133-152) and §7.1 (:840-883), README.md:173-182.

## Scope decisions to make when taking this

- **`-R` and `-D` as well, or `-L` only?** The user asked for `-L`. `-R` and `-D` are the same plumbing and the same gating; doing all three at once costs little more than one. Decide explicitly rather than by omission.
- **Runtime add/remove is out of scope.** Command mode (docs/DESIGN.md:694-745, dispatch at src/keys.rs:487) could plausibly grow a key, but there is no channel to reconfigure a *running* ssh: acs disables ssh's `~C` escape with `-e none` (src/ssh.rs:10) and disables the control socket (`ControlMaster=no`, `ControlPath=none`). Changing a forward would mean tearing the link down and redialling. Command mode also has no prompt or line editor, so there is nowhere to type `8080:localhost:80`. Note it as a non-goal.
- **Does `-L` suppress the `-o LocalForward` path?** No reason to; `-o` stays the unvalidated escape hatch. But the Session-only gating means the two behave differently, which the docs should say out loud.

Done when `acs -L 8080:localhost:80 box` forwards the port, the flag is repeatable, a bad spec is a clear acs error before any ssh is spawned, the forward is passed to the session ssh but **not** to the `Call::Side` and `Call::Batch` calls, it survives a reconnect, unit tests cover the argv for all three `Call` kinds plus spec parsing good and bad, and DESIGN §7.1 and the README document it along with the brief drop across a redial.
close_reason: Implemented in PR #155 (27cbc1e): repeatable -L, validated before any dial, emitted only for Call::Session, survives a redial

title: Resolve user@host through the host's configured entries, as that user
description:
Resolve `user@alias` through the alias too, using `user` as the login name.

User's ask: "if a user supplies 'me@devbox' as a destination, also check if 'devbox' is an alias, if so follow the normal flow and set 'user' to 'me'".

Today (src/alias.rs `resolve`): any destination containing `@` skips alias resolution on purpose, and DESIGN §7.3 and README ("`me@devbox`, or any name that is not an alias, is used as given") document `user@<alias>` as the way to reach a host whose name is also an alias. This change reverses that.

Proposed behaviour:

- Split the destination at the last `@`: if the host part is an alias, resolve it normally (entries in order, ping check, fallback) and connect as `<user>@<entry host>`. The given user overrides every entry's `user`.
- A redial resolves it again with the same user override.
- Names that are not aliases behave as before.
- The escape hatch goes away, so there needs to be another way to reach a host whose name equals an alias: for example its FQDN, or a documented form. Pick one and document it.
- `-v` shows that the login name came from the command line.

Done when tests cover `me@alias` (user override on the first and the fallback entry), `me@not-an-alias` unchanged, and the redial; DESIGN §7.3 and README are updated.
close_reason: Implemented with tests: user@alias resolves through the alias as that user, redial keeps it (PR #25)

title: Install acs and start the session on one ssh connection
description:
A new release ships after every merge, so every host pays first contact once per release: the dial that gets ACS-NEED, two install calls, then a redial — four handshakes without the user's multiplexing. After ACS-NEED, the prelude could read the payload from stdin on the same connection, finish the install and exec the proxy, so the whole thing is one handshake.
Touches ssh.rs prelude, install.rs, client.rs connect_and_serve, DESIGN §8/§8.1. The SHA-256 check before chmod +x must stay. The upload itself still dominates on slow links.
close_reason: Shipped in #375 (2114a1f): first contact installs and starts the session on one ssh connection

title: Find the early-redial window: the client redials with a 120s backoff configured
description:
Seen during the acs-trw pass (PR #176, 2579994), on a cold full-parallel
`cargo test --workspace` — compiling plus 24 test binaries at once. Three tests
failed together:

- `detach_works_while_the_link_is_down`
- `exit_needs_the_link`
- `a_session_ending_during_an_outage_leaves_no_status_behind`

In each, the client had entered a **redial** although `ACS_BACKOFF_MS` was
**120000**, so the command keys typed while offline were dropped as "typed
during a redial". Every later run was green — on the changed and on the
unchanged code alike — so this is not acs-trw's change.

**Why this is filed as a bug rather than as flakiness.** Those three tests all
sit behind acs-7wu (#174, 24b281a), which widened exactly this backoff to 120 s
precisely so that a loaded machine could not reach the end of the wait. If a
redial happens anyway, the wait is being cut short by something other than
elapsed time, and load alone does not explain it. The candidates, in rough
order of suspicion:

- **netwatch.** `offline()` watches for a network change and redials at once
  when it sees one; a spurious or self-inflicted wake (an interface flapping,
  or the test harness's own socket activity at 24-binary parallelism) would
  produce exactly this.
- **The backoff wait waking early** — a condvar or poll with a deadline that
  returns spuriously and is treated as expiry rather than re-waited.
- A takeover or session-end path re-entering `offline()` and restarting the
  attempt counter.

If it is netwatch, it is also a **user-visible** bug and not merely a test
problem: a laptop whose interfaces flap would redial repeatedly during an
outage, dropping every key typed offline — which is the thing DESIGN §5.2
promises not to do.

Interacts with acs-iyq (redial at once on the first attempt after a drop): that
bead deliberately shortens the first wait, so whoever takes it must not absorb
this window into the intended behaviour and hide it.

Done when the cause is identified and named, the wait cannot end before its
deadline except for a genuine network change, a regression test covers the
specific wake path found (driving it rather than waiting for load to produce
it), and the three tests above pass repeatedly under cold full-parallel
`cargo test --workspace`, which is how it was seen.
notes:
Diagnosis from the acs-iyq pass (PR #178, f565134), by reading the code rather
than reproducing. It eliminates two of the three candidates in the description:

- **Candidate 2 (wait waking early) is NOT present.** offline() re-checks
  `now >= deadline` at the top of its loop, so a spurious poll return is
  re-waited, never treated as expiry.
- **Candidate 3 (a restarted counter) is NOT present.** `backoff` is created
  once outside run()'s loop and is only reset()/spent(); no takeover or
  session-end path re-enters offline() with a fresh counter.
- **That leaves candidate 1, netwatch** — and `Offline::NetworkChanged` is the
  only path that can end the wait before its deadline.

Why it would present exactly as reported: the suite does not isolate the client
from the developer's real network. `NetWatch::new()` opens a PF_ROUTE socket on
macOS unless ACS_NETWATCH_FIFO is set, and only `a_network_change_redials_at_once`
sets it. `route_messages_matter` accepts RTM_NEWADDR/DELADDR/IFINFO, which a
laptop emits on Wi-Fi roams, VPN/utun churn and container interfaces. The FIRST
such event in a wait is always taken (`last_early` starts None), so the client
redials at once and keys typed at it are dropped as "typed during a redial" —
sporadically, on changed and unchanged code alike.

Ready-made isolation knob: ACS_NETWATCH_FIFO pointing at a path that does not
exist makes NetWatch::new() return None (the `.ok()?` on the open); a FIFO
nobody writes gives the same isolation while keeping the code path live.

IMPORTANT: that isolation was written into the harness during the acs-iyq pass
and then deliberately REVERTED, because applying it wholesale would hide the
symptom this bead has to reproduce. Isolate the tests that are not about
netwatch, but keep a reproduction of the real wake.

acs-iyq did not touch this window: `spent()` keeps a network change costing
exactly one dial, as before. Its three affected tests now use
`refuse_one_dial()` to enter the wait deterministically, but once in the wait
they are exposed to a netwatch wake exactly as they were.
close_reason: Fixed in PR #180 (f196120): NetWatch::changed() answered 'did the kernel say something' rather than 'did the network change'. A hint now counts only when netmatch::local_networks() differs from the previous hint. Reproduced deterministically and shown red before the fix

title: The prelude's candidate check kills the system-wide install path and mistakes a directory for a binary
description:
Three defects in the prelude's candidate handling, found during acs-gov
(PR #188, 595cdc7) while working on the same function. Grouped because one
pass over `acs_safe` and its caller fixes all three.

**1. The system-wide install path is unusable by anyone but its owner (the
serious one).** `acs_safe` requires `uid == $(id -u)`. DESIGN §8 describes
`/usr/local/lib/acs/<version>/acs` as "an optional system-wide location an
administrator can populate once for all users" — but an administrator
populates it **as root**, so every non-root user's prelude refuses it and
falls through to a per-user install. The second candidate is therefore dead
weight today: it can only ever be used by whoever owns it, which defeats the
entire point of a shared location.

This is pre-existing, from acs-08m, and it is a documented feature that does
not work rather than a security hole. The fix needs a judgement: a root-owned
file that is not group- or other-writable is arguably **more** trustworthy
than one's own, not less — but "owned by root or by me" is a wider rule than
acs-08m wrote, and its reasoning deserves re-reading before it is widened.
Whatever is decided, DESIGN §8 and the check must agree; today they do not.

**2. `[ -x "$b" ]` is true for a directory.** If a candidate path were a
directory with mode 755, the prelude would `exec` it, `sh` would exit 126, and
**no ACS-NEED marker would be printed** — so the client sees a silent failure
instead of a request to install. A `[ -f "$b" ]` alongside closes it. Cheap,
and the failure mode is bad out of proportion to the cause.

**3. The prelude clobbers unprefixed shell variables** — `u`, `b`, and now
`p`, `n`, `t`, `w` after acs-gov. Harmless as plain shell variables, but if
any of those names is *exported* in the ssh environment, the exec'd acs and
the user's remote shell inherit the changed value. `u` and `b` are
pre-existing; acs-gov kept the new names consistent rather than half-prefixing
them, deliberately, leaving the whole set to be renamed together.

Done when the system-wide candidate is usable by a non-owner under a rule that
acs-08m's threat model supports and DESIGN §8 states, a directory on a
candidate path yields ACS-NEED rather than a silent exit 126, the prelude's
variables cannot collide with an exported environment, and each has a test —
including one that actually populates the system-wide path as root, which
scripts/test_linux.sh is the place to do.
close_reason: Fixed in PR #190 (ae86191): an acceptable owner is the invoking uid or root, for the file and every directory on the path; the mode test is unchanged, so a root-owned file in a user-writable directory is still refused. [ -f ] added so a directory yields ACS-NEED; prelude variables are acs_-prefixed. DESIGN §8 and the check now agree

title: Create temp files with O_EXCL and full randomness instead of the process id
description:
Security, symlink and predictable-name attacks. Several temp paths are predictable and opened in a way that follows symlinks: upgrade.rs uses .acs-upgrade.<getpid()> with File::create (O_TRUNC, follows links) and 32-bit randomness elsewhere, update_check.rs uses .update-check.<getpid()>, scripts/install.sh uses "$2.new.$$" with cp and ln -s, and xtask/src/bump.rs uses /tmp/acs-release-<pid>-<version>.

This matters because both the upgrade and the installer tell the user to re-run under sudo into /usr/local/bin and /usr/local/lib/acs, which on Intel Homebrew and hand-managed hosts are routinely group- or user-writable. Pre-creating the predictable name as a symlink turns the root-run create or cp into an arbitrary-file overwrite, then chmod 755.

Also worth narrowing while here: upgrade::link_candidates adds <dir>/acs for every directory on PATH and relink writes into any that currently points at the running exe.

Done when every temp file is created O_EXCL with full-width randomness (never the pid), the installer uses install -m 755 rather than cp plus chmod, and a test or at least a comment records why.
close_reason: Implemented in #123: random_token and create_new at every temp path

title: Small client duplicates: reattach hint, interrupt+reset sequence, dead clear_status, column width
description: Found in review. The reattach hint is formatted four times (client.rs:1653-1656 and reconnect.rs:231-234 verbatim, the takeover variant client.rs:1508-1511, 'connection lost' reconnect.rs:161-164). 'Interrupt the open sequence, then reset the modes' is built three times (client.rs:1022-1023 leave, :1391-1392 Fresh, write_over_stream :1042-1047). reconnect.rs:225-226 calls clear_status then client::leave, which begins with clear_status. `sys::get_winsize(0).map(|s| s.rows).unwrap_or(24).max(1)` at reconnect.rs:445 and :469. wait_for_answer (reconnect.rs:285-291) re-implements the alias/plain-host split that client::host_answers encapsulates. The string-terminator step is duplicated byte-for-byte at keys.rs:330-342 and modes.rs:260-264. list::host_lines (318-338) and render_all (351-368) build the same rows; and table_lines pads by chars().count() (list.rs:281) while menu::width counts terminal columns (menu.rs:555-602), so a CJK or emoji identity in WHO misaligns IDLE/AGE in the table and inside the menu rows. Done when each has one home (reattach_hint, ModeObserver::leave_sequence, menu::width used by table_lines).
close_reason: Done in #385: reattach_hint/note_detached, ModeObserver::leave_sequence, dead clear_status gone, status_row shared, table_lines pads by menu::width (wide-identity regression test), host_lines/render_all share host_table. Left as is: wait_for_answer's alias split (redial_alias also reports a host change) and the keys/modes string terminator (no longer identical).

title: Decode frames just read before judging liveness, so a stdout stall is not a dead link
description:
The client loop (src/client.rs:959-972) reads the link into dec and immediately calls liveness.tick(), but liveness.heard() is only updated in the decode loop at the top of the next iteration (client.rs:734), so heard reflects the previous iteration. Normally microseconds, but write_output -> sys::write_all(STDOUT) (client.rs:657-674) blocks for as long as the terminal is not reading (emulator stalled, flow control). After a stall over 10 s the next poll returns at once, the new frames are read, and tick sees now >= heard + dead_after, so lost(link): a needless ssh kill, redial, status line and Ctrl-L although PONGs were sitting in the pipe.

Done when the client decodes after the read before ticking (or treats a readable link as heard), with a test that delays stdout consumption past the liveness deadline and asserts no redial.
close_reason: Implemented in #87 (d99d1d4)

title: A relative ACS_SOCKET_DIR resolves against two different directories
description: Found in review. The proxy resolves ACS_SOCKET_DIR=foo against its cwd; the master does set_current_dir("/") (master.rs:199) before SocketDir::open_at(args.dir) with --dir passed verbatim (master.rs:73-78, session.rs:179-184), so it tries /foo. It fails loudly ('cannot start session') rather than silently. Done when default_path() or spawn() canonicalises the directory once, with a test using a relative value.
close_reason: Fixed in #289 (b0c26da): SocketDir::open_at absolutises the path lexically; master absolutises --dir before chdir; regression test in tests/proxy.rs

title: Finish the timing work in tests/reconnect.rs: two elapsed bounds and the stalled-terminal settle
description:
What acs-o8h (PR #164, f4f2522) deliberately left, having been scoped to the
three tests acs-o8h named. Both items were found by sweeping the whole file.

**1. Two more `elapsed() < 5 s` assertions, each with only 4x discrimination.**

- `detach_works_while_the_link_is_down` (~:217)
- `a_network_change_redials_at_once` (~:408), which also has
  `wait_connections(2, Duration::from_secs(5))`

Each is distinguishing "at once" from "after the 20 s backoff", so the
assertion is genuinely about elapsed time and should stay an elapsed
assertion — but 5 s against 20 s is a narrow margin on a loaded machine. The
cheap fix keeps the discrimination and widens the slack: raise `ACS_BACKOFF_MS`
to 120000 and the bound to `T`, giving 6x the room for the same statement.
acs-o8h used exactly this move in `the_escape_window_is_the_same_offline`.

**2. `a_stalled_terminal_is_not_a_dead_link`'s settle.**

`sleep(8 s)` with the terminal paused, then `sleep(500 ms)`, then
`assert_eq!(remote.transport_pids().len(), 1)` and `!contains("reconnecting")`.

Its failure direction is the safe one — the 8 s is a *stimulus* that must
exceed `ACS_DEAD_MS` (800 ms), which load only lengthens, and the 500 ms is a
settle before a **negative** assertion, so a stalled host makes it pass rather
than go red. So this is loss of sensitivity, not a random gate failure: a real
regression could slip through, which is why it is worth doing and why it is
not urgent.

acs-o8h looked for an event-based settle and did not find a clean one: the
client emits nothing at the 400 ms-800 ms scale while offline, and waiting for
post-pause output matches the flood of buffered bytes drained on unpause rather
than newly produced ones. Doing it properly means giving the stimulus command a
counter so the test can wait for a specific later value — which perturbs a
carefully tuned acs-7k7 reproduction, and is the reason it was left alone.

Done when the two elapsed bounds keep their discrimination with room to spare
under load, the stalled-terminal settle waits for something observable rather
than 500 ms, the acs-7k7 reproduction still reproduces (show it), and each
still goes red for the regression it covers.
close_reason: Fixed in PR #174 (24b281a): the two elapsed bounds keep their discrimination with a 120s backoff and a T bound, and the stalled-terminal settle waits for a RESUMED marker produced after the unpause. The acs-7k7 reproduction survives — 5/5 red with liveness.heard() removed. Note the two elapsed asserts are now documentation rather than gates; the surrounding waits are what fire

title: Offer n and x in the session menu only on a row they act on
description:
User's words: "when the session list is presented. When the selected line is not a session but the 'exit' option, do not allow the 'n' key, nor display the option in the status bar. Same is true for the 'x' key."

What the code does now (src/menu.rs). rows() builds [sessions..., New (single-host menu only), Exit]. With the cursor on Exit:

- n (menu.rs:328) matches (false, _) in a single-host menu and returns Choice::New { host: 0 }, so it really does make a new session from the exit row. In the every-host menu the (true, _) arm only sets a note.
- x (menu.rs:313) is already a no-op off a session row (`if let Row::Session(..)`), but silently: nothing tells the user why.
- The key bar (menu.rs:447-450) is one fixed string, "1-9, or up/down jk and Enter: attach   .: <all|detached only>   x: end   n: new<there>   Esc: leave", drawn the same whatever the cursor is on.

Done when the bar lists only the keys that act on the row under the cursor (no "x: end" or "n: new" on Exit), n on the exit row does nothing instead of creating a session, and tests/menu.rs covers both: the bar's text on the exit row, and n on the exit row leaving the menu unchanged.

Open question for whoever takes it: the New row has the same shape (x does nothing there, and "Enter: attach" is wrong on both New and Exit). Worth deciding whether the rule is "hide keys that do not apply to this row" in general, or just the exit row the user named.

Follows acs-s0g, which built the menu.
close_reason: Implemented in #104: the key bar is built per row and n/x act only where they apply

title: List sessions on every host in the configuration
description:
Show the sessions on all configured hosts in one command.

User's ask: "add a way to display all the sessions on all hosts that are in the configuration".

Today `acs <host> --list` (src/list.rs) lists one host. The configuration's `hosts:` aliases (DESIGN §7.2, §7.3; src/config.rs, src/alias.rs) name every host acs knows.

Proposed shape (settle during implementation):

- `acs --list` with no host (or `acs list`, which would become a reserved first argument like `config` and `upgrade`) lists every alias.
- Each alias is resolved the way a connection would be (ping check, fallback hosts), then asked via the same `_proxy --list` side call. Hosts are queried in parallel with a timeout, so one slow or down host does not hold up the rest.
- Output: the existing table with a HOST (alias) column, or one block per alias. An unreachable host, or one without acs of our version, gets one line saying so rather than failing the whole command.
- Exit status: 0 if every host answered, non-zero (for example 255) if any did not.

Done when tests cover several aliases, including an unreachable one and one without acs installed, using the fake transport and ping; README and DESIGN document the command.
close_reason: Implemented with tests: acs --list without a host lists every alias (PR #21, feat: list sessions on every configured host)

title: Guard the children spawned in tty_restore, multiuser and harness tests so a failure does not leak them
description: Found in review. tests/tty_restore.rs and tests/multiuser.rs spawn current_exe() children with no Drop guard, so a panic in wait_for_raw (tty_restore.rs:62-72) leaves a child in `loop { sleep(1) }` forever; tests/harness.rs:20 and :58 take the Child from run_remote and only kill() on the success path. Everything that goes through Client/Proxy/TempDir is cleaned up correctly. Done when these use a kill-on-drop guard (testutil has the pattern) and a deliberately failing run leaves no process behind.
close_reason: Completed in #283: testutil::KillOnDrop guards the children in tty_restore, multiuser and harness tests

title: Honour the command keys while a dial is in flight, not only during the offline wait
description:
The offline wait is where command keys are honoured. While a dial is actually
in flight the client is in cooked mode for ssh's prompts and flushes stdin
(acs-qty), so `Ctrl-] Ctrl-] d` during a dial does nothing — and a dial against
a dead network can take ten seconds.

acs-iyq (PR #178, f565134) made this sharper rather than causing it. Before,
a drop bought you ~1 s of offline wait in which `d` detached; now the first
redial goes at once, so the dead window starts the instant a drop is noticed.
That is the right trade for latency — a detach during a dial was never
reliable — but it turns "mostly works" into "never works" for the first
attempt, and DESIGN §5.2 now has to say so.

The user-visible shape: the link drops, you want out, you type the detach you
have typed a hundred times, and nothing happens until the dial fails.

What makes this awkward, and why it is a feature rather than a bug: raw mode is
suspended precisely so ssh can prompt for a passphrase or a host key, and
acs-qty deliberately discards typed-ahead input on resume so a password does
not end up echoed or delivered to the program. Honouring command keys mid-dial
means reading stdin while ssh may also want it. Options worth weighing:

- only honour them while ssh has not yet asked for anything (the common case:
  key auth, no prompt), falling back to today's behaviour once it prompts;
- keep the detector fed from a separate path that does not consume the bytes
  ssh needs;
- accept the drop of typed-ahead but scan it for the escape sequence first.

Whichever way, the acs-qty guarantee must not regress: a passphrase typed at
an ssh prompt must never reach the program or the screen.

Done when Ctrl-] Ctrl-] d detaches during an in-flight dial in the common
no-prompt case, acs-qty's regression test still passes unchanged, a test covers
a detach during a dial, and DESIGN §5.2 and §6.1 say when command keys are live.
close_reason: Landed in #343 (474dad4)

title: Cover -L in the ssh e2e suite, which the Alpine image currently forbids
description:
`-L` landed in acs-6f5 (PR #155, 27cbc1e) with unit tests for the argv of all
three `Call` kinds and for spec parsing, plus a **by-hand** demonstration
against the e2e container: a real forward bound, the container's ssh banner
read back through it, no forward on the `Call::Side` call, and the forward
rebound after the session's ssh was killed. That hand check is recorded as a
row in docs/VERIFICATION.md and is the only end-to-end evidence there is.

It is by hand because `scripts/e2e/Dockerfile` inherits Alpine's sshd default
`AllowTcpForwarding no`, so `scripts/e2e_ssh.sh` cannot exercise a forward at
all. The hand check needed the setting flipped inside the running container.

The gating logic is exactly the part worth having a permanent test for: the
`call == Call::Session` condition in `ssh::argv` is what stops `acs list` and
the remote-install side calls from each trying to bind the same local port.
A unit test asserts the argv; only an e2e test asserts that a real ssh does
what the argv implies.

Done when the e2e image enables `AllowTcpForwarding` (sshd_config in
scripts/e2e/Dockerfile), `scripts/e2e_ssh.sh` gains a case that forwards a port
through an acs session and reads real bytes back through it, asserts the same
port is *not* bound by an `acs list` side call, and docs/VERIFICATION.md's `-L`
row moves from a by-hand result to an automated one.
close_reason: Implemented in PR #162 (caa3854): e2e_14 forwards a port, reads the container's real ssh banner through it, asserts the acs list side call never binds it, and rebinds after a redial; proven red two ways

title: One non-blocking flush loop, one events==0 pollfd skip, one pump_output
description: Found in review. The non-blocking flush loop is byte-identical in proxy.rs:389-401 (flush), client.rs:1183-1195 (write_link) and master.rs:284-296 (Conn::flush, plus a dead flag). 'Leave the fd out of the poll when events is 0' is written twice with the same acs-wza/acs-gkl rationale (proxy.rs:304-306 wait_for, master.rs:341-343 pty_pollfd) and relay_fds (proxy.rs:332) still uses the raw sys::pollfd with a possibly-zero ev. master.rs pump_output (1118-1137) and pump_output_all (1269-1288) differ only by the `c.out.len() < OUT_HIGH_WATER` term. proxy.rs:128-132 re-spells the ENOENT|ECONNREFUSED match that refused() (529-534) in the same file already is; the ring room for the active client is computed at master.rs:478-481 and 1043-1053. Done when sys::flush_queued(fd, &mut Vec<u8>) and a sys::pollfd that skips events==0 exist and the duplicates are gone.
notes: After #373: sys::wait_for (events==0 skip, now also the relay's master socket), one Master::pump_output(high_water), one Master::ring_room, and connect_or_start uses refused(). The master and the proxy already shared OutQueue::flush (#341). Left: client.rs write_link is the last copy of the non-blocking flush loop. Move it onto OutQueue::flush (or an equivalent) once acs-6k2 lets go of client.rs, then close.
close_reason: Done in #385: client.rs write_link removed; serve's queue is an OutQueue and the dial flushes via OutQueue::flush, the loop master and proxy share.

title: acs upgrade and install.sh leave the version directory group-writable under umask 002
description: Found in review. acs-iws fixed this for the remote install only: install.rs make_dir does `umask 022; mkdir -p; chmod 755`. upgrade.rs:417 Staged::new does a bare create_dir_all for root/<version>/ and scripts/install.sh:217 does `mkdir -p "$lib/$version" "$bin"`; place() chmods the file but neither directory. Under umask 002 (Ubuntu's login default with user-private groups, the lab-image case DESIGN 8.1 names) the directory is 0775; the prelude's acs_safe runs acs_ok on dirname of the binary (ssh.rs:448), the ?????w* pattern refuses it, the client prints 'acs: refusing to run ...: is writable by others', falls through to ACS-NEED and re-uploads the same version, whose chmod 755 then heals it. So install.sh's stated purpose on a remote ('a client of the same version finds it there and has nothing to upload') silently fails, and an upgraded host used as a remote gets a one-shot refusal plus re-upload. Test gap: tests/install.rs an_install_under_a_group_writable_umask_still_runs covers only the remote path; tests/upgrade.rs and tests/scripts.rs never set a umask. Done when Staged::new creates the directory 0755 regardless of umask (DirBuilderExt::mode or sys::Umask), install.sh sets umask 022 before the mkdir and chmods $lib and $lib/$version as make_dir does, and both have a umask 002 regression test.
close_reason: Fixed in #228 (c8e806d): Staged::new and install.sh make the version directory 0755 under any umask; regression tests under umask 002

title: Check by hand that a redial through a password-auth ProxyJump host still prompts
description: acs-8ax (PR #343) starts ssh in its own process group in the terminal's background during a redial; when ssh reaches for the terminal to prompt, the kernel stops the group (SIGTTOU/SIGTTIN) and acs hands the terminal over. For ProxyJump/ProxyCommand that relies on the jump ssh (or the proxy command) being in the same process group and leaving SIGTTOU/SIGTTIN at their default handling. The pass wrote that assumption into DESIGN but did not test it against a real host: if wrong, such a redial waits out the 30 s dial timeout instead of prompting. Done when a redial through a ProxyJump host that asks for a password (and one with a passphrase-protected key, no agent) is tried by hand, the result is recorded in docs/VERIFICATION.md's by-hand checks, and any failure is filed as a bug.

title: Reject a non-https ACS_RELEASES_URL and ignore it under elevated privileges
description:
Security, update integrity. release.rs takes the release base from ACS_RELEASES_URL with no scheme validation, so http:// and file:// are accepted (scripts/test_install.sh uses file:// deliberately). It is read by `acs upgrade`, by the detached `acs _update-check`, and by scripts/install.sh. Because the sums come from that same base, integrity checking is bypassed entirely, and the download is then executed.

Attack: a local user who can influence the environment of a privileged run (sudo -E, a sudoers env_keep, a poisoned shell rc, a CI step) points it at their own server and gets code execution as the upgrading user. The docs themselves suggest `sudo acs upgrade`. It also downgrades a mirror to cleartext for a network attacker.

Done when a non-https base is refused unless an explicit opt-out flag is passed, the variable is ignored when the effective uid differs from the real uid, the test suite's file:// use goes through the opt-out, and a test covers each case.
close_reason: Implemented in #115: https required unless flagged, and ignored under a privilege mismatch

title: Two small traps in the test harness: a private master-log path and a cached transport script
description:
Two minor hygiene items in `tests/common/mod.rs`, found while fixing acs-fzx
(PR #166, 80553cb). Neither is broken today; both are the shape of thing that
is cheap now and annoying later.

**1. `master_log_file()` is private, so tests cannot assert the exact path.**
`harness::remote_env_helpers_compose_in_any_order` can only assert that
`ACS_MASTER_LOG` *ends with* `master.log`, because the path it should equal is
not reachable from a test. A weak assertion like that passes while a path bug
sits under it.

**2. `Remote::transport()` caches the script on first call and never rewrites
it.** Safe as things stand, because every knob the script reads lives in a
separate file that the script sources at run time — which is exactly why
nobody will notice when it stops being safe. The first setting that needs to
change the script *body* will silently no-op whenever the script was already
materialised, and the symptom will be a test that configures something and
sees no effect, with nothing anywhere saying why.

Done when the master-log path is assertable from a test and the exact path is
asserted, and `transport()` either rewrites when its inputs change or fails
loudly (a debug assert and a comment naming the constraint is enough) if it is
called after the script exists with different inputs.
notes:
A third trap for this bead, from acs-odd (PR #216, 6397057).

**Three copies of "split a recorded ssh call at `--`" now exist in the test
harness:** `common::Ssh::keys`, an inline split in `tests/mux.rs`, and the new
`opts_of` in `tests/config.rs`.

Getting this wrong is **silently misleading rather than loudly wrong**, which
is what makes it worth fixing rather than tolerating. Everything after `--` is
the remote prelude, and the prelude contains text that looks exactly like ssh
options: `ls -ldnL`, `[ -L … ]`, `-i`-shaped fragments. A test that forgets to
split, or splits at the wrong place, will happily find `-L` in a call that
carries no forward at all — and pass, asserting something untrue.

acs-odd hit this directly while asserting the `Call::Session` forwarding gate,
which is precisely a test about whether `-L` is present, so a false positive
there would have hidden the thing being tested.

It belongs in `tests/common/mod.rs` once, beside the other shared helpers
acs-2dc consolidated (`numbers`, `assert_consecutive`, `last_number` moved
there for the same reason — a duplicated helper that had gone wrong in one
copy).
close_reason: Done in PR #218 (2440cef): master_log_file is public and the exact path asserted, transport() rewrites via temp+rename rather than caching, and one common::SshCall replaces four copies of the split-at---- helper. The copies agreed, so nothing had been asserting something untrue

title: Reuse an acs-owned ssh master for first connections and side calls
description:
A full ssh handshake (TCP, kex, auth, channel open: ~6-8 RTTs, plus a hardware-key touch) is paid on every acs <host>, detach-then-reattach included. §3 sets ControlMaster=no because a dead multiplexer hangs a reconnect; that hazard is the redial's, not a fresh start's.
Proposal: acs uses its own ControlPath + ControlPersist (not the user's) for the first connection and side calls only; a redial never multiplexes and runs ssh -O exit on the stale master first; if no marker arrives through the master within ~2 s, fall back to a direct dial. Revisits DESIGN §3 and needs a decision entry in §12. Wait for the per-phase timings to show the handshake is worth it.
close_reason: Implemented in PR #184 (cc1ab77): acs keeps its own master under a per-uid 0700 /tmp/acs-mux-<uid>, joined by first connections and side calls, never by redials or batch. Measured 43-52ms to 12-19ms to ACS-READY on loopback. Multi-user isolation tested as root

title: local_networks tests the wrong address: replace it with a caller-side per-host setting
description:
User's words: "the current implementation does not do what it's intended for.. File a bead to both remove current implementation and implement the correct one". On why a host entry cannot carry the setting: "The idea is that by specifying the local_networks on a host, the host will get preferred if the calling host is in any of the local_networks".

`local_networks` (acs-c9d, shipped in v0.11.0) tests the wrong address. It is a **target-side** filter when it needed to be a **caller-side** gate, and the difference is not cosmetic: as built, a configured network ranks a host first *wherever you are*.

## The defect

`prefer_local_network` on its own is correct and should stay. Its list comes from `getifaddrs`, so it is **self-gating**: the networks in it change as the machine moves, and "the host's address is on a network I am directly attached to" is a true statement about locality however you test it.

`local_networks` appends static entries to that same list (src/alias.rs:50):

```rust
n.local.extend(config.local_networks_for(alias).value.iter().copied());
```

and the match tests the **host's** resolved addresses against it (src/alias.rs:207, `addrs` from `resolve(&host, …)`):

```rust
on_net[i] = netmatch::matching(&network.local, &addrs);
```

So appending a static network destroys exactly the gating that made the interface-derived list meaningful. With `local_networks: [172.16.0.0/16]`, a host at 172.16.8.2 is ranked first from a coffee shop on 10.0.0.0/8 just as it is from the office, because the only address consulted is the host's. The caller's own address is never tested — the machine's interfaces merely *contribute entries to the list*.

The damage is bounded but real: the mis-ranked host still has to answer its ping, so you pay a `reachability_timeout` (500 ms default) and fall through to the right host. The ordering is simply wrong and the ping gate hides it.

## Why it got through review

acs-c9d's worked example — O at 172.16.1.65, T at 172.16.8.2, `local_networks: [172.16.0.0/16]` — gives the **same answer under both readings**: under the built rule T's address is in the /16, under the intended one O's address is. The one example in the bead, the README (README.md:345-353), DESIGN §7.3 and the tests could not tell the two apart. acs-c9d even flagged the ambiguity in as many words — "the user's phrasing, 'local for this host', reads as per alias (and maybe per host entry), while the example is about what O believes" — and then resolved it the other way.

## Remove

Not in production, so a clean break: no deprecated alias, no compatibility branch, no migration path. An existing config with a global or per-alias `local_networks:` should become a plain unknown-key error.

- src/config.rs: the `Config.local_networks` field (:129), `Alias.local_networks` (:99), `local_networks` from `KEYS` (:166) and `ALIAS_KEYS` (:199), the `NETWORKS` const (:211), `local_networks_for` (:510), the `networks_mut`/`networks_setting` arms (:420, :427) and the alias merge (:753).
- src/config.rs parsing: `networks_value` (:627), `parse_networks` (:649), `format_networks` (:659) — or keep them, since the new setting parses the same CIDR list; decide rather than delete blindly.
- src/config_cmd.rs: the `NETWORKS` branch in `typed` (:93), `networks_node` (:76), the `Seq` join in `value_text` (:108), and the alias-settings help text (:42, :47).
- src/alias.rs:50 — the `extend` that is the defect itself.
- Tests: the acs-c9d round-trip test `local_networks_read_as_a_list_globally_and_per_alias` (src/config.rs:1419), `a_configured_network_counts_as_local_in_either_family` (src/alias.rs:833), `networks_alone_do_nothing_without_prefer_local_network` (src/alias.rs:894), and the CLI test in tests/config_cmd.rs:162. Note that the single-scalar cases added in #137 go with them — that PR tested the parsing, which may survive, not the semantics, which do not.
- Docs: README.md:319-320 and :345-353, docs/DESIGN.md:906, :935, :1011-1032, :1180, :1184.

## Implement

`local_networks` becomes a **host-entry** setting (`HOST_KEYS`, src/config.rs:180, today `host, user, reachability_check, identity_file, persist, prefer`): a list of CIDR networks, IPv4 and IPv6, meaning *prefer this entry when the calling machine is on one of these*.

The test inverts. Instead of `matching(nets, host_addrs)`, it is the client's own `getifaddrs` addresses against the entry's list. `netmatch::LocalNet::contains` already masks both sides and handles both families (netmatch.rs:28-40), so the arithmetic is there; what changes is which value is passed as the address and which as the network. A caller-side hit needs no name resolution at all, which also makes it cheaper than the current path.

Ranking (`alias::rank`, src/alias.rs:215-224) keeps its shape — local first, then `prefer`, then configured order — with "local" now meaning *either* the interface-derived match *or* a caller-side `local_networks` hit.

## Scope decisions to make when taking this

- **Does the new setting require `prefer_local_network: true`?** Today `local_networks` is inert without it (`.then(network)` short-circuits, src/alias.rs:48). An explicit per-host statement arguably should stand on its own; the counter-argument is one switch governing all locality preference. Decide and document.
- **Is there still a global or per-alias form?** Probably not: "prefer *which* host when I am in network X" does not parse without naming the host, which is why per-entry is the right home. Say so explicitly rather than leaving the absence unexplained.
- **Several entries match.** Configured order, or the longest prefix? `rank` is a stable sort, so configured order is the no-work answer.
- **`-v` wording.** The existing line is "<alias>: <host> is on the local network <net>" (src/alias.rs:133), which describes the old direction. The caller-side one reads more like "this machine is on <net>, so <host> is preferred".

## Done when

A host entry accepts `local_networks`, that entry is ranked first exactly when one of **this machine's own** addresses falls in one of its networks, a global or per-alias `local_networks` is an unknown-key error, `prefer_local_network`'s interface-derived behaviour is unchanged, a bad CIDR is still a clear config error, and tests cover IPv4 and IPv6 plus the case the old design got wrong — **a host inside the configured network that is NOT preferred because the caller is somewhere else**, which is the regression test for this bead. README and DESIGN §7.3 describe the caller-side direction in a sentence that could not also describe the target-side one.

Supersedes acs-c9d; extends acs-sia.
close_reason: Fixed in #148: local_networks is now a caller-side per-host setting

title: Compare pre-release identifiers numerically in release::compare
description:
release::compare (src/release.rs:84-93) uses (Some(x), Some(y)) => x.cmp(y), so 0.3.0-rc10 < 0.3.0-rc2 ("rc10".cmp("rc2") is Less). Semver compares dot-separated numeric identifiers numerically. Impact is limited because find_asset refuses any archive whose version has a "-", so releases are never pre-releases; only decide()/should_link() for locally built -dev/-rc versions are affected. Related: archive_target("armv7-unknown-linux-musleabihf") (release.rs:27-32) yields the non-existent armv7-unknown-linux-musl; harmless while no armv7 archive is published.

Done when identifiers are split on "." and numeric ones compared as numbers, with a unit test for rc2 < rc10.
close_reason: Implemented in #89 (a3f0478)

title: Scrub the inherited ssh and agent environment from the session shell
description:
Security, credential reuse inside a shared account. master.rs start_child removes only ACS_SOCKET_DIR and ACS_MASTER_LOG, so the session shell inherits the creating ssh login's SSH_AUTH_SOCK, SSH_CONNECTION, SSH_CLIENT, KRB5CCNAME, DISPLAY, XDG_SESSION_ID and DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS, keeps them for the life of the session, and never refreshes them for later attachers.

So alice creates a session with agent forwarding, bob attaches on the same account, and bob's shell uses alice's forwarded agent for onward ssh as long as alice's connection lives. Everyone else's shell meanwhile reports alice's laptop in SSH_CONNECTION and DISPLAY. No privilege boundary is crossed, since the same uid could read /proc anyway, but acs hands it over invisibly and permanently.

Done when the forwarding and session variables are scrubbed from the child environment, or re-exported per attach from the attaching connection, whichever DESIGN §4.5 prefers, with the choice documented and a test.
close_reason: Implemented in #130: the session shell inherits no ssh or agent environment

title: A borrowed Decoder::next_data fast path for DATA to stdout
description: Found in review. proto.rs:529 and :535 to_vec() every DATA/INPUT payload on decode, unavoidable with the owned Msg API but one copy per frame on the client's hottest branch (DATA -> stdout). Done when a Decoder::next_data(&mut self) -> Option<(u64, &[u8])> serves that branch and the generic path keeps Msg.
close_reason: Done in #389: Decoder::next_data serves the client's DATA -> stdout branch with a borrowed payload; generic Msg path kept

title: Split EOF on the link by ssh's exit status, the last place a sibling is dropped for nothing
description:
acs-n1m (PR #197, bec3939) made the shared master survive a `LinkEnd::Channel`
loss — a decode error, where bytes demonstrably arrived a moment earlier. Every
other reason still ends the master, deliberately: silence is ambiguous, and a
wedged master stranding a user is worse than a dropped sibling.

`LinkEnd::Transport` — EOF on the link — is where most remaining collateral
comes from, and it is the one blunt case that could be sharpened with evidence
rather than guesswork. `Link` holds the `Child`, and OpenSSH has an exit-status
contract: **255 means ssh's own failure** (the connection), anything else is
the remote command's status (our channel). A bounded reap on EOF would let acs
tell those apart and keep the master in the second case.

Two reasons this is P4 rather than urgent, both from that pass:

- **It would almost never fire.** A clean channel end arrives as a
  `Msg::Exit`/`Msg::Error` frame — an `Outcome::Exit`, which never reaches the
  `-O exit` at all — long before EOF. The EOF path is mostly reached when
  something really did die.
- **It needs a decision this bead has to make**: what an *unreaped* child means.
  A bounded `try_wait` loop can time out, and "ssh has not exited yet" is a
  third answer the current two-way rule has no room for. Defaulting it to
  "end the master" keeps acs-n1m's bias; say so explicitly rather than letting
  the timeout decide by accident.

Do not let the reap block the redial. The whole point of acs-iyq (#178) is that
the first attempt after a drop goes at once; a reap that waits on a wedged ssh
would give that back.

Done when EOF with a non-255 ssh exit keeps the master, EOF with 255 or an
unreaped child ends it, the reap cannot delay the redial measurably, a test
covers all three, and acs-n1m's `a_channel_that_breaks_leaves_the_master_and_the_sibling_alone`
plus acs-9n3's `a_master_that_does_not_answer_is_ended_and_the_dial_made_again`
both still pass.
close_reason: Landed in #377 (a239464): EOF on a muxed link reaps ssh for up to 100 ms; a non-255 exit keeps the master, 255 or an unreaped/signalled ssh ends it

title: scripts/test_linux.sh fails tests/scripts.rs: the container has no git, and cargo then skips every later test file

title: Test-harness consolidation: spawn helpers, deadline polls, fixtures and parsers
description: Found in review. Four 'spawn a master/proxy, HELLO, expect WELCOME' helpers: tests/master.rs:22-42 (start_env), tests/proxy.rs:27-60 (proxy/session/hello_cmd/welcome), tests/multiuser.rs:78-103 (start_session), tests/harness.rs:20-39 (inline); two 'wait for EXIT'. T and exe() are re-declared in master.rs:9-15, proxy.rs:11-13, multiuser.rs:15-17 with the comment 'As common::T, which this file cannot reach' (it can; the natural home is acs::testutil beside TempDir/FrameConn). About 20 hand-rolled `deadline; loop { assert; sleep }` polls (client.rs:92,180, harness.rs:88, menu.rs:286, master.rs:77,95,196,460,490, persist.rs:29, update_check.rs:69, mux.rs:198, reconnect.rs:68,448,532, tty_restore.rs:64,111, e2e_ssh.rs:105, netns.rs:85) where Client::wait_until exists but is method-bound. Verbatim fixtures: FAST in reconnect.rs:13, redraw_on_reconnect.rs:17, host_aliases.rs:246,403, timing.rs:42, reconnect.rs:1196, master.rs:468; TICKER in reconnect.rs:24, timing.rs:13, e2e_ssh.rs:74 (master.rs:258 a third shape, acs-mkb); REPORTER in redraw_on_reconnect.rs:13 and e2e_ssh.rs:419 with received() reimplemented at e2e_ssh.rs:425/440; CMD/args() in config.rs:8-14 and install.rs:10-16; config.rs:16 env_refs == common::refs; menu.rs:16 echo() == e2e_ssh.rs:449; two row() parsers in list.rs:43 and :167; e2e_ssh.rs:465 vs menu.rs:49 last_screen; tests/client.rs:321 notes_at_a_boundary walks the same ModeObserver boundary logic as common::program_output (mod.rs:1089-1120); YAML alias fixtures built by string concatenation in a dozen places. Done when testutil carries T/exe/wait_until/MasterConn and the fixtures, and the copies are gone.
notes: 2026-10-27, PR #369 (2236f4a): acs::testutil now carries T, poll/wait_until, wait_idle, hello_running, start_master and FrameConn::ready_over/greet/expect_welcome/expect_exit; tests/common has the fixtures FAST, TICKER, REPORTER/received, UP_CMD/up_args, echo, last_screen, menu_row. The copies are gone from every test file except the ones listed next. Left: (1) tests/reconnect.rs: its own FAST, TICKER and hand-rolled deadline polls, out of scope while acs-io8c held it; (2) tests/host_aliases.rs: its two FAST copies and polls, held by acs-nhrq; (3) master.rs's echo-based TICKER (acs-mkb) and e2e_ssh.rs's 20 ms TICKER, which differ in shape or pace from common::TICKER; (4) client.rs notes_at_a_boundary vs common::program_output, which do not agree on what counts as a note; (5) YAML alias fixtures still built by string concatenation. exe() stays in tests/common: CARGO_BIN_EXE_acs exists only for integration tests, so the lib cannot hold it.
close_reason: Done in #369 and #371. acs::testutil now holds T, poll/wait_until, wait_idle, hello_running, start_master and the FrameConn ready/greet/welcome/exit helpers, and tests/common holds the shared fixtures. Every copy is gone, reconnect.rs and host_aliases.rs included. Four differences are deliberate: (1) master.rs's echo-based TICKER (acs-mkb) and e2e_ssh.rs's 20 ms TICKER differ in shape or pace, so changing them would change how those tests run; (2) client.rs's notes_at_a_boundary counts every 'acs: ' as a note and asserts it is at a boundary, while program_output skips only notes at a boundary, so merging them would weaken one; (3) the YAML alias fixtures stay literal, because their exact bytes (indentation, tabs, comments, a BOM) are what the tests check; (4) exe() stays in tests/common, because CARGO_BIN_EXE_acs exists only for integration tests.

title: a_network_change_ends_a_frozen_link_without_the_dead_timeout fails on cold full-parallel Linux, cause unknown
description:
Seen **twice**, both times on a **cold full-parallel Linux** run, both with the
same message:

    1 connections, waiting for 1 more than the 1 there were

- First during acs-ryz (PRs #194/#195), which then could not reproduce it in 40
  isolated plus 24 full-binary runs and said so honestly rather than claiming a
  fix.
- Again during acs-0n8 (PR #199, 491c637), on the first `scripts/test_linux.sh`
  run. Follow-ups were 3/3 green alone in the container, 5/5 green for the whole
  parallel `reconnect` suite there, and a clean full `test_linux.sh`.

**The leading theory is now eliminated.** acs-ryz suspected a swallowed network
hint; acs-0n8 fixed exactly that and the failure still happened. The path this
test exercises is a *welcomed* link, where acs-0n8 is semantically identical
(netcheck, then `acted()`), so that change can only have made this shape less
likely, never more.

What the test does: `SIGSTOP`s the transport so nothing flows and nothing
closes, with `ACS_DEAD_MS=60000` so only the netcheck can end the link, then
expects one more connection. The failure is that the second connection never
arrives inside `T`.

Remaining candidates, from the acs-0n8 pass:

- **The netcheck PING's write to a SIGSTOPped transport.** A stopped process
  does not drain its pipe; if the write blocks or is swallowed, the deadline
  that should follow it may never be armed. This is the most specific theory
  and the one to test first.
- **Plain starvation in the Docker VM** on a cold run, where the compile and
  30-odd test binaries land at once. If so it belongs with acs-2dc rather than
  here.

Note the environment matters: both sightings were Linux-in-a-VM, cold, fully
parallel. It has not been seen on macOS. Reproduce it there — `test_linux.sh`
after a `docker volume rm` of the target volume is the closest thing to the
conditions — before theorising further.

Done when the cause is named rather than suspected, the test either cannot lose
that race or the product bug behind it is fixed with its own regression test,
and a cold full-parallel `scripts/test_linux.sh` passes repeatedly — say how
many times.
close_reason: Fixed in PR #208 (28ee038): a real product bug. Liveness::tick_at cleared the netcheck probe on any byte arriving after the PING, but frames already in flight were written before the network moved. Only the PONG for that PING answers now. Reproduced deterministically 9/9 red, 0/8 after — not environmental, so not acs-hsw

title: Merge list::query and pick::Pick::list into one listing reader
description: Found in review. list.rs:155-232 query and pick.rs:183-223 Pick::list are the same reader: decode STATUS_REPLY via push_session, deadline, read-on-readable. They differ only in that one stops at EOF and ignores ERROR (the 'no sessions on host' bug) and the other stops at LIST_END and records ERROR. Done when one read_listing(dec, fd, deadline, until: End) -> Result<Listing, Failure> serves both and the ERROR behaviour is the same on both paths.
close_reason: Completed in #332: list::query and Pick::list share list::read_listing

title: Let prefer_local_network take explicit networks counted as local
description:
User's words: "as an extension to 'prefer_local_network' add the ability to specify one or more networks, ipv4 or ipv6 that are considered local for this host. As an example, the target T is at 172.16.8.2 and the origin O is on 172.16.1.65, it would not select T. However after specifying that 172.16.0.0/16 is local to T, O would match and use this host."

Today (acs-sia, DESIGN §7.3) the only networks that count are the ones this machine's own interfaces are on: netmatch::local_networks() reads getifaddrs and builds a LocalNet { addr, prefix } per address, alias::resolve filters to `!n.local.is_empty()`, and netmatch::matching() ranks a host first when one of its resolved A/AAAA addresses falls in one of those. So O on 172.16.1.65/24 never matches T at 172.16.8.2: the interface prefix is too narrow, although both are on the same site.

Wanted: a configured list of CIDR networks, IPv4 and IPv6, added to the machine's own for that match. With 172.16.0.0/16 configured, O ranks T as local and uses it.

Notes for whoever takes it:

- netmatch::LocalNet and contains() already do the arithmetic for both families, and usable() rejects a zero prefix, so the matching side needs little more than parsing "addr/prefix" into a LocalNet.
- The config side is the new part: every setting today is a scalar (bool or duration; see config.rs ALIAS_BOOLS and the tables config_cmd.rs uses for `acs config set`), so this is the first list-valued one. It needs a type in Setting, a parser with a real error for a bad CIDR, printing in `acs config show`, and a decision on `acs config set` syntax for a list.
- Decide the scope and say so in the doc: the user's phrasing, "local for this host", reads as per alias (and maybe per host entry), while the example is about what O believes. Global plus per-alias matches how prefer_local_network already resolves (config.rs:464), and per-entry is the third option.

Done when the networks can be configured, they are merged with the interface-derived ones for the ranking, a bad CIDR is a clear config error, netmatch and alias tests cover an IPv4 and an IPv6 case that only match through a configured network, and README plus DESIGN §7.3 document it.

Extends acs-sia.
close_reason: Implemented in #106 (v0.11.0): the local_networks setting, global and per alias

title: acs config host set refuses an empty value while acs config set accepts one
description:
`config_cmd::parse` guards the per-alias setter with `!value.is_empty()`, so

    acs config host set <alias> <key> ''

is rejected outright, while the global form

    acs config set <key> ''

is not. Found during acs-odd (PR #216, 6397057).

Two problems, the second worse than the first:

1. **No alias setting can ever be given an empty value**, whatever that setting
   means. Nothing about the per-alias path makes an empty value less meaningful
   than a global one — an empty value is how every other setting is told "take
   the default", and an alias is exactly where someone would want to undo an
   inherited one.
2. **The refusal is a generic "bad arguments"**, so it reads as a usage mistake
   rather than a deliberate rule. Someone will retype it, try quoting it
   differently, and conclude the CLI is broken.

It did not bite acs-odd, because `local_forwards` spells the empty case as the
literal `none` rather than as an empty string — so there is currently no
setting whose absence you can only express this way. That is luck, not design.

To settle when taking it: whether the guard should go entirely, or stay with a
message that says what it means. If some alias settings genuinely cannot be
empty, the check belongs with those settings rather than across the whole
command — the same way `local_forwards` validates its own value.

Done when an empty value is accepted per alias wherever it is accepted
globally, or is refused with a message naming the setting and the reason, and a
test covers whichever way it goes.
close_reason: Fixed in #285 (1bcf9d7): host set no longer refuses '' outright; each setting judges an empty value the same way globally and per alias (local_forwards: none; bools/durations/identity_file refused by name).

title: Remove the last upper-bound wall-clock asserts and the 50 ms double-tap gap outside reconnect.rs
description: Found in review. The client-side tests in tests/reconnect.rs were rewritten as lower bounds or events (acs-7wu, acs-o8h, acs-kip); four were not: tests/master.rs:418 kill_ends_a_normal_session_quickly asserts elapsed < 2 s; tests/list.rs:82 a_host_silent_after_its_marker_is_given_up_on asserts < 5 s around a 500 ms dial timeout plus a process start; tests/master.rs:712 and tests/proxy.rs:90 assert < 300 ms CPU over 1 s (CPU time, less exposed). tests/client.rs:245-249 double_tap sleeps 50 ms between the two presses inside the 400 ms window, used by three tests (l.257, 278, 298); tests/reconnect.rs:1256-1260 called the same gap 'the tightest wall-clock gap in this file' and removed it (one write plus ACS_ESCAPE_TIMEOUT_MS). Done when these are events or lower bounds, and double_tap is one write.
close_reason: Landed in #306 (abd65ca): upper wall-clock bounds in master/list/proxy/client tests are events or lower bounds; double_tap is one write

title: Quote the version in ssh::prelude and remote_candidates
description:
Security, latent command injection. ssh.rs remote_candidates interpolates the version into "$HOME/.local/share/acs/{version}/acs" with no quoting, and prelude puts that inside double quotes, where $, backtick and backslash are still live. Its sibling args all go through sh_quote, and install.rs does sh_quote the version, so this is an inconsistency rather than a deliberate exception. Verified by reading both.

Not exploitable today: every caller passes the compile-time crate::VERSION. But both functions are pub, take &str, and document no constraint, so one future caller passing a configured or remote-supplied version makes it remote code execution through both shell layers.

Done when the version is quoted the same way the other arguments are (or the function takes a validated type), with a test using a hostile version string.
close_reason: Implemented in #125: the version is quoted, and the prelude no longer re-wraps it

title: scripts/test_linux.sh is red on main for three unrelated reasons
description:
`scripts/test_linux.sh` — the suite run on Linux in a container, one of the
five checks CLAUDE.md lists — currently fails on `main`. Found during the
acs-6p8 pass (PR #180, f196120), which verified all three against a pristine
`origin/main` exported with `git archive` into a temp dir and run in the same
container: **all three reproduce without that change**.

Three independent causes:

1. **`signature::tests::*` (6 tests) — `ssh-keygen: No such file or directory`.**
   The `rust:alpine` container installs only `musl-dev`, and the signature
   tests shell out to `ssh-keygen -Y`. Either `apk add openssh-keygen` in the
   script, or skip those tests when `ssh-keygen` is absent — but skipping
   silently would hide a real failure, so prefer installing it.
2. **`a_stalled_terminal_is_not_a_dead_link` hard-codes
   `transport_pids().len() == 1`.** In the container the remote has to install
   acs first, which spends two extra transport calls, so it is 3. The count
   should be taken from a baseline captured at the start of the test, not
   from the literal 1. The acs-6p8 pass hit exactly this trap in its own new
   test and fixed it that way, so the pattern to copy is in that commit.
3. **`frozen_link_is_declared_dead_and_replaced` — "declared dead too early".**
   A wall-clock floor (`>= 500 ms`) the container misses. This is the class
   acs-o6x (#158), acs-o8h (#164) and acs-7wu (#174) have been retiring from
   `tests/reconnect.rs`; it wants the same treatment.

Why P2 rather than P3: a gate that is red for reasons nobody is tracking stops
being read, and this one is the only thing in the repo that runs the suite on
Linux and as root for the multi-user isolation check. Everything else runs on
macOS. The longer it stays red, the more likely a genuine Linux-only or
permissions regression lands unnoticed behind the three known failures.

Done when `scripts/test_linux.sh` passes on `main`, each of the three causes is
fixed rather than skipped or suppressed (or, where skipping is right, the skip
is loud and conditional on the missing binary), and the two reconnect tests
still go red for the regressions they cover — show it.
notes:
Likely root cause of most of the container failures, found during acs-9n3
(PR #184, cc1ab77), which ran the whole Linux suite with --no-fail-fast on its
branch AND on a pristine origin/main export in the same container. The same
set fails on both; main actually failed slightly more. Beyond the three causes
in the description, the failing set includes `proxy`, `host_aliases`, `list`,
`menu`, `timing`, `update_check` and `upgrade`.

**`Remote::installed()` symlinks the host binary into the fake remote's HOME,
and in `rust:alpine` the prelude's `acs_safe` check rejects it** — so every
harness test in the container pays an extra first-contact install dial it does
not pay on macOS. That single difference plausibly explains `list`, `menu`,
`host_aliases` and `proxy` together, and it is the same trap that made
`a_stalled_terminal_is_not_a_dead_link` wrong (cause 2 here): assertions that
hard-code an absolute dial or transport count are wrong on any remote that
must install acs first.

Two consequences for whoever takes this:

- Fix `installed()` for the container and a batch of these may go green at
  once. Try that before fixing them one by one.
- Where a count is genuinely being asserted, count from a baseline captured at
  the start of the test rather than from a literal. acs-9n3 did this in
  tests/mux.rs — it made its assertions property-based for exactly this reason
  and they pass 6/6 in the container.
close_reason: Fixed in PR #186 (a5d3274): 36 failures to 0. Root cause was Remote::installed() symlinking the binary, which the prelude's acs_safe refuses on Linux; the rest was a missing ssh-keygen in the image. src/ untouched

title: Null-check pw_dir in sys::user_by_name before CStr::from_ptr
description: Found in review. sys.rs:52-93: user_name checks pw_name.is_null(); user_by_name checks only result.is_null() and then does CStr::from_ptr(pw.pw_dir). A passwd entry with an empty or missing home from an NSS backend can yield a null pw_dir, and CStr::from_ptr(null) is undefined behaviour. The SAFETY comment ('pw_dir points into buf and is NUL-terminated') assumes what it should check. Done when a null pw_dir returns None, ideally by sharing the getpw*_r boilerplate between the two functions so the check lands in both.
close_reason: Fixed in #247 (a45d951): shared getpw helper null-checks pw_dir and pw_name

title: Ignore frames from a taken-over or detached (Closing) connection
description:
`handle()` (src/master.rs ~L553-591) has no check for `ConnState::Closing`. A Closing conn is not polled for POLLIN, but POLLHUP is always reported, so when the old client's proxy closes, `read_conn` decodes whatever was still buffered and applies it as for the active client: INPUT goes to the pty and advances `InputDedupe::written`, so the new client's first keystrokes at the same sequence are dropped as duplicates (DESIGN §5.1 says clients taking turns never collide); RESIZE resizes the new client's pty; KILL kills the session. Trigger: the old client types or resizes between the takeover and its exit on TAKEOVER, or its proxy holds unsent input when the link died.

Done when Closing conns are drained without handling (or skipped in read_conn), with a test that a late INPUT/RESIZE/KILL from a taken-over conn is ignored and the new client's input_seq stays consistent.
close_reason: Fixed with regression tests (bugs-master branch)

title: The release key is validated at build time and its twin the URL is not
description:
An asymmetry noted during acs-okz (PR #212, 9ce69b0), which made the key's
build-time validation testable and in doing so made the gap visible.

**`ACS_DEFAULT_RELEASE_KEY` is validated** — one line, a known key type, a
base64 body of at least 16 characters — and a bad value **fails the build**.

**`ACS_DEFAULT_RELEASES_URL` is not.** It is trimmed and has a trailing `/`
stripped, and otherwise taken as given. That is deliberate ("taken as given",
per acs-5em), and for a URL there is less to check. But the consequence is that
a fork which sets both and **mistypes the URL** gets a silently unreachable
update channel rather than a build error — the binary builds, ships, and only
fails at a user's `acs upgrade`, which is the worst place to find out.

A cheap check would catch the realistic mistakes: a scheme that is not https
(the runtime override already refuses non-https, so a build-time value that is
http is almost certainly a slip), an obviously unparseable value, or an empty
host. Not a validator for URLs in general — just enough that a typo is a build
error like the key's is.

**Second, smaller item on the same check:** the key's body test is shape-only.
`ssh-ed25519 AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA` passes, and so does `ssh-rsa <an ed25519 body>` —
nothing base64-decodes the blob or checks its embedded type string against the
declared one. That fails closed (every release is then refused) and is the
"wrong-but-well-formed" case DESIGN already accepts, so it is not a hole. But a
decode-and-compare would catch a truncated or mismatched paste at build time
rather than at the user's upgrade — the same argument as the URL above.

Note acs-x57 may change what these values feed: if the build's URL is
substituted into the packaged `scripts/install.sh`, an unvalidated value starts
reaching a shell script, which raises the stakes. Check what that bead landed
before deciding how much validation is enough.

Done when a mistyped releases URL fails the build the way a mistyped key does,
with the same shape of message, and the decision about how far to decode the
key body is recorded in DESIGN §9 either way.
notes:
**The stakes are NOT raised by acs-x57 (PR #214, 1d00169)** — resolving the
question this bead flagged as open.

That pass does substitute the build's releases URL into the packaged
`scripts/install.sh`, but it emits both the URL and the key as **single-quoted
POSIX shell words**, with `'` escaped as `'\''`. `sh` expands nothing inside
single quotes — no `$`, no backtick, no backslash, and a newline is literal — so
the value becomes exactly that string and can never become a command. It is
tested: `a_build_time_value_cannot_inject_shell` drives `'; touch <canary>;
echo '`, `$(touch …)`, backticks, `"; rm -rf /; "` and a pile of metacharacters
through the real script, runs the resulting assignments under `sh`, and asserts
each round-trips as text with the canary never created.

One thing that pass **does** refuse in the value: an embedded line break.
Harmless inside quotes, but it would split the assignment across two lines and
leave nothing able to read the value back for the drift guard.

So this bead is purely the **ergonomics** question it started as: should a
mistyped releases URL fail the build the way a mistyped key does, instead of
producing a silently unreachable update channel that is only discovered at a
user's `acs upgrade`? Nothing about safety depends on it.
close_reason: Done in PR #360 (786aa26): ACS_DEFAULT_RELEASES_URL must be one https URL with a host and the key body is base64-decoded with its embedded type compared, both in src/build_channel.rs shared by build.rs and xtask; decision recorded in DESIGN §7.5/§9

title: Fix the env-scrub test: every Input frame has seq 0, so nine of ten names never reach the shell
description: Found in review. tests/master.rs:994-1046 the_session_shell_does_not_inherit_the_creating_logins_environment (acs-aps's regression test) sends each of ten variable names as Msg::Input{seq: 0, ...}. InputDedupe::accept (resume.rs:191-200) drops a frame whose end <= written and otherwise writes only bytes[written - seq..], so after SSH_AUTH_SOCK\r (14 bytes) SSH_CONNECTION\r contributes one \r and every later shorter name contributes nothing. The shell is only asked about SSH_AUTH_SOCK; the nine other assert!(!text.contains(v)) are vacuous. The later d connection correctly uses seq: w.input_seq. The test also waits for one 'got:' and sleeps 400 ms before the negative asserts, the settle-then-assert shape acs-7wu/acs-o8h removed elsewhere. Done when a running seq is tracked (or one frame is sent), the test waits for ten got: lines, and it is shown red against a master that leaks one of the later variables.
close_reason: Fixed in #273 (5a092d9): one Input frame at the WELCOME's input_seq, waits for ten got: lines, shown red against a master leaking XDG_SESSION_ID

title: Cut the test suite's fixed costs: gzip per call, a keygen per server, 100 serial masters, an 8 s sleep
description: Found in review; measured 65.4 s wall for `cargo test --workspace` on a warm macOS build, 627 passed. Binaries run serially so wall is the sum: reconnect.rs 20.7 s, list.rs 6.2 s, host_aliases.rs 5.3 s, shared.rs 3.4 s, harness.rs 3.3 s, redraw_on_reconnect.rs 3.1 s, master.rs 3.1 s, proxy.rs 2.7 s, install.rs 2.5 s.
