Within reconnect.rs, a_redial_into_a_silent_host_returns_to_the_backoff is 20.5 s by construction (ACS_DIAL_TIMEOUT_MS=10000, two silent redials) and is unblocked by acs-p46 (a separate redial timeout would make it ~2 s); a_stalled_terminal_is_not_a_dead_link sleeps 8 s against ACS_DEAD_MS=800 (2-3 s is still 3x). Fixed costs: common::complete_client (mod.rs:1232) gzips the whole 4 MB binary with an external gzip -9 on every call and install.rs calls it six times (a OnceLock per test binary); ReleaseServer runs ssh-keygen per server and `-Y sign` twice per release(), upgrade.rs starts 14 servers and update_check.rs 9 (a process-wide key except where sign_with_another_key needs its own); tests/master.rs:666-682 the_last_output_before_exit_is_never_lost starts 100 masters serially. Done when the suite is measurably shorter and no test's assertions weakened.
notes: 2026-10-27, PR #348 (f73b412) landed the shared fixed costs: complete_client gzips once per test binary (OnceLock), ReleaseServer signs with one keypair per test binary (impostor key still per call), and the 100 masters in the_last_output_before_exit_is_never_lost run ten at a time (still 100 runs). Measured: that test 1.43 s -> 0.45 s; install.rs user CPU 12.1 s -> 10.6 s; the per-binary sum 76.0 s -> 75.4 s (each binary's wall is set by its slowest test). Still left before done-when: a_redial_into_a_silent_host_returns_to_the_backoff (20.5 s, reconnect.rs; blocked on acs-p46) and the 8 s sleep in a_stalled_terminal_is_not_a_dead_link (reconnect.rs; 2-3 s is still 3x ACS_DEAD_MS). Seen but not in the bead: master.rs wall is about 3.1 s from kill_escalates_to_sigkill_for_a_group_ignoring_sighup (a grace period of at least 2.5 s, product behaviour) and a_hangup_while_the_client_is_stalled_does_not_spin_the_master.
close_reason: Done across #348 (shared gzip and keygen, 100 masters ten at a time) and #358 (ACS_REDIAL_TIMEOUT_MS: the silent-redial test 20.7 s -> 2.7 s, the stalled-terminal sleep 8 s -> 2.4 s); reconnect.rs 20.7 s -> 8.4 s, no assertion weakened

title: Let sys::poll_retry accept -1 as no deadline instead of panicking
description: Found in review. sys.rs:522-523: `Duration::from_millis(timeout_ms as u64)` turns -1 into ~u64::MAX ms and `Instant::now() + ...` overflows, a panic in debug and release. The only caller passes 50 (master.rs:352), so it is latent, but the sibling sys::poll accepts -1 and the signatures are identical, so the first future caller that swaps one for the other aborts the master. Done when timeout_ms < 0 means no deadline, as poll(2) does, with a unit test calling poll_retry(-1) on a fd that becomes readable.
close_reason: Fixed in #253 (ce483eb): negative timeout means no deadline, with unit test

title: Let a held command key survive a redial attempt, instead of a fresh Detector forgetting it
description:
`reconnect::offline()` constructs a fresh `keys::Detector` on every entry, so a
command-key press held across a backoff expiry is silently forgotten: the first
Ctrl-] of a double tap is dropped and the user's escape does not arm.

With the default 400 ms escape window this is invisible — a backoff expiry is
very unlikely to fall inside it. It becomes reachable with a long configured
`ACS_ESCAPE_TIMEOUT_MS` and a short backoff, which is not an exotic combination
for someone who has deliberately widened the window because they find 400 ms
too quick.

Found while doing acs-o8h (PR #164, f4f2522): it is why that PR had to raise
`ACS_BACKOFF_MS` from 20 s to 120 s in `the_escape_window_is_the_same_offline`.
The test configures a 30 s escape window, and without the longer backoff the
redial attempt expires inside it and eats the held press. So the workaround is
already in the suite, which is a good sign the behaviour is real and a bad sign
that it is only recorded as a magic constant.

The question to answer is whether the detector should outlive one redial
attempt — carry it across `offline()` entries rather than rebuilding it — and
what that means for a press held across a *successful* reconnect, where the
client transitions out of the offline path entirely. DESIGN §6.1 describes the
command-mode state machine and is where the answer belongs.

Done when a command key held across a backoff expiry still arms command mode, a
test asserts it with a backoff shorter than the escape window (the inverse of
the constant acs-o8h had to set), and DESIGN §6.1 says what the detector's
lifetime is.
close_reason: Fixed in PR #168 (04e4e22): the Detector moves to client::State and lives as long as the client, so a held press survives a redial attempt and a reconnect; the escape window is the only thing that ends a gesture. acs-o8h's ACS_BACKOFF_MS workaround reverted to 20s

title: The Linux suite fails on a remote exec answering Text file busy: Remote::install's copy races test forks
description: Seen running scripts/test_linux.sh on main 39d070e (2026-10-27): tests/client.rs leaving_ends_a_sequence_the_program_left_open timed out waiting for 'ready' with 'sh: exec: line 0: /tmp/acst-.../h/.local/share/acs/0.17.0/acs: Text file busy' then 'acs: the connection closed before acs started on the remote'. cargo stopped at that binary, so every later test file went unrun. Cause: in the container Remote::install (tests/common/mod.rs ~L528) cannot hard_link across the target volume (EXDEV) and falls back to std::fs::copy, which holds the destination open for write; a parallel test thread that forks in that window carries the write descriptor until its exec, and the fake remote's exec of that file fails ETXTBSY. output_of already retries ETXTBSY for commands the test runs itself, but this exec is inside the fake ssh's sh, out of reach of that retry. Suggested fix: copy exe() once per test binary (OnceLock) into the suite's temp filesystem, before any test forks, and hard_link every remote's install from that copy, so no per-test write descriptor ever exists. Done when Remote::install never holds a written-to fd while other tests fork, and scripts/test_linux.sh passes the client binary (ideally several runs) without this error.
close_reason: Fixed in #295 (89e05fa): Remote::install hard-links one staged copy made by a child cp; the harness's fake executables are written out of process (write_executable). Container load: 3 Text file busy in 48 processes before, 0 in 180 after; scripts/test_linux.sh passes.

title: Drain queued output to the client before failing on a master write error
description:
In `relay()` (src/proxy.rs ~L266) `flush(m, &mut to_master)?` propagates EPIPE when the master closed between this iteration's `read(m)` — which just queued the EXIT frame into `to_client` — and the write. `session()` then errors out without `drain(STDOUT, &to_client)`, so the client sees "link lost" and later NO_SESSION instead of the child's exit status. Needs queued client input (a PING or INPUT) in the same iteration, so the window is narrow.

Done when a write error to the master falls through to the drain path instead of `?`, with a test for EOF-with-pending-output ordering.
close_reason: Fixed with regression tests (bugs-master branch)

title: Do not ACK input the master has not written to the pty
description:
The master ACKs INPUT when it enters pty_in (src/master.rs:622-630), not when it is written; write_pty (master.rs:860-878) clears pty_in on any error or when !pty_open, so acked input can be silently lost. The client then never resends it on resume because it believes the master has it. Only observable on a pty write error, so rare, but it breaks the §5.2 guarantee that an ACK means written.

Done when the ACK is sent after the write succeeds (or the sequence is only advanced by written bytes), with a test that fails the pty write and asserts no ACK.
close_reason: Implemented in #99 (d6cfc12)

title: Keep command mode working after Alt+_ and other ESC-prefixed keys
description:
In Lex::Esc (src/keys.rs:226-230) any of ] P _ ^ X after ESC switches the input lexer into Lex::Str, which (keys.rs:283-290) forwards every byte raw until a BEL or ESC \, and Lex::Str has no timeout (deadline()/tick() only cover seq_since and held state). It exists for terminal replies (OSC 52/11, DCS), but a keyboard Meta+key produces the same two bytes.

Scenario: in bash press Alt+_ (readline's default yank-last-arg, sent as ESC _). From then on Ctrl-] Ctrl-] d, legacy or kitty encoding, is forwarded to the program and never detaches, silently, until the user types Ctrl-G. Verified in a scratch harness: ESC _ then 5 s later 1D 1D 64 gives action=None with all bytes forwarded; with a 07 in between it detaches. Contradicts the README's "press Ctrl-] Ctrl-] quickly, then d".

Done when only the string introducers the replies actually use are treated as strings and the string state is bounded by a short timeout like PENDING_MS, with a test for ESC _ followed by the command key.
close_reason: Implemented in #73 (0f6159f)

title: The -v phase names have no single source, and DESIGN's list has been missing three of them
description:
Found while adding `HELLO sent` in acs-ftn (PR #222, a311e0d), which inserted
its phase and deliberately left the pre-existing gaps alone.

**DESIGN §7's phase list names six phases. The code marks nine.** Missing from
the doc: `shared ssh master checked` (acs-9n3), `acs installed` (the ACS-NEED
install path), and `ACS-NEED seen`, which is the alternative to `ACS-READY
seen` rather than an addition to it. So someone reading `-v` against the doc
today sees phases the doc does not mention, and — worse for the ACS-NEED case —
does not see one the doc leads them to expect.

**The cause is that there is no single source of truth.** Phase names are
string literals spread across `client.rs`, `pick.rs`, the install path, `mux`
and now `timing.rs`. Nothing links a name to the doc, so the doc drifts quietly
and only someone adding a phase notices.

Two halves, and the second makes the first stay fixed:

- add the three missing phases to DESIGN §7 (and check none of the six named
  there has since been renamed);
- give the names one home — an enum, or at least consts on `Timing` — so a new
  phase cannot be added without touching the place the doc is checked against.

A third thing falls out of the same change: **`tests/timing.rs` and
`tests/e2e_ssh.rs` each re-parse the `-v` timing line format independently.**
That is the shape acs-9jv just consolidated for the ssh-call splitter — two
copies of a parser, where one drifting from the other is silent. One home for
the names makes one shared parser natural.

Low priority because nothing is wrong today: every phase acs prints is correct,
and the doc's six are all real. It is the drift that is the problem, and it is
cheap to close.

Done when DESIGN §7 lists every phase the code can mark, the names live in one
place the doc is checked against, and the two test parsers share one.
close_reason: Landed in #381 (45c2b8c): timing::Phase is the one list, DESIGN §7 checked against it by tests/timing.rs, one shared timing-line parser

title: Probe an alias host's ssh port with a TCP connect instead of ICMP
description: Split from acs-zpj. Alias reachability (DESIGN §7.3) is a system ping: hosts that drop ICMP need reachability_check: false, and networks that filter ICMP report a reachable sshd as down. A TCP connect to the host's ssh port is the truer signal (it is what the dial needs) and works for those hosts. Cost: the port must be known per entry, which means ssh -G <host> (Port, and HostName), and an entry reached through ProxyJump/ProxyCommand cannot be probed directly at all (fall back to ping, or to taking it unchecked). Touches alias.rs ping/run_ping, client.rs resolve_alias, DESIGN §7.3. Done when an entry can be probed by TCP with the same deadline semantics as the ping, with tests through a fake listener, and DESIGN says how ProxyJump entries are handled.
close_reason: Landed in #338 (655382a): reachability_tcp checks an alias's hosts on their ssh port via ssh -G + TCP connect; proxied entries are pinged

title: Require a handshake and authorize KILL on the master
description:
Security, missing authorization. master.rs handles `Msg::Kill if pending` by setting the connection to Ending and calling start_kill() with no HELLO, no identity and no force flag. Verified by reading the arm. The BUSY path leaves the connection Pending, so a client that was just refused ("busy, alice@laptop is attached") can send a 5-byte KILL frame on that same connection and destroy the session it was denied. More simply, any process running as that uid can write the frame into any session socket. The menu's confirmation is client-side courtesy only.

The socket permission is therefore the entire trust boundary, which DESIGN §4.5 accepts for a shared account while still promising nobody ends someone else's session by accident.

Done when KILL requires a completed HELLO and is subject to the same identity and force rules as a takeover, a KILL on a connection already answered BUSY is refused, the proxy's END_SESSION path still works, and tests cover the refused-then-kill sequence.
close_reason: Implemented in #111: KILL carries its asker and is held to the takeover rule

title: install.sh re-points ~/.local/bin/acs unconditionally where should_link deliberately does not
description: Found in review. scripts/install.sh:219 `link "$lib/$version/acs" "$bin/acs"` does mv -f over whatever is at ~/.local/bin/acs: a user's own regular file or a link to a newer version is replaced, and ACS_VERSION=older moves the link backwards. install.rs:423-463 should_link (acs-tb1) only moves a link of ours forward and leaves a user's file alone; DESIGN 8 describes that rule. Arguably intended for an explicit installer run, but undocumented. Done when the installer either follows should_link's rule or its header comment ('Running it again upgrades in place') says it also re-points the link, and tests/scripts.rs covers the chosen behaviour.
close_reason: install.sh now follows should_link: link forward only, user's file left alone (#347)

title: Check GitHub weekly for a newer acs release and show a message
description:
Check GitHub for a newer acs release once a week and tell the user.

User's ask: "have the acs binary check for a new release on github once a week, if a new release is available display a message".

Proposed design:

- Only the local client checks; the remote roles (`_proxy`, `_master`, `_install`) never do.
- At most once every 7 days, recorded in `$XDG_STATE_HOME/acs/update-check` (default `~/.local/state/acs/update-check`). It queries `https://api.github.com/repos/michel-onstein/acs/releases/latest` and compares `tag_name` to our version with semver.
- acs has no HTTP/TLS client, and adding one would break the 1 MB size budget (DESIGN §9). So it shells out to `curl` with a short timeout (for example `-m 3`) and never blocks or delays connecting: run it in the background and show the result on the next start, or finish within the timeout before raw mode.
- The message goes to stderr outside the session stream, e.g. `acs 0.3.0 is available (you have 0.2.0) — run: acs upgrade`. It is shown once per new version, not on every run.
- Can be turned off with `ACS_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1`, and with an `update_check: false` option once the YAML config file (acs-xfk) exists. Being offline or rate-limited stays silent.

Done when: unit tests cover the interval, the version comparison and the "shown once" state; an integration test injects the API response (e.g. a fake curl on PATH); README documents it and how to turn it off.
close_reason: Implemented: weekly background _update-check (SHA256SUMS via curl, 3 s), state in XDG_STATE_HOME, message once per new version before connecting, off via ACS_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1 or update_check: false; silent offline

title: Explain the README's two alias shapes: a host list, or a mapping
description:
Wanted: the README's example configuration uses two shapes for an alias without saying why. `devbox` and `nas` are a list of host entries, while `lab` is a mapping of its own settings with the entries under `hosts:`. A reader asked whether the example is even correct.

Verified (v0.8.1): the example is valid. Loaded as-is with the installed acs, `acs config host list` resolves all five hosts with the expected user, check and key. Both shapes are by design (DESIGN §7.2, "An alias's own settings"): YAML cannot make one node both a list and a mapping, so an alias with a setting of its own (`identity_file`, `redraw_on_reconnect`, `reachability_timeout`, `persist`, `reachability_interval`) must be a mapping, and its hosts then need a key. The list form stays the short, usual one. `acs config host set` / `unset` convert between the two. The README's only hint is the comment "an alias with settings of its own", plus the settings-table row for `hosts`.

Change: one or two sentences in README "Configuration" next to the example (or under "Host aliases"): an alias is a list of hosts, or, when it has settings of its own, a mapping of those settings plus `hosts:` with the list. The mapping form is always allowed, and `acs config host set` rewrites a list-form alias into it. Word it to match the top-level key's name at the time; a rename of that key is being proposed separately.

Done when the README explains both shapes and when each is needed, markdownlint passes (scripts/verify.sh), and nothing else changes.
close_reason: Done in PR #60 (8a9e909): the README explains the list and mapping alias shapes

title: Watch for network changes while connected, not only while offline
description:
netwatch is only polled in reconnect.rs offline(); while connected, a Wi-Fi switch or wake from sleep waits out the full 10 s dead-link timeout before the redial starts. Poll the netwatch fd in client.rs serve() too: on a change, send a PING at once and treat the link as dead if no frame arrives within a short deadline (~2 s), so real drops are caught in 1-2 s and a surviving link costs nothing.
Also covers macOS wake, where Instant pauses during sleep so the 10 s window restarts from zero. Done when a netwatch event during serve triggers the early ping, with a test using ACS_NETWATCH_FIFO.
close_reason: Implemented in PR #182 (ecd5d5e): serve() polls the netwatch fd; a real change sends a PING at once and gives the host ACS_NETCHECK_MS (2s) to answer. A surviving link costs nothing; a dead one is found at ~2s instead of 10 and recovers via acs-iyq's free redial

title: Give Timing a HELLO sent phase, now that the greeting has its own moment
description:
acs-pgn (PR #172, d093139) added per-phase connect timings under `-v`.
acs-trw (PR #176, 2579994) then moved the HELLO to immediately after spawn,
before `ACS-READY` is seen — so the greeting now has a moment of its own that
the phase list does not name.

The acs-trw pass left the documented phase list alone on purpose, to keep churn
against acs-pgn low, and measured its own win with a temporary external relay
harness that is not in the commit. That is the gap: the change is not
self-measuring. Anyone asking "did moving the HELLO actually help on this
link?" has to rebuild that harness instead of reading `-v`.

Adding a `HELLO sent` phase would make the acs-trw win visible from the client
itself, and would also show the case acs-trw's non-blocking write is designed
for — a transport that has not connected yet, where part of the greeting stays
in `Link::pending` and is written later by `serve()`. Worth deciding whether
the phase marks the first write or the moment the whole greeting has gone,
since with `pending` those differ and the difference is the interesting bit.

Done when `-v` names the greeting as its own phase, the pending case is
distinguishable from the fits-in-one-write case, and DESIGN's phase list and
the README's `-v` description match.
close_reason: Done in PR #222 (a311e0d): one phase, HELLO sent, always meaning the whole greeting is out — its position in the order is the information. A pending greeting adds HELLO partly sent, so the unusual case is told rather than being a silent reordering. acs-trw's win is now readable off one -v run

title: Make the test remote-env helpers append instead of one silently overwriting the others
description:
`tests/common/mod.rs::Remote::remote_env()` **overwrites** the remote-env file,
while `Remote::remote_umask()` and `Remote::log_master()` (added by acs-o6x,
PR #158) **append** to it. So calling `remote_env` after either of the others
silently discards their setting: no error, no warning, just a test that no
longer configures what it says it configures.

Nothing is broken today — `remote_env` has one caller, and it happens to be
the only thing that caller sets — which is exactly why this is worth fixing
now rather than when it bites. The failure mode is a test that still passes
while no longer testing what its name claims, which is the most expensive kind
of test bug to find.

Found while fixing acs-o6x; left alone there to keep that change to one test.

Done when all three helpers compose — any order, all settings present — with a
test that sets two of them and asserts both reached the remote environment.
close_reason: Fixed in PR #166 (80553cb): every write to the remote-env file goes through one private append-only helper, so there is no whole-file write left to get the order wrong with

title: Validate the version parsed out of SHA256SUMS in the installer script
description:
Security, path traversal in the shell installer. scripts/install.sh greps SHA256SUMS with a pattern whose filename part is [^ ]+, which permits / and .., so the extracted version can be something like 1.0/../../../../etc/cron.d/x. That value then reaches mkdir -p "$lib/$version" and the place call, as root in the root branch. The Rust side is strict about this (release::find_asset then parse_version, digits and dots only), so the two implementations of the same logic disagree.

Reaching it needs full control of the release channel, so this is hardening behind the signing item rather than an independent hole, and the fetch into $tmp/$file fails first for most traversal shapes.

Done when the script requires X.Y.Z exactly, as the Rust code does, and tests/scripts.rs or test_install.sh covers a hostile sums line.
close_reason: Implemented in #126: the sums pattern requires X.Y.Z, with a case guard behind it

title: One atomic write / symlink helper in sys for the seven hand-rolled create_new + rename sites
description: Found in review. The 'create_new temp, write, set mode, rename' dance is spelled in upgrade.rs:422-432 (Staged), upgrade.rs:461-470 (relink), install.rs:381-397 (write_exe), install.rs:405-417 (link_bin), update_check.rs:137-149, config_cmd.rs:1135-1144 and signature.rs:167-182. sys::create_new exists but write_exe and write_allowed_signers re-spell OpenOptions because they need .mode(). A sys::create_new_mode(path, mode), sys::write_atomic(path, mode, bytes) and sys::symlink_atomic(target, link) would replace all of them, and the two umask/scratch-mode bugs become one-line fixes in one place. Done when the sites call the helpers and the existing tests pass.
close_reason: Landed in #363 (f05ba7f): sys::create_new_mode, write_atomic, symlink_atomic replace the hand-rolled create+rename sites

title: Make e2e_ssh.sh --no-build refuse or warn when dist/ is stale
description:
`scripts/e2e_ssh.sh --no-build` reuses whatever is in `dist/` with no check that
it was built from the current source tree. A red e2e failure from a stale
binary is **indistinguishable** from a real one: same test, same assertion,
same message.

Found during acs-8kv (PR #162, caa3854). While deliberately breaking the
`Call::Session` gate to prove `e2e_14` could fail, a `--no-build` run handed
back a red result from a binary built two edits earlier — after the break had
already been reverted. It was only noticed because the person running it knew
exactly what they had just restored. Anyone bisecting an e2e failure, which is
precisely when `--no-build` is worth using, has no such luxury.

The obvious fix is a stamp: `cargo xtask dist` writes the source tree's state
(a git sha plus a dirty marker, or a hash of the inputs it packaged) beside the
artifacts, and `--no-build` compares it and either warns loudly or refuses.
Refusing is probably right — the flag exists to save a minute, and a wrong
answer costs far more than the minute — with a way to say "yes, I mean it".

Note `--no-build` is genuinely valuable: it takes the suite from ~1:03 to ~20 s,
which is what makes iterating on an e2e case bearable. This is about making it
honest, not about removing it.

Done when `cargo xtask dist` records what it built from, `--no-build` compares
and refuses (or warns unmissably) on a mismatch including an uncommitted change,
there is a way to override deliberately, and a test covers the mismatch case.
close_reason: Fixed in PR #170 (2d0a719): cargo xtask dist writes a content hash of the sources to dist/source.stamp, and --no-build refuses on a mismatch unless --allow-stale-dist is passed

title: Fix master spinning on pty POLLHUP while the ring is full
description:
With an active client stalled and the ring full (`room_before_overwrite(next) == 0`) the master polls the pty with `events = 0` (src/master.rs ~L384-395), but Linux `n_tty_poll` reports POLLHUP once the slave side closes, regardless of `events` and even with unread data. Poll then returns immediately, `read_pty` bails at `want == 0` (~L793-796), the drained heuristic does not apply because `asked` is false, `pump_output` cannot add (client at high water), and the loop spins hot until the client drains a chunk or the connection dies. Trigger: `acs host -- cat big.log` over a stalled link when cat finishes.

Done when the pty fd is omitted from the poll set (or the loop sleeps) while `room == 0`, with a test covering hangup-while-stalled.
close_reason: Fixed with regression tests (bugs-master branch)

title: The prelude's acs_safe check reads the symlink, not its target, and is wrong on both platforms
description:
`acs_safe` in the ssh prelude decides whether a remote acs binary is safe to
execute. It reads the mode with `ls -ldn` — **without `-L`** — so on a symlink
it inspects the *link*, never the target.

Found during acs-cu8 (PR #186, a5d3274), where it was the mechanism behind 11
of 36 container failures. It is wrong in opposite directions on the two
platforms:

- **Linux**: a symlink is `lrwxrwxrwx`, so the `?????w*|????????w*` pattern
  matches and the binary is **always refused** — with the message "it or its
  directory is writable by others, or not yours", which is not the reason. A
  user who symlinks acs into place gets a refusal that sends them looking for
  a permissions problem that does not exist.
- **macOS**: a symlink is `lrwxr-xr-x`, so the check **passes** and the
  target's mode and owner are never examined at all. That is precisely the
  hole acs-08m was meant to close: a world-writable binary reached through a
  symlink is executed without complaint.

**Impact today is low**, and that is why this is worth doing calmly rather
than urgently: `acs _install` writes a real file, and the Homebrew symlink is
not on `remote_candidates`, so no real install is a symlink. The test harness
was the only thing producing one, and acs-cu8 changed it to write a real file
(hard_link, falling back to copy) the way a real install does. So nothing is
currently exploiting it.

But a check that silently does not check is worse than no check: it reports
safety it never established, and the next person to add a candidate path or
package acs differently inherits the hole with no warning.

The fix follows the link — `ls -ldnL`, or resolving it first — and then has to
decide what to do about the *link's own directory*, which is a second place an
attacker could substitute the target. Worth re-reading acs-08m's reasoning
before choosing, since this is its check.

Done when the mode and owner examined are the target's, a symlinked binary
whose target is safe is accepted on both platforms, a symlinked binary whose
target is unsafe is refused on both, the refusal message names the actual
reason, and tests cover all four combinations on at least one platform.
close_reason: Fixed in PR #188 (595cdc7): acs_safe walks the chain with readlink and judges the final file plus every directory on the path. Both halves demonstrated before the fix; ls -ldnL verified on busybox, GNU and BSD

title: Replace the fixed 500 ms settles in tests/update_check.rs with events
description: Found in review. tests/update_check.rs:139-159 a_check_is_made_once_a_week (l.145) and :162-177 it_can_be_turned_off (l.174) sleep 500 ms and then assert s.server.hits().is_empty(): a background _update-check not scheduled within 500 ms passes the negative assertion without having run. :180-190 offline_is_silent sleeps 500 ms and positively asserts st.starts_with("checked="), so the same stall fails a correct client under load. The file already has wait_state() (l.68) for the positive case. Done when the positive case waits on wait_state and the negative cases wait on an event (a second start that would show the message, or a checked= write) rather than a clock, per acs-7wu/acs-kip.
close_reason: Landed in #264 (61438a1): update-check tests wait on a witness pipe instead of 500 ms sleeps

title: Table-driven settings in config.rs / config_cmd.rs instead of nine match sites per setting
description: Found in review. Adding a setting today touches Config::bool_setting/bool_mut/duration_setting/duration_mut (config.rs:409-448), AliasSettings::bool_mut/duration_mut/merge_into (:750-781), the Alias and AliasSettings structs that mirror each other field-for-field (:84-110, :739-747), show()'s hand-pushed alias settings (config_cmd.rs:504-558), scalar() (:65-78), typed() (:107-119), apply() (config.rs:328-353), and the USAGE prose in cli.rs and config_cmd.rs. Also: config_cmd::parse_bool (736-742) duplicates config::bool_value (534-549); the host-name rule is written three times (validate_alias config.rs:520-531, host_entry :894, user :904) and host add does not run it before emitting (so a bad CLI argument is reported as a broken file at a line in the unsaved text, config_cmd.rs:1105); aliases -> alias navigation is hand-rolled four times in config_cmd.rs (defined_in :687, HostUnset :839, HostRemove :893, aliases_mut/alias_node :959-989) with the 'remove alias and aliases when empty' tail twice; config_cmd::parse (181-298) hand-rolls --opt=value next to lexopt. Done when a (key, kind, scope) table drives storage, get/set, show and usage, so a new setting is one row.
close_reason: Landed in #327 (4bbd9f2): one SETTINGS table drives file reading, alias merge, get/set/unset/show and host set/unset; helpers merged; release 1,024,000 -> 1,022,392 bytes

title: Make the 25 tests that return early on macOS visibly skipped instead of passing
description: Found in review. tests/e2e_ssh.rs (16 tests, `let Some(h) = host() else { return }`), tests/multiuser.rs (8, `if !enabled() { return }`) and tests/netns.rs (file-level cfg plus an env gate) count as passed in `cargo test --workspace` on macOS: the summary shows `16 passed ... 0 ignored` for e2e_ssh. By design and documented in the headers, but scripts/verify.sh green on a Mac then says nothing about them, and a broken scripts/test_linux.sh goes unnoticed, which is exactly how acs-t8t's installer suite went dark. Done when a skipped test says so (an eprintln as netns.rs does, or a runtime ignore that shows in the summary) and the verify output makes the gap countable.
close_reason: Landed in #287 (191a784): the 25 tests are #[ignore], the scripts pass --include-ignored, verify.sh prints the ignored total

title: Harden the session socket: fchmod 0600 and an O_NOFOLLOW directory handle
description:
Security, defence in depth. Two small gaps sit under an otherwise solid cross-uid boundary. master.rs bind creates the unix socket at 0777 masked by the inherited umask and never chmods it; the 0700 directory and the SO_PEERCRED/getpeereid check on every accept are the only controls. session.rs checks the directory with symlink_metadata and then calls set_permissions by PATH, a chmod that follows symlinks applied after the lstat, and only the leaf's ownership is checked, never its ancestors.

Neither is exploitable at the default path: /tmp is sticky, a pre-created directory fails the uid check, and tests/multiuser.rs deliberately loosens the directory to 0755 and the socket to 0777 and proves the peer check still refuses. It becomes reachable only with ACS_SOCKET_DIR pointed at a path whose parent others can write, where swapping the leaf for a symlink between the check and the connect redirects the client to an attacker's master.

Done when the socket is fchmod'd 0600 after bind, the directory is verified and chmod'd through an O_DIRECTORY|O_NOFOLLOW handle rather than by path, a socket directory with other-writable ancestors is refused, and multiuser tests cover it.
close_reason: Implemented in #131: socket created 0600, dir held by an O_NOFOLLOW handle, ancestors checked

title: Let acs list over every alias join an existing master without starting one
description:
acs-9n3 (PR #184, cc1ab77) gave first connections and side calls a shared
master. Batch calls — `acs list` over every alias (§7.3) — were deliberately
left out: they neither start nor join one.

The reason was sound. A batch fans out to every alias at once, so letting each
one *start* a master would mean a dozen masters appearing simultaneously, plus
a race where several calls to the same host each decide to be the master. That
is exactly the footprint and the race acs-9n3 was warned about.

But **joining** has neither problem. `ControlMaster=no` with the path set means
"use the master if one is there, otherwise dial normally" — no creation, no
race, and the fan-out is what makes it worth having: a batch over a dozen
aliases is a dozen handshakes, and any host you already have a session to
would answer from its existing master instead. On a real link that is the
difference between a listing that takes a second and one that takes several.

Cheap to do — `control_opts()` already distinguishes starting from joining, and
`Call::Batch` is already its own variant — but worth a deliberate look at:

- whether a batch joining a master can slow down the *interactive* session
  sharing it (ssh multiplexes channels, so mostly no, but a dozen channels
  opening at once on one connection is not nothing);
- whether the 2s `ACS_CONTROL_FALLBACK_MS` check per host is worth paying when
  most hosts in a batch will not have a master — `ssh -O check` costs ~5ms, so
  probably yes, but measure rather than assume;
- whether a batch should skip the check entirely and just set the path, letting
  ssh fall back on its own.

Done when a batch call joins an existing master where one is there, never
starts one, the fan-out does not degrade an interactive session on the same
master, and the win is measured with acs-pgn's timings rather than asserted.
close_reason: Landed in #356 (5529031): acs list over every alias joins a master that is up (ControlMaster=no after ssh -O check), never starts one; 33 vs 50 ms per listing on loopback

title: acscp: scp for acs
description:
Implement `acscp`, scp for acs, as designed in docs/ACSCP_DESIGN.md (draft PR #226): the `acs` binary under a second name (`acscp`, and `acs cp` with no link), running a fourth role. Copies survive a network drop and resume from the part on disk; the remote end is `acs _cp`, started by the session prelude and self-installed like a session — no sftp-server, no remote shell expansion of paths.

The plan is §12 (refactors, then phases 1–6 in dependency order), the decisions §13. Done when the refactors and phases 1–4 and 6 are closed and ACSCP_DESIGN.md's Status says Built; phases 5a/5b are optional.

title: Refactor session code for acscp: from_argv, Connection, -P, Framer
description:
The four refactors ACSCP_DESIGN.md §10.3 (items 1–4) asks of the session code before the copy role is added. No behaviour change.

1. `Role::from_argv(&args)` in lib.rs: consult argv[0]'s basename for `acscp` before today's `from_first_arg`; add `cp` to the reserved first arguments.
2. `cli::Connection`: split the reaching-a-host part of `ClientArgs` (transport, verbose, config, alias, entry) out, so `client::dial`, `client::resolve_alias`, `install::install` and `install::not_installing` take `&Connection`. `ClientArgs` embeds one.
3. The ssh option passthrough in cli.rs becomes a function of the port option's letter (`p` for acs, `P` for acscp), keeping one list and one validation.
4. `proto::Framer` split out of `proto::Decoder` (§5.1); `Decoder` = `Framer` + `Msg::decode`. Existing frame tests apply to both.

Done: scripts/verify.sh green, with unit tests for from_argv (acscp basename, `acs cp`, existing roles unchanged) and the P/p passthrough.
close_reason: Landed in #393 (dfb9de6): Role::from_argv, cli::Connection, port-letter passthrough, Decoder::next_frame per the design's 2026-10-28 revision (no Framer type)

title: acscp: the copy measures 64 KB of x86_64 slim, over its 50 KB budget (decision 13)
description:
Measured by acs-hofu.9 (2026-10-28, at 792c178, `cargo xtask dist` with phase 1's cfg(debug_assertions) gates on src/cp removed for the measurement only): phase 1's copy alone — the local copy, no remote end, no ssh dial yet — adds 63,984 B to the slim x86_64-unknown-linux-musl build (1,046,120 -> 1,110,104 B) and 124,875 B to the complete one (2,097,809 -> 2,222,684 B). aarch64 Linux slim +50,488 B, aarch64-apple-darwin +50,016 B, x86_64-apple-darwin +57,704 B.

ACSCP_DESIGN decision 13 / goal 7 budgets the whole copy role at 50 KB of x86_64 slim and §10.4 estimated 30–60 KB with phase 2 included; phase 1 is already 14 KB over, and phase 2 (acs _cp, Call::Session dial, install on ACS-NEED) adds more. acs-hofu.9 raised the enforced budget to slim 1.15 MB / complete 2.3 MB to leave room, so the gate is not what blocks — the design's figure is.

Either find where the 64 KB goes (cargo bloat / `--emit` symbol sizes on the musl slim build: argument parsing, the walker, the progress meter, formatting machinery pulled in by them) and trim it toward 50 KB, or revise goal 7 / decision 13 to the measured figure. Done: the measurement and the choice recorded in ACSCP_DESIGN §10.4 (or DESIGN §8.1 once the design doc is on main), and the copy's x86_64 slim cost either under 50 KB or the decision revised to what it is.
close_reason: Trimmed in #403: phase 1's x86_64 slim cost 63,984 -> 49,960 B, under decision 13's 50 KB; measurement in DESIGN §8.1

title: acscp: the copy role measures 56.8 KB of x86_64 slim — raise decision 13's 50 KB or trim further?
description:
acs-hofu.3 (phase 2: `acs _cp`, upload and download over ssh) landed its code and tests, but measured by `cargo xtask dist` with the `cfg(debug_assertions)` gates in `src/lib.rs` lifted for the measurement only, the whole copy role (phases 1 + 2) is **56,840 B of x86_64 musl slim** against ACSCP_DESIGN decision 13's **50,000 B**. Phase 1 alone was 49,960 B (acs-hofu.10), so phase 2 costs about 6,900 B. The copy therefore stays gated out of release builds; removing the gate (and the README "Use" section that goes with shipping it) waits on this decision.

Measured at f0299a0 plus the phase-2 change, release without the copy -> with it (DESIGN §8.1 has the table):

- x86_64-unknown-linux-musl: slim 1,046,248 -> 1,103,088 (+56,840); complete 2,097,787 -> 2,212,459 (+114,672)
- aarch64-unknown-linux-musl: slim 931,824 -> 980,320 (+48,496); complete 1,983,363 -> 2,089,691 (+106,328)
- aarch64-apple-darwin: slim 774,032 -> 824,064 (+50,032); complete 1,836,640 -> 1,919,264 (+82,624)
- x86_64-apple-darwin: slim 853,184 -> 902,720 (+49,536); complete 1,920,992 -> 2,028,752 (+107,760)

Every build stays within the size budget `cargo xtask dist` enforces (slim 1.15 MB, complete 2.3 MB), so only decision 13's figure is exceeded.

Where phase 2's bytes go (llvm-nm --size-sort on unstripped x86_64 builds, with vs without the copy): the copy's dial `cp::over_ssh` 2.3 KB; `acs _cp` itself, inlined into `run`; and outlining. The session's install step (`client::ready_or_install`, ACSCP_DESIGN §10.3 item 7) is now one 6.2 KB function with two callers where it used to be inlined into the session alone. The session side shrank by about as much, so the copy-less release grew only 288 B over 792c178. But that cost shows in the copy's figure, and so do `update_check::on_client_start` (1.6 KB) and `prune::touch_own` (0.8 KB), each outlined now that it has two callers.

Options:

1. Raise decision 13 to about 60 KB of x86_64 slim. That leaves room for phase 3 (resume, redial) only if phase 3 is small, and phase 3 will need its own figure.
2. Trim further. No single cheap trim closes 6.8 KB. Candidates: drop the copy's weekly update check (about 1.5 KB, against §10.1); share more of `over_ssh` with the session's first-connection path; look again at phase 1's 37 KB of code (the command line's 6.5 KB inlined into `run`, the receiver's `hashbrown` map at 3 KB).
3. Restate decision 13 as a budget for the copy's own code, net of shared session code it makes outlined (here about 8.6 KB).
close_reason: Maintainer set the copy budget to 100 KB of x86_64 musl slim (2026-10-28), replacing 50 KB; recorded as DESIGN decision 13 and §8.1

title: acscp: a lost link's acs _cp can still write the part a redial is resuming
description:
Found while building acscp phase 3 (resume, acs-hofu.4).

A redial's `acs _cp` receiver opens `.<name>.acscp-part`, hashes the prefix it finds and appends from there. Nothing stops the lost link's own `acs _cp` — still alive on the host until its liveness (ACS_DEAD_MS, 10 s) or sshd notices — from writing bytes it still had buffered to the same part after the new one has hashed it. Two writers at different offsets can leave a part whose bytes past the hashed prefix are wrong, and nothing re-checks them: the file is renamed into place as whole.

The window is small (the old end only has what reached its socket before the drop, and the client redials after detecting the drop, usually seconds later), but the result is a silently wrong copy, which is the one thing the part's hash exists to prevent.

Possible fixes: an exclusive `flock` on the part while a receiver holds it, with the new receiver waiting a bounded time for it (the old one exits within ACS_DEAD_MS) or answering FAIL "in use by another copy"; or the old end closing the part on a lost link before the client can have redialled.

Done: a test with two receivers on one part — the first still writing when the second opens it — shows the second waits or refuses, never interleaves; ACSCP_DESIGN §7 states the rule.

title: acscp phase 1: copy protocol, sender and receiver, local copies
description:
Phase 1 of ACSCP_DESIGN.md §12: the copy itself, proven with no ssh involved. §4–§6; new files per §10.2: src/cp/{mod,cli,proto,sender,receiver,walk,progress}.rs.

- cli.rs: scp-compatible arguments (§4, `-p` preserves, port is `-P`), `split_remote` (§4.1), the pre-ssh checks (§4.2), usage text.
- proto.rs: the copy messages (§5.2) as their own enum over `proto::Framer` (decision 11).
- sender.rs: walk sources, run headers ahead of data by a window of 64 (§5.3), stream DATA.
- receiver.rs: scp's placement rules (§6), writing `.<name>.acscp-part` and renaming when whole; name checks (§5.4: single components, DIR/DIR_END nesting, top-level names must be those requested).
- walk.rs: the local tree, metadata, symlink and loop rules. progress.rs: the stderr meter.
- Local-to-local runs sender and receiver in one process over a socketpair (§10.2).

Done: §11's unit bullets, tests/cp_local.rs (byte-for-byte tree equality over the listed sizes, -r, -p, symlinks, fifo, unreadable file) and the pipelining test (100 one-byte files over a 50 ms-delayed transport in well under 100 round trips) all pass.
close_reason: Landed in #399

title: acscp phase 2: acs _cp remote end, upload and download over ssh
description:
Phase 2 of ACSCP_DESIGN.md §12: the first thing a user runs — `acscp file host:` to a host that has never seen acs. §8 and §3.

- remote.rs: `acs _cp`, started by the session prelude so it is always the client's version; marker, HELLO, pick the endpoint, run it on stdio. Paths travel in HELLO, never on the command line (decision 4); `_cp` expands `~` and relative paths itself.
- The first connection is a `ssh::Call::Session` on acs's ssh master (decision 9, revised 2026-10-28: not a `Call::Side`) via `client::dial`, with the existing self-install on `ACS-NEED` on the same connection (`install::plan/install/not_installing`, the step lifted out of `client::connect_once`, §10.3 item 7).
- Upload and download, several sources on one host. Until phase 3 a drop ends the copy with the part kept.

Done: tests/cp_remote.rs (fake remote via --transport-cmd and tests/common::Remote) covers upload, download, several sources, first-contact install, the `install_on_remote: false` refusal, and refusal of hostile names from the far end (`/`, `..`, a top-level name not asked for, `.bashrc` in answer to `host:notes.txt`). The binary-size delta in `cargo xtask dist`'s table is recorded in DESIGN §8.1: the copy within its 50 KB of the slim x86_64 Linux build (decision 13), and every build within the budget acs-hofu.9 raised (slim 1.15 MB, complete 2.3 MB; §10.4).
notes: 2026-10-28: phase 2's code and tests landed (acs _cp, upload and download over ssh as a Call::Session, install on ACS-NEED on the same connection via client::ready_or_install; tests/cp_remote.rs), still behind the cfg(debug_assertions) gates in src/lib.rs, extended to _cp, so release builds are unchanged. Only removing the release gate is left (plus the README Use section that goes with shipping). It waits on the size decision in acs-hofu.11: the copy role measures 56,840 B of x86_64 slim against decision 13's 50,000 B (DESIGN §8.1). Deviations from ACSCP_DESIGN: a download whose remote path has no name of its own (host:, host:~, host:~/, host:a/.., host:/) is refused before dialling rather than accepting whatever name the far end sends. The copy marks no 'WELCOME received' -v phase, and dials without a network watcher (phase 3, §7).
close_reason: Phase 2 shipped in #405; release gate removed in this PR (acscp / acs cp / acs _cp in release builds, README Use section)

title: acscp phase 3: resume from the part, redial with backoff
description:
Phase 3 of ACSCP_DESIGN.md §12: resume — what makes acscp an acs tool. §7, §10.3 item 6.

- The part on disk is the only state: on (re)connect the receiver sends `HAVE` with the part's size and prefix hash; the sender answers `RESTART` at that offset, or from zero on a mismatch (decision 6). A later run resumes an earlier one by the same mechanism.
- The receiver's hashing is sliced inside the poll loop so a long HAVE never looks like a dead link to the session's pings (decision 12).
- Redials go on their own connection (`ssh::Call::Redial`) with `reconnect::Backoff`, `reconnect::Liveness` and `netwatch::NetWatch` in a loop of the copy's own — not `reconnect::run`, which carries terminal state.

Done: in tests/cp_remote.rs, the transport killed mid-file and the copy resumed with the trees equal and the part reused (asserted by the bytes the second connection carried); a part with a wrong prefix restarted; Ctrl-C leaves the part and a second run finishes from it.

title: acscp phase 4: install the acscp link everywhere acs goes
description:
Phase 4 of ACSCP_DESIGN.md §12: put the `acscp` name everywhere acs is installed — no new artifact, only a relative link. §9, §10.3 item 5. Can land in parallel with phase 3.

- `install::link_bin` grows a companion that makes the relative `acscp` link, shared with upgrade.rs, so the remote install finisher and `acs upgrade` both create it.
- install.sh creates the link in every layout (default, pinned, re-run, ACS_INSTALL_DIR, root).
- The Homebrew formula installs the link; `brew test` runs `acscp --version`; `brew audit --strict` passes on the generated formula.
- README "Use" documents acscp / `acs cp`.

Done: scripts/test_install.sh asserts `acscp --version` after each layout and that the link is relative (the suite was repaired under acs-t8t); the formula checks pass.

title: acscp phase 5a: two-host copies relayed through the local machine
description:
Phase 5a of ACSCP_DESIGN.md §12 (optional, last): copies between two remote hosts, routed through the local machine like `scp -3`. §5.6, decision 10.

relay.rs splices the two links' frames, peeking at headers only for the name checks and the progress meter; no file handling in the middle and no resume in this form. Taken when someone misses it.

Done: a host-to-host copy over two fake remotes in tests/cp_remote.rs yields equal trees, and hostile names from either side are refused.

title: acscp phase 5b: remote wildcards expanded by acs _cp
description:
Phase 5b of ACSCP_DESIGN.md §12 (optional, last): remote wildcards, e.g. `acscp 'host:logs/*.gz' .`. §5.4.

`acs _cp` expands the pattern itself (there is no remote shell — decision 4); the receiver's top-level name rule admits only names matching the pattern the user wrote. Taken when someone misses it.

Done: unit tests for the matcher, and an integration test where a wildcard download fetches the matching files and a far end answering with a non-matching name is refused.

title: acscp phase 6: e2e over ssh, verification and docs to Built
description:
Phase 6 of ACSCP_DESIGN.md §12: close the loop end to end and bring the docs to Built.

- scripts/e2e_ssh.sh (§11 end-to-end bullet): `acscp` to a fresh container host installs acs on first contact; upload and download of a tree with `-r -p` compared with `diff -r`; `sshd-session` killed mid-copy of a 200 MB file and the copy completing with the part visibly reused; the copy joins the session's master (`-v` shows no second handshake, `ssh -O check` one pid); `acscp` and `acs cp` both present after the install; `acs _cp`'s version directory touched.
- scripts/test_linux.sh: as root with alice and bob, a copy into another user's directory fails; the per-version install and prune touch work for copies.
- By hand: 2 GB over Wi-Fi with the lid closed for a minute halfway, and an `scp -r` timing comparison — recorded in docs/VERIFICATION.md.
- Docs: DESIGN.md §3 role table and §9 layout rows; ACSCP_DESIGN.md Status line to Built; the CLAUDE.md index row.

title: acscp: raise the complete size budget so the copy can ship in release builds
description:
ACSCP_DESIGN §10.4 and §12 (node B, 'the maintainer's call'): the complete x86_64 Linux build has about 3 KB of room under xtask's COMPLETE_BUDGET (2,100,000 B), and every byte the copy adds to the slim build is carried again, gzip'd, in both Linux payloads, so a 30-60 KB copy costs the complete build about twice that. No bead tracked this precondition of phase 2.

Phase 1 (acs-hofu.2) therefore compiles src/cp only under cfg(debug_assertions): tests and dev builds have it, release builds still answer 'copying files is not built yet'. Phase 2 removes that gate (lib.rs: the cfg on 'pub mod cp' and on the two Role::Copy arms, and tests/cp_local.rs's #![cfg(debug_assertions)]) once this lands.

Also: acs-hofu.3's text predates the 2026-10-28 design revision — it says the first connection is a Call::Side and the budget is 100 KB; the design now says Call::Session (decision 9) and 50 KB slim with the complete budget raised (decision 13).

Done: COMPLETE_BUDGET (and the xtask doc line) raised, to about 2.2 MB per the design or as the maintainer decides; DESIGN §8.1's size table brought up to date in the same change.
close_reason: Budget raised to slim 1.15 MB / complete 2.3 MB on measurement (#401); DESIGN §8.1 updated

title: Guard the input-dedupe sequence arithmetic against overflow
description:
Security, peer-steerable arithmetic. resume.rs InputDedupe::accept computes `let end = seq + bytes.len() as u64;` with no guard, where seq comes straight from a peer's INPUT frame, and master.rs written_to_pty then does a plain `self.input.written() - self.pty_in.len() as u64`. Verified by reading both, and Cargo.toml sets no overflow-checks, so release builds wrap.

An INPUT frame with seq near u64::MAX wraps end to a small number while bytes are queued, so written_to_pty underflows to roughly 2^64 and poisons the ACK the client uses to decide what it may forget. A debug build aborts the master outright, ending the session.

Done when the addition is checked and a frame whose sequence cannot be valid is refused as a protocol error rather than wrapping, with a test for the wrapping sequence.
close_reason: Implemented in #127: accept refuses a sequence whose end does not fit

title: The load failures that are left are all the dial, and T is the only lever
description:
After acs-o6x, acs-o8h, acs-7wu, acs-ryz and acs-2dc, the tests that still fail
under heavy load have **one** cause between them, and it is not a window any of
those passes could close: the dial is starved, and the test has nothing left to
wait for.

Measured during acs-2dc (PR #205, 661e1dc), under 6 `dd` loops plus 10
fork/exec loops:

- `tests/client.rs` — 86 failures in 850. The two biggest are
  `unsupported_remote_platform_is_reported` (34) and
  `the_verbose_command_line_reaches_the_acs_arguments` (30). Both wait for the
  program's first byte and there is no earlier observable event.
- `tests/menu.rs` — 64 in 700, i.e. **worse** than client.rs (9.1% against 2.7%)
  with the identical empty terminal, so this is not a property of one file.
- `host_aliases` — 13 in 60 on `timed out waiting for "new session 's' on "`,
  after that bead's own failures went to zero.
- `alias::tests::ping_is_one_packet_with_a_backstop_past_the_deadline` — 4 in 32
  full-lib runs: a `fork` + `exec` + shell startup taking more than the **10 s**
  acs-ryz had already widened it to.
- `tests/reconnect.rs::a_redial_into_a_silent_host_returns_to_the_backoff` — 9 in
  522, independent of any of these changes.

The diagnosis is established, not guessed: holding the load fixed and moving `T`
from 30 s to 300 s took client.rs from 86 failures to 6, and **removing the I/O
pressure while keeping load average ~20 gave 850/850 green**. It is I/O
starvation of two shells plus a cold 4 MB debug binary — nothing subtler.

So the question this bead exists to answer is a policy one, not a debugging one:

- **Is `T` (30 s) the right suite-wide deadline?** It is four times smaller than
  the client's own first-dial timeout (120 s), so a starved dial is
  indistinguishable from a hang. Raising `T` makes a genuine hang slower to
  report, which is the trade.
- **Or is "the suite is not expected to pass under deliberate I/O starvation" the
  honest answer?** If so it should be written down, so the next person does not
  spend a day rediscovering it. acs-2dc's numbers are the evidence either way.
- A third option worth weighing: make the dial itself cheaper in tests — a
  release-profile test binary, or a fake transport that does not fork two shells.

Note what is NOT in scope: the five clients that were **SIGKILLed externally**
under memory pressure (swap at 3.4/4 GB), zero bytes written, 1.2-1.9 s after
spawn. No deadline addresses that and it is not acs's doing.

Done when the suite's deadline policy is decided and recorded — either `T` moves
with a stated reason, or the starvation limit is documented as expected — and
the four beads above stop being re-filed as individual flakes.
notes:
Re-weighted P4 to P3 on frequency, not on new analysis.

Three separate passes hit `tests/client.rs` timeouts on this machine in quick
succession — acs-z22, acs-9jv's neighbours and acs-0pr, the last seeing *two
different pairs* of tests time out in three consecutive runs
(`modes_left_on_are_reset_on_detach` + `output_is_byte_exact_including_escape_sequences`,
then `new_session_is_announced_and_raw_mode_applies`).

That does not change the diagnosis — acs-2dc established it is the dial being
starved, with the deadline as the only lever, and acs-0pr's reds were on a
machine also running docker builds. What changes is the cost: every pass now
pays time deciding whether a red run is its own doing, and a run that has to be
repeated to be believed is not much better than no run.

The decision this bead exists to make is unchanged and still the right one:
either `T` moves with a stated reason, or "the suite is not expected to pass
under deliberate I/O starvation" gets written down. What is new is that the
second answer now needs to say something about the *ordinary* case too, because
these reds are not all under deliberate starvation — a concurrent docker build
is a normal thing to be doing in this repo.

Keep acs-br2's lesson in view when settling it: "only fails under load,
unreproducible in isolation" was consistent with starvation there too, and it
turned out to be a real ordering bug that starvation merely exposed.
close_reason: Decided and recorded in PR #391 (71e9b7a): T stays 30 s; the I/O-starvation limit is documented as expected at T (src/testutil.rs), DESIGN §9.1 and decision 11, with a unit test holding T to half the suite's minute timers. Follow-up acs-3sk9 derives those timers from T.

title: On macOS, unlinking a hard link of the acs binary while a test thread spawns it kills the spawned client
description: Found during acs-e86g (2026-10-27). Every Remote drop removes a hard link of exe() (tests/common/mod.rs Remote::install links it). If another test thread spawns exe() as a client at that moment, the client dies at once without output: it becomes a zombie child of the test binary, and the test times out after 30s waiting for its first line (for example new_session_is_announced_and_raw_mode_applies). There is nothing in the unified log. A test in tests/client.rs that created two Remote::installed() and dropped them at once failed several times in 6 runs. Remote::new() (no link) and forgetting the remotes both gave 0 hangs in 25. That test now keeps its remotes until exit (remove_at_exit). The race is still there for every other test's drop and makes a rare macOS flake. Fix candidates: defer every Remote's directory removal to exit (remove_at_exit), or have the client spawn a link rather than exe() itself. Done when dropping remotes during other tests' client spawns no longer kills a client (a stress test that drops remotes in a loop while spawning clients passes repeatedly).
close_reason: Remote's Drop ends sessions now and defers directory removal to exit, so no drop unlinks a hard link of the binary while a client spawns (PR #318). tests/client.rs: 10/270 failing runs before, 0/150 after.

title: Add acs config subcommands to edit the configuration
description:
Add `acs config …` subcommands to manage the configuration file from the command line.

User's ask: "add options to the cli to allow configuration of acs through the command line, something like `acs config host add <alias> <hostname> --reachability-check`".

Proposed shape (settle the details during implementation):

- `acs config show`: prints the merged configuration and which file each value came from.
- `acs config get <key>` and `acs config set <key> <value>`, e.g. `acs config set install_on_remote false`.
- `acs config host add <alias> <host> [--user U] [--no-reachability-check]`: appends an entry, so repeated adds give an alias fallback hosts in order.
- `acs config host remove <alias> [<host>]` and `acs config host list`.
- Writes go to the local file (`~/.config/acs/config.yaml`); `--global` targets `/etc/acs/config.yaml` and needs the right permissions.

Notes:

- `config` becomes a reserved first argument. Today it would be read as a host name (src/cli.rs), so a host literally called `config` needs a way through, e.g. `acs -- config` or `user@config`. Document it.
- Writing must keep the file readable and stable (no reordering of what it did not touch); comments are nice to keep but not required.

Done when: every subcommand works against a temp HOME in tests; errors (unknown key, wrong type, missing alias) are clear; README documents it.
close_reason: Implemented: acs config show/get/set/unset/path and host list/add/remove, --global, comment-preserving validated atomic writes; config reserved as first arg

title: On Linux, a_stalled_terminal_is_not_a_dead_link never actually blocks the client
description: Found by the acs-p46 pass (#358). The test trickles output into a paused terminal so the client blocks in write_output for longer than ACS_DEAD_MS, then asserts the link is not declared dead. A macOS raw pty holds ~1024 B (measured), so the trickle fills it in the first dead interval and the client really blocks. A Linux pty holds ~20 KB (measured in the test container); at the trickle's rate (~1.5-2 KB/s, estimated) it never fills, even in the old 8 s, so on Linux the test has never exercised the stall it claims to — before or after #358. Done when the test blocks the client on Linux too (e.g. fill the pty to a measured capacity first, or size the trickle from the measured buffer), with a check that the client was in fact blocked (e.g. the -v timing or a write that cannot complete), and it still passes on both.
close_reason: Test now proves the client blocked (resize probe unhandled for 3 dead intervals) on Linux and macOS; fails on both with acs-7k7 reverted. PR #365.

title: Treat a failure to link ~/.local/bin/acs as a warning, not an install failure
description:
install::finish() (src/install.rs:266-278, 302-314) renames the binary into place and only then calls link_bin; any error there (HOME unset in the ssh environment, ~/.local/bin existing as a regular file or not writable, symlink failing) returns Err, the finisher exits 1 without printing ok, and the client reports "installing acs failed" and exits, although ~/.local/share/acs/<v>/acs is complete and every later connection works. DESIGN §8 says nothing in the protocol depends on that link.

Done when link_bin failure is reported as a warning after ok, the install still counts as successful, and a test makes ~/.local/bin a file and asserts the install succeeds with a warning.
close_reason: Implemented in #83 (80cf8d5)

title: Install creates its directory under the umask, then refuses to run from it
description:
Reported by the user against v0.11.4, connecting to a host that worked before:

    acs: installing acs 0.11.4 on tolot (Linux x86_64)…
    acs: installed acs 0.11.4 on tolot
    acs: refusing to run /home/michel/.local/share/acs/0.11.4/acs: it or its
      directory is writable by others, or not yours
    acs: acs was installed on tolot but the remote still cannot run it
      (is $HOME the same for ssh commands?)
    exit 254

acs-08m (#132) added the prelude's acs_safe check, which refuses a candidate
whose file OR its directory is group/other writable, or not owned by the
caller (ssh.rs prelude()). It did not change the install, which still creates
the directory with a bare `mkdir -p` under the remote's umask
(install.rs:129,138 — `set -e; mkdir -p {dir}; …`).

The binary is fine: the upload chmod 755's it, and write_exe sets 0755 for
real past the umask (acs-28b). Only the directories are left to the umask.

On the reported host (umask 002, uid 1000, per-user group):

    drwxr-xr-x  /home/michel                       fine, predates acs
    drwxr-xr-x  /home/michel/.local                fine
    drwxr-xr-x  /home/michel/.local/share          fine
    drwxrwxr-x  /home/michel/.local/share/acs      made by acs, group write
    drwxrwxr-x  /home/michel/.local/share/acs/0.11.4   made by acs  <- checked
    -rwxr-xr-x  /home/michel/.local/share/acs/0.11.4/acs   fine

acs_safe checks `dirname "$b"`, the version directory, so it refuses the
directory acs itself has just created. Every host with umask 002 is bricked
by an install: it succeeds and the very next exec is refused, 254. The
ownership half of the check passes (uid 1000 owns all of it); only the group
write bit trips it. Here the group is the user's own per-user group, so it is
harmless in fact — but the check cannot know that, and should not have to.

Wanted: the install creates the directories it owns with 0755 explicitly,
past the umask, as it already does for the binary — the version directory
and its ~/.local/share/acs parent. Do not touch $HOME, ~/.local or
~/.local/share: acs did not create them, and chmod'ing a user's own
directories is not acs's business (the check does not look at them either).

Note for whoever takes it: an existing install on such a host stays broken
until its directory is fixed, since the directory is only created when a
version is new. Upgrading to the fixed version creates a new version
directory, so it heals itself; the stale ~/.local/share/acs parent should be
chmod'd by the install too so it does not linger group-writable.

Done when the install sets the mode on the directories it creates, a test
runs the real install script under umask 002 and asserts the resulting
directory is not group- or other-writable and that the real prelude then
execs it, and DESIGN §8 says the directories are created 0755 past the umask.

Regression of acs-08m; the mode-past-umask reasoning is acs-28b's.
close_reason: Fixed in #138 (v0.11.5): the install sets 0755 on the directories it makes

title: Redial at once on the first attempt after a drop
description:
Backoff::new(1000) in reconnect.rs makes even the first redial after a lost link wait 1 s. Most drops are momentary (a Wi-Fi blip), so the first attempt should go immediately and the 1 s -> 30 s backoff start from the second. Saves 1 s on every resume.
Done when the first redial after a LinkLost has no wait, later ones keep the backoff, and a unit test on Backoff covers it (ACS_BACKOFF_MS still sets the base).
close_reason: Implemented in PR #178 (f565134): Backoff.next is Option, the first attempt after a drop goes at once, and NetworkChanged uses spent() so a watcher-driven redial still costs one dial. Measured cut-to-resumed median 1030ms to 43ms

title: cargo xtask dist fails its size budget on x86_64 Linux, so no release can be cut
description: Found 2026-10-27 by the acs-hdj4 pass running scripts/e2e_ssh.sh: cargo xtask dist stops with 'xtask: over the size budget' for x86_64-unknown-linux-musl — slim 1005216 B against SLIM_BUDGET 1000000, complete 2018338 B against COMPLETE_BUDGET 2000000 (xtask/src/main.rs:38-39). dist is the first step of scripts/release-binaries.sh, so the next version bump cannot publish binaries, and scripts/e2e_ssh.sh without --no-build fails too. The budgets are design goal 2 (DESIGN.md: 'Slim build < 1 MB; with the embedded Linux payloads < 2 MB'); DESIGN §8.1's size table is stale (still says 602 KB / 1.21 MB). The release profile is already opt-level z, lto, codegen-units 1, panic abort, strip, and the only dependencies are libc and lexopt, so there is no build knob left: either code comes out (measure what grew — e.g. cargo bloat or comparing v0.17.0's slim size against main, and the ~40 merges of 2026-10-27) or the budget in goal 2 is raised. That choice is the maintainer's. Done when cargo xtask dist passes on every target, DESIGN goal 2 and the §8.1 table match what is built, and the chosen budget is the one xtask enforces.
close_reason: Maintainer chose to raise the budget: #330 sets slim 1.1 MB / complete 2.1 MB in xtask and DESIGN goal 2, refreshes the §8.1 size table; cargo xtask dist passes on every target

title: Make the timing-sensitive tests survive a loaded machine
description:
Two integration tests fail intermittently when the whole suite runs at once, and pass on their own every time. Seen twice during the security burn-down of 2026-09-20:

- tests/master.rs::a_client_that_vanishes_without_closing_is_dropped — pushes 3 MB through a pty and waits on a marker file within a 10 s deadline.
- tests/reconnect.rs::ctrl_c_during_a_redial_clears_the_status_line — depends on a redial landing inside a window.

Neither was a real failure: re-running scripts/verify.sh passed both times, and the changes in flight (an installer digest check, an input-sequence guard) cannot touch either path. But a gate that fails one run in several teaches people to re-run rather than to read, which is how a real failure eventually gets waved through.

Done when both are steady under `cargo test` with the whole suite running in parallel — a generous deadline driven by an environment knob as the liveness tests already use, waiting on a condition rather than a sleep, or serialising the few that need the machine to themselves — and the reason is written next to whichever mechanism is chosen.
close_reason: Implemented in #135: generous deadlines, a condition instead of a sleep, a wider parallel margin

title: Test SHA-256 at the padding boundaries 55, 56, 63, 64, 65 bytes
description: Found in review. The implementation was verified correct against hashlib for 212 lengths (0..=200 and powers of two to 1 MiB, one-shot and chunked), but the in-tree tests cover lengths 0, 3, 56, 10,000 and 1,000,000 only. 55, 63, 64, 65 and 119/120 are the one-block/two-block padding boundaries in finish() (sha256.rs:108, `fill = (64+56-(buf_len+1)%64)%64`), and a future change there would not be caught. Done when a loop test checks 0..=130 bytes against known digests (or shasum -a 256 at test time).
close_reason: Landed in #269 (9657f15): SHA-256 tested at every length 0..=130, one-shot and byte-at-a-time, against shasum/openssl digests

title: Draw the session menu's selection bar at one width for every row
description:
Wanted, in the user's words: "in the session selection menu, make the bar that shows your current selection the same width across all the entries, covering the largest width needed among the entries."

Verified (v0.5.0, src/menu.rs `Menu::render`): each selectable row is `"{mark} {key}  {text}"` and the cursor's row is written as `\x1b[7m{text}\x1b[0m`, so the reversed bar is exactly as long as that row's text. It is short on "new session" and "exit", and differs between sessions whose last `--list` column (the command) differs in length. It jumps in width as the cursor moves.

Fix: pad the cursor's row with spaces to the widest selectable row (sessions, new session, exit) currently shown, clipped at the terminal width (`cols`) as lines already are, so the bar never wraps. Measure in terminal columns rather than chars if a command can hold wide characters; `render` truncates with `chars().take(cols)` today.

Done when the reversed bar has the same width on every row, equal to the widest entry (or the terminal width if that is narrower), with a unit test next to the existing render tests in src/menu.rs asserting the padded width on a short row (exit) and a long session row.
close_reason: Implemented in PR #42 (01c9b5c): the selection bar is padded to the widest row, clipped at the terminal width, measured in columns

title: Let a fork set its release signing key at build time, as it now can the releases URL
description:
Follow-up to acs-5em (PR #153, be220ed), which made the default releases URL
settable at build time via `ACS_DEFAULT_RELEASES_URL`. The signing key did not
move with it, and the two are only useful together.

`signature::key_for(base)` returns the built-in `RELEASE_KEY` when `base ==
DEFAULT_RELEASES_URL`, and only otherwise consults `ACS_RELEASE_KEY`. So a fork
that bakes in its own releases URL and keeps acs's key **cannot verify its own
releases**: `acs upgrade` reaches the fork's SHA256SUMS and then refuses them,
because the key it checks against is upstream's. The fork's two options today
are to patch `src/signature.rs` (a merge conflict on every upstream sync — the
exact problem acs-5em removed for the URL) or to tell every user to export
`ACS_RELEASE_KEY` forever.

The mechanism to copy already exists and is one commit old: `build.rs` passes
the variable through with `cargo:rerun-if-env-changed`, `src/release.rs` has
`const fn default_releases_url(Option<&'static str>)` with an empty value
counting as unset, and `release::tests::the_default_releases_url_can_be_set_at_build_time`
is the shape of the test.

Note this is *not* a loosening of acs-95w or of acs-o9v's verification. The
runtime `ACS_RELEASE_KEY` override and its guards stay exactly as they are; a
compile-time key is chosen by whoever builds the binary, who already decides
what it does. Say so in the doc comment, as acs-5em did for the URL.

Done when the default release key can be set at build time and falls back to
today's `RELEASE_KEY` when unset, an empty value counts as unset, a test covers
both cases the way the URL's does, and the Forking table in docs/VERSIONING.md
moves the key from "source edit" to "build-time knob".
close_reason: Implemented in PR #160 (df58317): ACS_DEFAULT_RELEASE_KEY at build time, empty falls back to acs's own key, a malformed key fails the build; demonstrated against a locally signed release

title: Take the create lock in check_socket, and shorten the 60 s window that can fork a session
description: Found in review. master.rs:1181-1206 check_socket re-binds the socket after a tmpfiles deletion (DESIGN 4.1) every 60 s. If a client reconnects inside that window the proxy sees ENOENT, spawns a second master for the same name under the create lock, which binds a fresh socket and starts a new shell. The old master then finds 'socket path now belongs to something else; leaving it' (line 1185) and runs its shell unreachable forever (no socket; nothing can attach or kill it except by pid). check_socket also calls bind() (line 1196) without dir.create_lock(&self.session), unlike Master::bind (line 381) and write_statuses (proxy.rs:451), so even the microsecond race between two binds is unguarded. Done when check_socket takes the lock and connect-probes before re-binding (closing the small race), and the interval is shortened or replaced by a directory watch (the design gap); a test deletes the socket, reconnects inside the window, and asserts one shell.
close_reason: Fixed in #267 (c4d7581): .master lifetime lock + SIGUSR1 prod, locked/probed re-bind, 5 s backstop

title: Take the create lock before --list removes a stale socket
description:
`list()` (src/proxy.rs ~L317-325) removes a socket after ECONNREFUSED/ENOENT without holding `create_lock`, while master start (src/master.rs ~L304-315) does check → unlink → bind under that lock. Interleaving: list connects (refused, old stale file) → master A unlinks the stale file and binds a fresh socket → list unlinks A's *live* socket. A is unreachable for up to `rebind_every()` (60 s); any proxy in that window spawns master B; when A's `check_socket` runs it sees another inode and leaves it — A is orphaned forever with its shell still running.

Done when the refused → unlink step takes `dir.create_lock(name)` (try_lock; skip if busy), with a test for list racing a bind.
close_reason: Fixed with regression tests (bugs-master branch)

title: Copy each output byte once in the master, not four times
description: Found in review. Per output byte the master does ring.push (master.rs:1061), `[x, y].concat()` per 32 KiB chunk (1128/1280: an allocation plus a copy), encode copies again into c.out (1131), and out.drain(..n) memmoves the remainder on every partial write (289). The ring already hands back two slices. Done when the DATA header is encoded directly and x then y are extend_from_slice'd, and drain is replaced by a read cursor as Decoder already does (start); the byte-exact tests stay green.
close_reason: Landed in #337 (e6f1418): DATA encoded from the ring's two slices, out buffer written from a read cursor

title: Replace acs --list without a host by an acs list subcommand
description:
Wanted, in the user's words: "`acs --list` lists the sessions on all hosts. This is wrong: --list is an option style, not a command. It should be `acs list`. This does increase the number of reserved aliases/hosts."

Verified (v0.7.0): `acs [ssh options] --list` (or `-l`) with no host lists every alias's sessions (src/cli.rs, "Only `--list` goes without a host"; src/list.rs `run_all`; DESIGN §7.3 "Every alias at once"; README "Use"; `acs --help`). The other whole-program actions are already subcommands: `config` and `upgrade` are reserved **first** arguments (DESIGN §7.4, §7.5), and a host literally named like one is reached as `user@config` or with an option before it (`acs -p 22 config`). `list` becomes the third reserved first argument, with the same escape.

Change: `acs list` (taking the ssh options, as `acs --list` does today, e.g. `acs -p 2222 list` or `acs list -v`, whichever the parser settles on) runs today's all-alias listing (parallel, BatchMode, the HOST table). Drop the hostless `--list` outright, with no alias kept (not yet a compatibility contract; say so in the PR). Open point: whether the per-host `acs <host> --list` stays as an option (it is a modifier of a host) or moves to `acs list <host>` for symmetry. Decide and write it down in DESIGN.

Done when `acs list` lists every alias, a hostless `acs --list` is a usage error that points to `acs list`, `list` is documented as reserved with the `user@list` / option-before escape, cli.rs tests cover the parse (including a host named `list`), and DESIGN §4.4/§7.3/§7.4, the README, the module docs in cli.rs and `acs --help` are updated.
close_reason: Implemented in PR #45 (f5164ab): acs list [host] replaces the -l/--list option; list is a reserved first argument

title: Stop str::trim_end silently stripping trailing Unicode whitespace from YAML values
description: Found in review and reproduced: `acs config host add a b --identity-file $'k\xc2\xa0'` reports 'with identity_file k<nbsp>', the file holds `identity_file: k<nbsp>`, and it reads back as `k`. yaml.rs:191 raw.trim_end(), :478 t[..end].trim_end() and :677 .trim_end() use str::trim_end, which removes U+00A0, U+3000, U+2028 etc. (YAML whitespace is only space and tab), while plain_ok only refuses an ASCII trailing space, so the emitter writes the char bare and the parser eats it. Keys too: key_text("k\u{a0}") emits k. identity_file only rejects control chars (config.rs:725), which is how it reaches the CLI. Done when the parser trims only [' ', '\t'] and/or plain_ok refuses any trailing char::is_whitespace (single-quoting it), with a round-trip test for a value and a key ending in U+00A0.
close_reason: Fixed in #251: reader trims only space/tab, writer quotes values/keys with Unicode whitespace at an end

title: Automatic semantic versioning (scripts/version-bump.sh)
description: Bump the version automatically after each merge: PATCH for small fixes, MINOR for larger fixes and features, MAJOR only on explicit instruction (resets MINOR and PATCH). Reads unreleased commits since the last vX.Y.Z tag, updates Cargo.toml/Cargo.lock, pushes a chore(release) commit and tag to origin/main via a throwaway worktree. Run by the ship skill.
close_reason: cargo xtask bump + scripts/version-bump.sh: PATCH small fixes, MINOR features/larger fixes (>=300 shipped lines, Semver trailer or semver label), MAJOR only via --major (resets minor/patch); release commit + annotated tag pushed atomically from a throwaway worktree; idempotent; docs/VERSIONING.md; unit tests + end-to-end lifecycle test

title: Publish release binaries to GitHub Releases
description: Attach per-platform archives (acs-<version>-<target>.tar.gz), SHA256SUMS and install notes to a GitHub Release for each vX.Y.Z tag, built from the exact tag. scripts/release-binaries.sh does it; scripts/version-bump.sh calls it after cutting a release so shipping publishes binaries. Packaging lives in cargo xtask package (tested).
