close_reason: cargo xtask package (archives with acs + README, SHA256SUMS, NOTES.md) + scripts/release-binaries.sh (build tag in throwaway worktree, gh release create/upload) + version-bump.sh publishes new tags; tests for packaging; v0.1.0 dry run verified (checksums, macOS and Linux binaries run)

title: Configure an ssh identity file per alias and per alias host
description:
Wanted, in the user's words: "add the option to specify the SSH identity file in the configuration, either at alias level and/or at alias>host level. The identity configuration supplied through the commandline has precedent, then the one at alias>host level, followed by the alias level."

Today the identity only comes from `-i <identity_file>` on the command line (src/cli.rs, forwarded by src/ssh.rs; repeatable, ssh tries them in order) or from ~/.ssh/config. Config `hosts` entries (src/config.rs `HostEntry`, `HOST_KEYS`) accept only `host`, `user` and `reachability_check`, and an alias is just a list of entries (or one entry), so there is nowhere to put an alias-wide setting yet.

Precedence, highest first: `-i` on the command line; `identity_file` on the chosen host entry; `identity_file` on the alias. Only the winning level is passed to ssh as `-i`. It applies to every ssh call that uses the resolved destination (session, --list, install, redial).

Open design points: the YAML shape for an alias-level setting, keeping today's list form valid (for example `devbox: {identity_file: …, hosts: [...]}`); whether one level may hold several files, like repeated `-i`; `~` expansion; how global and local files merge an alias-level value (local replaces, as with other settings); and `acs config host add --identity-file` plus `config show` / `host list` output.

Done when the config validates and `acs config` edits the new key at both levels, the precedence is covered by tests, and DESIGN §7.2–7.4 and the README describe it.
close_reason: Implemented with tests: identity_file per host entry and per alias, -i > host > alias, acs config edits both (PR #30, which replaced #28)

title: tests/master.rs has its own numbers() with the trailing-torn-line bug acs-2dc just fixed
description:
acs-2dc (PR #205, 661e1dc) moved `numbers` / `assert_consecutive` /
`last_number` into `tests/common` — `tests/e2e_ssh.rs` had held a byte-identical
copy — and fixed two real faults in them: a note tearing a number, and the
snapshot itself cutting one in half (`c.text()` is a prefix of a live stream, so
its last bytes are as likely as not to be `#17` of `#175#`).

`tests/master.rs` has **its own** `numbers`, which that pass did not touch, and
it has the second fault: `split(['\r','\n'])` plus `strip_prefix('n')` happily
parses a truncated `n17` as the number 17. Same class, same consequence — a torn
number reported as lost output, which is the `174 → 17` shape acs-ryz chased and
could not explain.

It has not been seen failing, which is why this is P4 rather than P3. But it is
the last copy of a helper that has now been demonstrated wrong twice, and the
fix is known: drop a trailing fragment the snapshot may have cut, exactly as
`tests/common` now does.

Worth checking while there whether `master.rs`'s copy should simply use the
shared one. Its prefix differs (`n` rather than `#…#`), so it may need a
parameter rather than a straight substitution — decide rather than duplicating
the fix a third time.

Done when no copy of this helper can report a torn value as a gap, `master.rs`
either shares the common implementation or has a stated reason not to, and a
test covers the truncated-fragment case the way `numbers_leaves_out_what_the_snapshot_cut_in_half`
does.
close_reason: Fixed in PR #292 (9006546): tests/master.rs uses common::numbers via a #i# ticker; cut-in-half tick test added

title: ACS_ESCAPE_TIMEOUT_MS widens the double tap but not the window to choose the command key
description:
`ACS_ESCAPE_TIMEOUT_MS` widens the window *between* the two presses of the
command key. The window to then choose what to do — `d` to detach, and the
rest — is `keys::Config::command_timeout_ms`, a bare 2 s constant with no
environment knob and no config setting.

So someone who widens the escape window because 400 ms is too quick for them
has said, in effect, "I am slower than the default" — and acs answers by
widening the half of the gesture they did not complain about while leaving the
other half exactly as it was. The setting does not do what its name suggests
to the person most likely to set it.

Found during acs-ryz (PRs #194/#195), which could not remove this window: it
is the one wall-clock window left in `the_bell_rings_while_the_link_is_down_too`
and `the_escape_window_is_the_same_offline`. The test cannot merge the two
writes either, because a feed ending with the action key never leaves the
detector armed and so never rings the bell those tests are named for. Closing
it needs a `src/` change, which is why acs-ryz documented it in the tests
instead.

To settle when taking it: whether the two windows should be one setting or
two. One is simpler to explain and matches what a user means by "give me
longer"; two is more precise and lets the double tap stay tight while the
choice is relaxed. `ACS_ESCAPE_TIMEOUT_MS` is the existing name, so widening
its meaning is a behaviour change for anyone already setting it — small, since
the default is unchanged either way, but say so in DESIGN.

Done when the command-mode window follows the configured escape timeout (or
has its own knob, decided deliberately), DESIGN §6.1 says which windows the
setting covers, and the two acs-ryz tests can drop their documented wall-clock
window.
close_reason: Fixed in PR #203 (33e6fdc): ACS_ESCAPE_TIMEOUT_MS sets the gap outright and the command-key window as that value or 2s whichever is longer, so it widens both and narrows only the first. command_timeout_ms removed. Both acs-ryz wall-clock windows dropped

title: Rename the top-level hosts: configuration key to aliases:
description:
Wanted: the top-level `hosts` key is confusing, since `hosts` and `host` appear at several levels of the hierarchy. Rename it so each word means one thing.

Today (v0.8.1): the word "hosts" means two things. The top-level `hosts:` maps **alias names** (what you type: `acs devbox`) to their definitions, and inside an alias's mapping form `hosts:` is the list of host entries, the ways to reach it, tried in order. Each entry's `host:` is one address given to ssh. Everything else already says "alias": the README's "Host aliases" section, DESIGN §7.3, `-v` output and errors ("no host for 'lab' is reachable"), and `acs config host add <alias> <host>`.

Change: the top-level key becomes `aliases:`. Nothing else changes: an alias's `hosts:` list, the entry key `host:`, and `acs config host …` (it adds a host to an alias) all keep their names. The hierarchy then reads aliases → <name> → hosts → host.

```yaml
aliases:
  devbox:
    - host: devbox.lan
  lab:
    identity_file: ~/.ssh/id_lab
    hosts:
      - host: lab.lan
```

A clean break, since the project is not in production: no alias kept for the old key. A top-level `hosts:` stays an unknown key and is refused, but with a specific message so existing files are easy to fix: `<file>:<line>: 'hosts' is now 'aliases': rename the key`.

Touches: src/config.rs (`KEYS`, the parser and the `hosts` match arm), src/config_cmd.rs (host list / add / remove / set write the top-level key when rewriting the file), the `(hosts:)` hint in `acs --help` (src/cli.rs), the README example and settings table, DESIGN §7.2–7.4, and the config tests.

Done when `aliases:` is the only accepted top-level key for aliases, a file with `hosts:` fails with the rename message (tested), `acs config` edits write `aliases:`, all docs and help say `aliases:`, and scripts/verify.sh passes. The README's explanation of the two alias shapes (added by #60 for the closed bead "Explain the README's two alias shapes: a host list, or a mapping") keeps its inner `hosts:` wording, but its settings-table row for the top-level `hosts` must become `aliases`, and the example must use `aliases:`.
close_reason: Implemented in PR #63 (8fb5f72): the top-level key is aliases:; a hosts: file is refused with a rename message

title: acs list <host> reports a proxy ERROR as 'no sessions on host' with exit 0
description: Found in review. list.rs:155-232 query() has `Ok(Some(_)) => continue` for every non-STATUS frame, so a Msg::Error from `_proxy --list` (written by write_statuses' failure path, proxy.rs:412-416: unreadable socket dir, a non-refused connect error) is skipped; the proxy then exits, the client sees EOF at list.rs:226, returns Ok(Some(vec![])) and prints 'no sessions on <host>' with exit 0. The sibling reader pick::Pick::list (pick.rs:197) does record Msg::Error. Done when query treats Msg::Error as a Failure (BadReply with the message, or a new variant) with a non-zero exit and a test that makes the proxy answer ERROR; consider doing it by merging the two readers (see the listing-reader task).
close_reason: Fixed in PR #241 (7bd5a11): _proxy --list sends ERROR on failure; acs list reports it as a failure

title: A sibling session on the shared master dies when another session's link is lost
description:
Consequence of acs-9n3 (PR #184, cc1ab77), prescribed by that bead and
documented in DESIGN §7.1 — filed so it is tracked rather than only described.

When a link is lost, the redial runs `ssh -O exit` on the master the lost link
ran on. That is correct when the TCP connection itself died: the master is
holding a dead connection and everything on it is doomed anyway. It is wrong
when only *our channel* died — the master and the network are fine, and any
**other** acs session sharing that master is dropped as collateral.

The user-visible shape: two sessions to the same host, one hiccups, both
reconnect. On the second one you lose whatever you had typed, because a redial
discards typed-ahead input (§5.2). Nothing tells you why.

acs-9n3 chose the blunt version deliberately: ending the master is what
guarantees a redial gets a genuinely fresh connection rather than re-joining a
wedged one, and the wedged-master case is the one that actually strands a user.
Getting it wrong in the other direction — keeping a dead master — costs the
2s fallback on every subsequent join.

The fix is to distinguish the two, which needs the `Outcome` reason plumbed
into `connect_and_serve` so the redial knows whether the link ended because the
transport died or because the session ended/was taken over. Only the former
should end the master.

Note the blast radius is bounded by `ACS_CONTROL_PERSIST` (default 300s) and
by how many sessions a person actually runs to one host — this is a papercut,
not a stranding, which is why it is P3.

Done when a redial ends the master only when the evidence says the connection
itself failed, a sibling session on the same master survives a channel-level
loss (test it with two clients on one master), the wedged-master case still
recovers — acs-9n3's `a_master_that_does_not_answer_is_ended_and_the_dial_made_again`
must still pass — and DESIGN §7.1's note is updated to say what now happens.
close_reason: Fixed in PR #197 (bec3939): Outcome::LinkLost carries a LinkEnd reason, and the master is ended unless the loss was LinkEnd::Channel — a decode error, the one case with positive proof the connection was alive. All silence and all transport deaths stay blunt

title: Assert that an ACK arrived in input_is_acked_only_as_fast_as_the_pty_takes_it
description: Found in review. tests/master.rs:561-587: the body is a loop that asserts seq < end for any Ack it receives within 1 s. There is no assertion that at least one ACK was seen, nor a lower bound on the acked count, so a master that stopped acking entirely passes. Done when the test asserts saw_ack (and ideally that the acked count is roughly the pty buffer size), and fails against a master with acks disabled.
close_reason: Test now requires an ACK and an acked count about a pty input buffer; fails with acks disabled (PR #278)

title: Keep the hosts: line comment when host unset removes an alias's last setting
description:
config_cmd host unset (src/config_cmd.rs:781-787): when only hosts is left, `node.value = hosts.value; node.flow = hosts.flow` copies the value but not hosts.comment or hosts.before.

Scenario: file `d: # dev\n    identity_file: k\n    hosts: # the list\n      - host: a`, then `acs config host unset d identity_file` gives `d: # dev\n    - host: a`; "# the list" is gone. README and DESIGN say comments survive edits. The d: comment and the item comments are kept correctly.

Done when the comment and before-lines move with the value, with a round-trip test.
close_reason: Implemented in #93 (71f6dda)

title: reachability_tcp: give ssh -G the command line's ssh options and --ssh
description: reachability_tcp (acs-fbes, DESIGN §7.3) runs ssh -G <user@host> with ACS_SSH or ssh, but the alias is resolved without the client's transport, so a command-line -p, -F, -J or -o Port=/ProxyJump= and --ssh are not seen: acs -p 2222 devbox probes the ~/.ssh/config port and may report a reachable host as down. Pass Transport.user_opts and Transport.ssh into alias resolution (client.rs resolve_alias -> alias::resolve_remembering) and put them before the destination in the ssh -G argv. Done when a test with -p on the command line probes that port, and DESIGN §7.3 drops the 'not seen by it yet' caveat.
close_reason: Shipped in #366 (acb2d7f)

title: Ping an alias's hosts in parallel, with a configurable 0.5 s deadline
description:
Wanted: when checking which of an alias's hosts is reachable, ping them in parallel instead of one after another, and make the ping deadline configurable, defaulting to 0.5 seconds.

Verified (v0.5.0): `pick` in src/alias.rs loops over the alias's entries and pings each checked host in turn with `ping -c 1` and a fixed 2 s deadline (`ping`, src/alias.rs), stopping at the first that answers. Every host that does not answer adds up to 2 s before the next is tried: home/office/public entries where only the last answers take about 4 s to choose. It happens again on every redial (DESIGN §7.3), and nothing reachable costs 2 s × N before the error. `acs --list` with no host already runs aliases in parallel threads (src/list.rs), but each alias's hosts are still sequential.

Parallel, keeping the configured order as the priority: start every checked host's ping at once; take host k as soon as it has answered and every checked host before it has failed. A host with `reachability_check: false` still wins without a ping as soon as the hosts before it have failed. The result is exactly what the sequential loop would choose, in at most one deadline. Log lines (`-v`) and the "tried …" error keep the configured order.

Deadline: a new setting, for example `reachability_timeout` (duration or milliseconds; default 0.5 s), global and probably per alias like `identity_file`, possibly with an `ACS_*` env override. Portability: macOS `ping -t` and BusyBox `-W` take whole seconds only (macOS `-W` is per-packet milliseconds; iputils `-W` takes fractions only in newer releases). So acs should enforce the deadline itself: start `ping -c 1` with a generous own timeout, and kill and reap the child when acs's deadline passes, counting that as no answer. `ACS_PING` (the test hook) keeps working.

Done when the hosts are pinged concurrently with order-preserving selection, the deadline is configurable (validated, shown and edited by `acs config`) with a 0.5 s default, tests cover the selection order (a later host answering first must not beat an earlier host that answers within the deadline) and the timeout path, and DESIGN §7.2/§7.3 and the README describe it.
close_reason: Implemented: parallel pings with order-preserving selection and the reachability_timeout setting (default 500ms, global and per alias)

title: Fix the flaky reconnect test that makes scripts/verify.sh non-deterministic
description:
`tests/reconnect.rs::a_client_busy_with_output_answers_the_masters_ping` fails
intermittently under load:

    assertion `left == right` failed: the link was dropped
      left: 2
     right: 1

Observed 2026-09-23 during the acs-5em work (PR #153): one failure in a full
`scripts/verify.sh` run on a loaded laptop, then passing on its own immediately
afterwards and in two later full runs. The change under test was `build.rs`,
`src/release.rs` and `src/install.rs` — nothing on the reconnect path — so this
is the test, not a regression.

Why it matters more than one flaky test usually does: `scripts/verify.sh` is
this repo's *only* gate. There is no `.github/workflows` at all, so a red run
is the single signal that stops a change landing. A gate that fails at random
teaches people to re-run it until it is green, which is the same as not having
one — and it will eventually swallow a real failure.

The assertion counts dials, so the likely shape is a timing budget: the client
is deliberately busy with output, and under load the master's ping is answered
later than the deadline allows, so the client concludes the link dropped and
redials. Worth checking whether the test asserts on wall-clock at all, and
whether the timeout it depends on can be driven by the test rather than by the
machine's mood.

Done when the test no longer depends on the host's load — either the timing is
injected rather than real, or the assertion is on the behaviour rather than on
the dial count — it fails for a genuine regression on the reconnect path (show
this, e.g. by reverting the relevant guard and watching it go red), and it
passes repeatedly under artificial load (a few hundred runs, or the suite run
alongside a busy machine).
close_reason: Fixed in PR #158 (106a2c8): the test waits for 8 answered pings on one link instead of a 3s wall-clock budget; 360/360 under the load that failed 2/120 before

title: Remove the remaining wall-clock windows from tests/reconnect.rs
description:
acs-o6x (PR #158, 106a2c8) fixed one load-sensitive test in `tests/reconnect.rs`
by waiting for an observable event — 8 answered pings on one link — instead of
sleeping 3 s and asserting on a dial count. Three tests in the same file still
have the old shape, found while doing it and left alone to keep that change to
one test.

`scripts/verify.sh` is this repo's only gate (there is no `.github/workflows`),
so each of these is a way for the gate to go red at random.

1. **`keys_typed_during_a_redial_are_dropped`** — the clearest one.
   `remote.slow_dial(Some("1.5"))`, then `sleep(300ms)`, then `c.send(…)`: the
   key has to land inside a 1.5 s window that the test has already spent 300 ms
   of before it starts. `ctrl_c_during_a_redial_clears_the_status_line` solved
   exactly this under acs-kip with
   `c.wait_until("the client is in cooked mode", |c| c.echo_on(), T)`; the same
   substitution fits here and removes the window outright.
2. **`a_silent_host_is_given_up_on`** — `assert!(t0.elapsed() < Duration::from_secs(5))`
   with `t0` taken before `c.wait(T)`, so process start, the dial, the 500 ms
   dial timeout and exit all have to fit in 5 s. Tight on a loaded machine.
3. **`the_escape_window_is_the_same_offline`** — a real `sleep(1000ms)` inside a
   configured 3000 ms command-key window; 2 s of slack against a starved client.

The pattern to apply is acs-o6x's: wait for the thing the test is actually
about, so a stalled host only makes the test slower, never red. Where the
assertion really is about elapsed time (2), the question is whether it can
assert the behaviour — that the host was given up on — rather than the clock.

Done when none of the three depends on the host's load, each still goes red for
a genuine regression (show it, by breaking the guard it covers), and the file
has no remaining `sleep` that gates an assertion.
close_reason: Fixed in PR #164 (f4f2522): the redial is gated by the test rather than a 1.5s window, the silent-host clock assertion is replaced by the behaviour, and the bell's two bytes go in one write; all four proven red by breaking their guard

title: Let a host entry be preferred when several of an alias's hosts answer
description:
Wanted, in the user's words: "add functionality to a host which indicates which of the alternative is the primary one to pick if both are reachable. Something like 'prefer': true".

Verified (v0.8.1): an alias's host is chosen in src/alias.rs `pick` (DESIGN §7.3): every checked entry is pinged at once and the first entry **in configured order** that answers within `reachability_timeout` wins; an entry with `reachability_check: false` wins as soon as the entries before it have failed. The order is therefore the only way to say which host is primary, and it cannot always be set: when both files define an alias its entries concatenate, **global file first** (src/config.rs `apply`), so a user's local file cannot put its own host ahead of the global ones without redefining them.

Change: a host entry key `prefer: true` (src/config.rs `HostEntry`, `HOST_KEYS`, validated like `reachability_check`). When several entries answer, a preferred one wins over an unpreferred one; among preferred (or among unpreferred) entries the configured order still decides. So selection waits for the preferred hosts' pings up to the deadline before taking an earlier unpreferred host that answered first; with no preferred entry answering, today's order-based choice is unchanged.

Open points:
1. A preferred entry with `reachability_check: false`: it cannot answer a ping; say whether it wins outright (it is "reachable" by fiat) or is refused as a contradiction at load time.
2. Several `prefer: true` entries in one alias: allowed (order among them) or an error.

Done when `prefer` is parsed, validated and shown (`acs config show`, `acs config host list`, and settable with `acs config host add --prefer`), `-v` says a host was chosen because it is preferred, unit tests in src/alias.rs cover a preferred later host beating an earlier one that answered first, an unanswering preferred host falling back to order, and the unchecked case as decided, and DESIGN §7.2/§7.3 and the README describe it. The bead about choosing a host by the networks this machine is on also changes selection; state how the two combine if it lands first.
close_reason: Implemented in PR #56 (5dcc31f): prefer: true on host entries, tried first

title: Sign release artifacts and verify the signature before running the download
description:
Security, supply chain. SHA256SUMS and the .tar.gz are fetched from the same base URL with no signature, no attestation and no pinned key (release.rs, upgrade.rs, scripts/install.sh). Confirmed: a grep for minisign/cosign/gpg/signature/attestation over src, scripts and xtask finds nothing but a gpgsign=false line in a test. The checksum therefore proves only that the tarball matches what the same server said it should be.

Attack: anyone able to write to the GitHub release (a leaked token, a compromised account, a hostile runner) replaces both files. Every `acs upgrade` verifies happily, then EXECUTES the binary (upgrade::check_runs runs it with --version) and renames it over the destination and the ~/.local/bin and /usr/local/bin links. scripts/install.sh does the same. acs then installs that binary onto every remote host the user connects to, so it fans out.

Done when SHA256SUMS is signed with a key embedded in the binary (minisign/cosign) or GitHub artifact attestations are verified, the check runs before the downloaded binary is ever executed, the release script signs as part of publishing, and a test covers a good signature, a bad one and a missing one.
notes: PARKED 2026-09-20, blocked on a decision only the user can make. Two things are needed before the code can be written: (1) the signing scheme — neither minisign nor cosign is installed on this machine, and GitHub artifact attestations are not available because the repo has no .github/workflows and releases are published from a laptop by scripts/release-binaries.sh; ssh-keygen -Y sign/verify is present and would fit, since acs already requires ssh; (2) which key signs releases and where its private half lives. Implementing the machinery against a placeholder key would ship a verification path that verifies nothing, which is worse than none. Everything else in the bead (verify before check_runs, sign in the release script, tests for a good, bad and missing signature) is mechanical once those are settled.
close_reason: Implemented in #140 (v0.12.0): SHA256SUMS signed with ssh-keygen -Y, checked before the sums are read

title: A local_forwards setting, global and per alias, so a host can always forward its port
description:
Step 5 of acs-6f5, deliberately left out of PR #155 (27cbc1e) because it is a
differently-shaped change from the command-line flag and would have doubled
that PR.

`acs -L 8080:localhost:80 box` is now the way to forward a port, and it has to
be retyped every time. The motivating case is standing, not ad hoc: "this host
always needs its database forwarded". That belongs in the config beside the
other per-host facts, the way `identity_file` (acs-mbd) and `local_networks`
(acs-9yv) already do.

`local_networks` is the exact precedent to copy, and the work is mechanical:
a `Config` field, an `Option` field on `Alias`, an entry in `KEYS` and in
`ALIAS_KEYS`, a type const beside `NETWORKS`, a `*_for(alias)` accessor, and a
branch in `config_cmd::typed`.

Two things to decide when taking it, rather than by omission:

- **Do command-line `-L` and the setting merge, or does the flag replace the
  list?** Merging matches how ssh treats repeated `-L`, and matches the flag
  already being repeatable; replacing gives a way to suppress a configured
  forward. Merging is probably right, with a documented way to say "none".
- **Validation happens at config-read time**, not at dial time. `-L` is checked
  before any ssh is spawned (`ssh::check_local_forward`); a bad spec in the
  config should be a normal config error naming the line, not an ssh stderr
  line mid-reconnect. Reuse the same checker.

The `Call::Session` gating from acs-6f5 applies unchanged: a configured forward
must reach the session ssh only, never the `Call::Side` and `Call::Batch` calls,
or several children fight over the same local port.

Done when `local_forwards` can be set globally and per alias, is validated when
the config is read with an error naming the offending line, is applied only to
the session ssh, merges with (or explicitly overrides) command-line `-L` as
decided above, has tests covering the config round-trip and the three `Call`
kinds, and is documented in README and DESIGN §7.1 and §7.4 alongside `-L`.
close_reason: Implemented in PR #216 (6397057): local_forwards global and per alias, merging with command-line -L, validated at config-read time through ssh::check_local_forward. Both invariants tested — the Call::Session gate and acs-9n3's master veto, the latter proven red by reordering

title: Make the master ping its client so a vanished client stops blocking the pty
description:
DESIGN §5.3 says each side sends PING after 3 s of silence, but src/master.rs only ever answers with Pong (master.rs:632): no timer, no Ping, and an Active conn is only dropped on read EOF/error (master.rs:553-567) or takeover. The client ignores an incoming Ping too (client.rs:853, the "other =>" arm). Backpressure is applied against the Active conn (master.rs:416-422, 833-846): once room_before_overwrite is 0 the pty is no longer read.

Scenario: laptop lid closed and powered off, no FIN reaches the host. sshd keeps the TCP session for the keepalive period (2 h by default, ClientAliveInterval 0), so proxy and Active conn live on. A build or tail -f in the session stalls after 1 MiB of output until the next attach takes over. §4.2 says a detached program never blocks, but the master cannot tell "detached" from "dead client".

Done when the master pings after 3 s of silence, the client answers, the master drops a conn silent for 10 s (freeing the pty), and a test covers a client that stops reading without closing.
close_reason: Implemented in #68 (b3e517f)

title: Test build.rs's release-key validation, which no test target covers
description:
acs-ktm (#160, df58317) added `build.rs::check_release_key`, which rejects a
malformed `ACS_DEFAULT_RELEASE_KEY` by failing the build: it requires one line,
a key type starting `ssh-`/`ecdsa-`/`sk-`, and a base64 body of at least 16
characters. The multi-line rejection is the load-bearing one — a value with an
embedded newline would write a second allowed-signers line, which nobody means,
and would corrupt the `cargo:rustc-env=` directive as well.

None of it is covered by a test. Build scripts are not a test target, so its
branches were exercised only by a by-hand `cargo build` during that pass, and
the evidence is a paragraph in the PR rather than something that runs again.
The validation can therefore rot silently: a later edit that loosens it, or a
refactor that stops calling it, breaks nothing any suite would notice.

The obvious shape is an integration test that shells out to `cargo build` with
a bad key and a throwaway `--target-dir`, asserting the build fails and the
message names the variable. The cost is honesty about runtime: that is a slow
test, and it would want to be behind the same arrangement as anything else
expensive in this suite. An alternative worth weighing first is moving
`check_release_key` into a tiny module that both `build.rs` and a unit test can
include, so the logic is tested at unit speed and only the wiring stays
untested — `build.rs` already has the precedent of emitting `ACS_TARGET`.

Done when each branch of the key validation is covered by a test that runs in
`scripts/verify.sh` (empty, single well-formed key, wrong type, short body,
embedded newline), the test fails if the validation is removed — show this —
and whichever approach is taken, the by-hand paragraph is no longer the only
record that the check works.
close_reason: Done in PR #212 (9ce69b0): the whole decision moved to src/release_key.rs, include!d by build.rs and compiled under cfg(test) by the crate, so all five branches are unit-tested. Empty was in main() not the check, so extracting the check alone would have left that branch untested

title: Send Ctrl-L on reconnect to refresh the screen, configurable per alias
description:
Wanted, in the user's words: "when reconnecting to a session, send a Ctrl-L to refresh the screen first thing, unless disabled in the configuration, globally or per alias."

Today (DESIGN §5.2, §5.4): a fresh attach or a resume gap clears the local screen and the master SIGWINCHes the foreground group (src/master.rs `resize(.., force_redraw)`); a lossless resume redraws nothing unless a status line was shown while offline, and then the client sends two RESIZE frames (src/reconnect.rs `on_welcome`). Nothing sends Ctrl-L. Ctrl-L (0x0c) is input to the program, not a terminal operation: shells and most TUIs repaint on it, but a program reading raw input receives a form feed. That is why the off switch matters.

Config: a global boolean (for example `redraw_on_reconnect`, default true, next to `command_bell` in `KEYS`/`BOOLS` in src/config.rs) and the same key on an alias (`ALIAS_KEYS`, the alias-mapping form that `identity_file` introduced). The alias value wins over the global one. Probably also an `ACS_*` env override, as `ACS_COMMAND_BELL` has.

Open points: whether "reconnecting" means the automatic resume after a drop, a re-attach by a new client (`acs host session`), or both; how it sits with the existing SIGWINCH / double-RESIZE redraw (replace it or add to it); and sending it right after WELCOME as INPUT, so it goes through the resend/ACK path and is never typed twice.

Done when the client sends Ctrl-L after reconnecting unless disabled, both config levels validate and `acs config` shows and edits them, tests cover the precedence and the on/off cases, and DESIGN §5.2/§5.4/§7.2 and the README describe it.
close_reason: Implemented with tests: Ctrl-L on any attach to an existing session, after resent input, never into an open paste; redraw_on_reconnect global and per alias, ACS_REDRAW_ON_RECONNECT (PR #32)

title: A silent host is redialled back-to-back: a timed-out redial resets the backoff
description: Found in review (2026-10-27). reconnect.rs:114 takes `started` at the top of the loop, before the dial; reconnect.rs:185 resets the backoff when `started.elapsed() >= 30 s`. The redial dial timeout (client.rs:639, answer_timeout(true)) is also 30 s, so a redial into a host that accepts TCP but never prints the marker or never WELCOMEs returns LinkLost after >= 30 s, the backoff resets, step() yields 0 and the next 30 s dial starts at once. The backoff never climbs while the host stays silent, and keys typed into a dial are dropped (acs-qty), so there is never an offline wait where the command keys work, contrary to DESIGN 5. Only the persist && pingable path escapes. acs-iyq made the first redial immediate and said later ones keep the backoff; this defeats that. tests/reconnect.rs a_redial_into_a_silent_host_returns_to_the_backoff sets ACS_DIAL_TIMEOUT_MS=10000, below the threshold, so it cannot see it. Done when the 'connection lasted' test measures served time (WELCOME to loss), a dial that took its full timeout with no WELCOME does not reset the backoff, and a test with the dial timeout at or above the threshold shows the backoff climbing.
close_reason: Fixed in #232: the backoff reset counts served time from the WELCOME, so a silent redial no longer resets it

title: Guard against tcgetpgrp returning 0 so hard_kill cannot kill the master
description:
Linux `tiocgpgrp` on a pty *master* fd returns `pid_vnr(real_tty->ctrl.pgrp)`, which is 0 when the slave has no foreground group (after TIOCNOTTY, after a hangup, or during the leader's exit between `disassociate_ctty()` and reaping). `hard_kill` (src/master.rs ~L886-888) only filters `p != ch.pid`, so `kill(-0, SIGKILL)` == `kill(0, SIGKILL)` signals the master's own process group — the master is a session leader after setsid, so it dies and takes the user's session with it. `start_kill` (~L871) and `resize` (~L772) hit the same value harmlessly. Rare (child ignores SIGHUP and dropped its ctty, or exits at the 3 s deadline) but the consequence is total.

Done when every tcgetpgrp result is filtered with `p > 0`, with a unit test on the filter.
close_reason: Fixed with regression tests (bugs-master branch)

title: Stop trusting the self-asserted identity and record attaches, takeovers and kills
description:
Security, impersonation and no audit trail. client.rs takes the identity from ACS_IDENTITY with no validation beyond non-empty, and the master compares it as a string to decide whether a takeover is the same person's second terminal. Verified by reading both.

Attack, inside the one-account model DESIGN §4.5 describes: person B sets ACS_IDENTITY=alice@laptop and the master treats B's attach as alice's own, taking over SILENTLY with no prompt, while acs list's WHO column and every BUSY message name alice. Sending an EMPTY identity is worse: the takeover comparison short-circuits on non-empty, so while B is attached anyone takes over silently and WHO shows a dash, leaving no mark at all. The only record is an mlog! that writes nothing unless ACS_MASTER_LOG is set, and last_identity is overwritten rather than appended to.

The design accepts no security boundary here, but it does claim the identity mechanism prevents accidents, and it does not survive even trivial intent. Follows acs-5v9.18, which built the mechanism.

Done when an empty identity cannot suppress the takeover prompt, the identity is bounded and control-free, and every attach, takeover and kill is appended unconditionally to a per-session record with the peer uid and pid, so the shared-account model has a trace even without a boundary. Tests for the empty-identity path and the trail.
close_reason: Implemented in #129: an empty identity matches nothing, and every attach/takeover/kill is recorded

title: Verify SHA256SUMS.sig before update-tap.sh vX.Y.Z renders the formula from it
description: Found in review. scripts/update-tap.sh vX.Y.Z does `curl -fsSL -o .../SHA256SUMS` then `cargo xtask formula` with no .sig check. The normal path (release-binaries.sh) renders from the file it just built, so only the retry path is affected, but Homebrew users never see the signature, so the tap is where a tampered release would be laundered into pinned sha256s. Done when the script runs ssh-keygen -Y verify against RELEASE_KEY as install.sh does, and refuses otherwise.
close_reason: Landed in #313: update-tap.sh vX.Y.Z verifies SHA256SUMS.sig against the build's release key (cargo xtask channel) before rendering

title: ACS_DIAL_TIMEOUT_MS sets the first connection and the redial deadline together
description:
The defaults differ 4:1 for a stated reason — **120 s** for a first connection
(which may prompt for a passphrase, touch a hardware key, or install acs on the
remote) against **30 s** for a redial (which should give up and back off). But
`ACS_DIAL_TIMEOUT_MS` sets both, so anything that shortens one shortens the
other.

The consequence acs-ryz hit: a test that wants a short *redial* deadline must
also shorten the *first* dial, and the first dial is the one that has the most
work to do. That is the residual window in
`a_redial_into_a_silent_host_returns_to_the_backoff`, which acs-ryz could only
widen (4 s to 10 s) rather than remove, and which still failed 9 times in 63 at
extreme load.

It is not only a test problem, though that is where it shows. A user who
shortens the dial timeout because their redials hang too long also shortens the
window their first connection has to accept a hardware-key touch — which is the
one dial that genuinely needs a human.

Two candidate fixes: honour the same 4:1 ratio when the variable is set, so one
knob keeps its meaning for both; or add a second knob and let the variable set
only the first dial. The ratio is less to explain and cannot be set
inconsistently; two knobs are more honest about there being two things.

Done when shortening the redial deadline does not shorten the first
connection's, whichever way it is spelled, the README environment table and
DESIGN agree, and `a_redial_into_a_silent_host_returns_to_the_backoff` can use
a short redial deadline without giving its first dial an unrealistic one.
close_reason: Landed in #358 (b3648224): ACS_REDIAL_TIMEOUT_MS is its own knob; ACS_DIAL_TIMEOUT_MS sets only the first connection and the acs list batch limit

title: acs's own writes to the terminal can land inside a sequence the program left open
description:
acs-z22 (PR #201, da1368c) held `-v` notes to a boundary of the program's
stream. Three of acs's **own** writes to the terminal have the same hazard and
no boundary check:

- `reconnect::show_status` / `clear_status` — the bottom-row status line;
- `client::leave`'s `observer.reset_sequence()`;
- the `\x1b[H\x1b[J` a Fresh or Gap attach writes.

The window is narrower than acs-z22's but real, and the status line is the
worst of the three: it goes up **after a link is lost**, and the decoder only
delivers whole frames — the one that was cut is discarded, and the last one it
did deliver may well end mid-CSI or mid-OSC. So the explanation the frozen
terminal is owed can itself be what corrupts it.

**Why this is not simply acs-z22 applied again, and is the harder problem:** a
note can wait, and acs-z22's whole fix is waiting. A status line cannot — it
exists to explain a terminal that has just stopped responding, and holding it
for a boundary that may never come is the opposite of what it is for.

That leaves aborting the program's unfinished sequence first (`ESC \`), which
is a real design decision rather than a mechanism: it throws away the bytes
that would have completed the sequence. And note what happens next — a
`Resumed` attach really does deliver the rest of that sequence afterwards, so
aborting turns the remainder into printed junk on screen. Doing nothing leaves
a corrupted sequence; aborting leaves visible garbage. Neither is obviously
right, which is why acs-z22 documented the hazard in DESIGN §7 rather than
guessing.

Things that might make it tractable: the observer already knows *what kind* of
sequence is open, so a CSI could be closed differently from an OSC; and the
status line's `ESC 7` / `ESC 8` save-restore may already limit the damage for
some sequence kinds — check before assuming it does not.

Done when acs's own terminal writes cannot corrupt a sequence the program left
open, or the decision to accept it is recorded in DESIGN with the reasoning and
the cases where it shows; either way a test should demonstrate what a status
line drawn mid-sequence actually does to the screen today.
close_reason: Fixed in PR #210 (ad04421): acs ends the program's open sequence before its own write and hands it back after, per kind — CSI, bare ESC and partial UTF-8 replayed exactly; OSC/DCS/APC ended but not replayed because the body may already have acted. leave and the attach clears end only; the signal handler opens with an unconditional ST

title: Say that no configuration file exists when acs list finds none
description:
Wanted: when there is no acs configuration at all, `acs list` should say so, instead of the message for a configuration without aliases.

Verified (v0.8.0, installed binary with throwaway XDG_CONFIG_HOME / ACS_GLOBAL_CONFIG): with no config files, with an empty file, and with an empty `hosts:`, `acs list` prints the same line and exits 2 without dialling: "acs: no host aliases in the configuration: list one host with acs list <host>, or add an alias with acs config host add <alias> <host>". Both paths use it: src/list.rs `run_all` (piped table) and src/pick.rs `every_host` (terminal menu), via `list::NO_ALIASES`. With no files the wording is misleading, since there is no "the configuration".

Change: when no configuration file exists (`Config.files` is empty; `config::global_path()` is /etc/acs/config.yaml or `ACS_GLOBAL_CONFIG`, `config::local_path()` is `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/acs/config.yaml` or ~/.config/acs/config.yaml), print a distinct message naming both paths it looked in, with the same hints, e.g. "acs: no configuration (looked for /etc/acs/config.yaml and ~/.config/acs/config.yaml): list one host with acs list <host>, or add an alias with acs config host add <alias> <host>". Keep today's message when a file exists but defines no aliases. The exit code stays 2 (usage) in both cases, and both the table and the menu path use the new message.

Done when the two cases print their own messages from both paths, with unit or integration tests for no files vs. a file with no aliases (tests/ already sets ACS_GLOBAL_CONFIG and XDG_CONFIG_HOME for config tests), and DESIGN §7.3 ("Every alias at once") mentions the no-configuration case.
close_reason: Implemented in PR #52 (a418b49): acs list names the files it looked for when there is no configuration

title: Report per-phase connect timings under -v
description:
Measure before optimising connect latency. Under -v, print how long each phase of a connection took: alias resolved (pings, lookups), ssh spawned, ACS-READY marker seen, WELCOME received, first output byte. Applies to the first connection, the menu path (_proxy --pick) and every redial. Today -v shows none of this, so it is unknown whether the ssh handshake, remote startup files or the reachability deadline dominates on real hosts.
Touches client.rs (dial, serve), pick.rs, reconnect.rs. Done when -v prints one timing line per phase and a test asserts the lines appear in order.
close_reason: Landed in #172: -v prints one timing line per connect phase (alias resolved, ssh spawned, ACS-READY seen, session list received, WELCOME received, first output byte) for the first connection, the menu path and every redial; tests/timing.rs asserts the order.

title: Fix flaky acs_list_in_a_terminal_ends_and_creates_on_the_rows_host in tests/menu.rs
description:
The `tests/menu.rs` integration test `acs_list_in_a_terminal_ends_and_creates_on_the_rows_host`
failed once in a full `cargo test --workspace` run: after sending `n` on nas's row,
`e.nas.session_exists("1")` was false and the screen had fallen back to the menu header
("\x1b[Hacs: detached sessions on every host").

It passes in isolation (3/3) and the full suite went green on rerun, so this is timing-
dependent. The test sequences on explicit `std::thread::sleep` calls (20ms/200ms in the
same file) and on a race in which "the cursor follows whichever host answered first"
(the comment on the `> 1  nas` cursor assertion).

Fix: make the menu interaction deterministic in the test — deadline-based waits /
harness coordination instead of sleeps, and/or deterministic fake-host answer ordering.
If the failure is a real race in the menu code rather than the test, fix that instead;
capture the full screen bytes from a failing run for the diff.
close_reason: Implemented in #101 (2dd175d)

title: Let scripts/test_linux.sh run one test file instead of the whole suite
description:
`scripts/test_linux.sh` runs everything: the full suite, the multiuser pass as
root, and now the netns pass under CAP_NET_ADMIN. There is no way to run one
test file.

That matters because the script is now the **only** place three things are
exercised at all — Linux `ls` behaviour in the prelude (acs-gov), the
root-populated system-wide install (acs-6w9), and the kernel netlink watcher
(acs-4i2). Anyone debugging one of those pays the whole suite per iteration.

The acs-4i2 pass hand-reconstructed the script's `docker run` to iterate on
`tests/netns.rs`, including re-deriving the `cksum`-based target-volume name.
That is both slow and a good way to accidentally run with different flags from
the real thing and draw a wrong conclusion.

A pass-through argument — `scripts/test_linux.sh --only netns`, or simply
forwarding extra arguments to the inner `cargo test` — would cover it. Points
to settle: whether `--only` should also skip the image build and volume setup
when they are already current (the acs-gb4 staleness stamp is the precedent
for doing that honestly), and whether the privileged passes stay opt-in by
env var as they are now.

Small and purely developer-facing, hence P4 — but it is paid by every person
who touches the three things only this script covers.
close_reason: Landed in PR #298 (5bd1b93): scripts/test_linux.sh --only NAME [-- ARGS] runs one test target with the full run's container, volumes and flags

title: Create the config temp file 0600 and bound YAML nesting depth
description:
Security, two small local issues in config handling, filed together because they share the config path (say so if they want splitting).

config_cmd::write creates its temp file with std::fs::write, so it lands at the process umask (typically 0644) in the config directory and only then copies the real file's permissions onto it. If the config file does not exist yet, the new file keeps 0644 permanently. The content is host names, login names and identity_file paths: not secrets, but a private host inventory on a shared machine.

yaml.rs Flow::value and block_node/seq/map recurse with no depth limit, so a config with a few thousand nested brackets, which fits on one line, overflows the stack. With panic = abort in the release profile that is an immediate abort rather than an error.

Done when the temp file is created 0600 before any content is written and widened only to match an existing file, the parser rejects nesting past a fixed depth with a normal config error, and both have tests.
close_reason: Implemented in #133: config created 0600, and both parsers bounded at 64 deep

title: Pass -t 1 to the wget fallback in release::fetch
description: Found in review. release.rs:303-311 passes -T <secs> but not -t 1; wget's default is 20 tries, so the '3 s' background update check can hold a connection-refused mirror for ~60 s and the upgrade for up to 100 min on a stalling server. Done when the wget fallback tries once, with the argument asserted in the fetch tests.
close_reason: Landed in #354 (49e1e00): wget -t 1, curl --retry 0, asserted in release tests

title: Write acs config edits through a symlinked config instead of replacing the link
description:
config_cmd::write() (src/config_cmd.rs:1014-1025) writes a temp file and renames it over the path. read_doc follows a symlink, but rename replaces the link itself.

Scenario: ~/.config/acs/config.yaml -> ~/dotfiles/acs.yaml (stow, chezmoi). `acs config set update_check false` reports success; afterwards config.yaml is a regular file with the new content and ~/dotfiles/acs.yaml still says update_check: true. Same for a hard link: the other name keeps the old content. DESIGN §7.4 promises "replaces the file (atomically, keeping its mode)".

Done when write resolves the path (fs::canonicalize) before the temp-and-rename, and a test edits a symlinked config and asserts the target changed and the link survived.
close_reason: Implemented in #75 (5251a06)

title: Fix payload install failing when the login shell prints to stdout
description:
Step 1 of the payload install plan (`gzip -dc > tmp`, src/install.rs ~L114) prints nothing, and `side_call` (src/install.rs ~L150) errors with "unexpected reply while installing" whenever stdout is non-empty and no line is exactly `ok`. Any `.bashrc` echo or motd script that writes to stdout for non-interactive sessions — the very noise the ACS-READY marker was designed to tolerate (DESIGN §3) — therefore fails the macOS → Linux self-install after the upload succeeded, leaving `acs.new.<token>` behind. The self-copy path only passes because the finisher happens to print `ok`.

Done when the upload step is judged on exit status alone (or prints its own marker) and tests/install.rs has a case with a chatty login shell.
close_reason: Fixed with regression tests (bugs-install branch)

title: Under -v, log why each of an alias's hosts was not chosen
description:
User's words: "when verbose mode is selected '-v' log why a particular host is not selected as a target for the alias".

Today `-v` explains the **winner** and nothing else. `alias::pick` logs why the chosen entry was chosen, but most of the losing entries produce no line at all, so from the output you cannot tell whether a host was beaten, skipped, or never considered.

## What is logged now (v0.13.0)

`client::resolve_alias` (src/client.rs:192) passes a `log` closure into `alias::resolve`, printed as `acs: …` notes when `-v` is given. The lines it can emit, all in `src/alias.rs`:

- `:66` `<alias>: logging in as <u>, from the command line`
- `:168` `<alias>: <host> is on the local network <net>` (`prefer_local_network`)
- `:170` `<alias>: this machine is on <net>, so <host> is local` (`local_networks`, acs-9yv)
- `:195` `<alias>: using <dest> (reachability_check is off, …)`
- `:211` `<alias>: <host> answers ping, using <dest> (…)`
- `:217` `<alias>: <host> does not answer ping within <timeout>`
- the error `no host for '<alias>' is reachable (tried a, b, c)`

So exactly **one** "why not" line exists — `does not answer ping` — and it only covers entries tried *before* the winner.

## The three silences

1. **Everything ranked after the winner.** The trial loop (`src/alias.rs:180`) returns as soon as a host is taken (`:196`, `:215`). Entries ranked below it are never visited, so they are never mentioned. With four hosts where the first answers, `-v` says nothing at all about the other three — a host missing from the output looks identical to a host that is not configured.

2. **Entries pruned before any ping.** `candidates` (`src/alias.rs:131`) truncates the order at the first entry with `reachability_check: false`, because nothing after an unchecked host can ever be chosen. Those entries are not pinged and not logged. This is the most confusing case: the host is configured, reachable, and silently unreachable-by-construction.

3. **Why an entry ranked where it did.** Rank is local, then `prefer`, then configured order. `-v` says why a host *is* local or preferred, never why it is not — there is no line for "on no local network", "not preferred", or "listed third".

## Wanted

Under `-v`, every entry of the alias accounts for itself: taken, beaten, not answering, or never eligible — with the reason. Roughly:

    devbox: devbox.lan does not answer ping within 500ms
    devbox: devbox.vpn answers ping, using devbox.vpn (preferred)
    devbox: devbox.example.com not tried: devbox.vpn was chosen first
    devbox: nas.lan not tried: it is listed after devbox.old, whose
            reachability_check is off

Scope decisions for whoever takes it:

- **Where the lines come from.** The pruned set is known at `candidates`, before any ping; the "chosen first" set is known only once the loop returns. Emitting both means either logging after the choice (one pass over `order`, easy) or threading the reason out of `candidates`. The first is likely simpler and keeps the configured order in the output, which the existing lines already preserve.
- **Ordering.** Today's lines come out in rank order as the loop walks. Adding the untried ones at the end keeps that; interleaving them in configured order reads better. Pick one and say so.
- **`-v` vs `-vv`.** `args.verbose` is a `u8` and `-v` is repeatable (src/cli.rs:181), but nothing currently distinguishes the levels — `let verbose = args.verbose > 0` (src/client.rs:193). Per-host "not tried" detail is a plausible first use of `-vv` if the single-level output gets noisy for a long alias. Decide rather than default into it.
- **Does the failure path change?** When nothing answers, every entry is already tried and logged, and the error names them (`tried a, b, c`). That path is fine; this is about the success path.

## Done when

`acs -v <alias>` accounts for every entry of the alias — one line each, naming the entry and why it was not used — including the entries ranked after the chosen one and the entries pruned for sitting behind a `reachability_check: false` host. Unit tests in `src/alias.rs` assert the full log for at least: a winner with hosts ranked after it, an alias pruned by an unchecked entry, and the existing no-host-answers path (unchanged). README's `-v` line and DESIGN §7.3 describe what the output now covers.

Extends acs-sia and acs-9yv (which added the locality lines this builds on).
close_reason: Implemented in PR #151 (2ca89da): under -v every entry of an alias accounts for itself

title: Accept a tab after a YAML key and strip a UTF-8 BOM in the config parser
description:
yaml::split_key (src/yaml.rs:379) only accepts a colon followed by a space or end of line; YAML 1.2 also allows a tab. `install_on_remote:<TAB>false` is not recognised as a key, block_node (yaml.rs:245-264) returns a root scalar, and config.rs:288-296 reports "config.yaml:1: expected settings as 'key: value' lines, found a single value", pointing nowhere near the tab. The parser detects tab indentation (yaml.rs:170-172) but not this. Related: a UTF-8 BOM is not stripped (yaml.rs:166-173), giving "unknown setting '\u{feff}install_on_remote'" for a file every other YAML reader accepts.

Done when a tab after the colon separates the key, a leading BOM is skipped, and tests cover both.
close_reason: Implemented in #91 (bca5b96)

title: Pop the title stack and status line when the session ends during an outage
description:
After a link drop, `offline()` (src/reconnect.rs ~L207-219) draws the bottom status row and pushes the xterm title (`CSI 22;0 t`), setting `status_shown`. The pop (`clear_status`) only runs from `on_welcome` and the offline Detach path. If the redial gets `Error{NO_SESSION}`, `Exit`, or `Takeover` before any WELCOME (src/client.rs ~L487-529), `serve` returns and `run()` calls only `leave()` (~L301), which never pops. The terminal keeps the "acs: host — connection lost" title and the inverse-video status row after acs exits — a DESIGN §5.4 violation. tests/reconnect.rs only covers the detach-while-down path.

Done when `leave()` (or those return paths) calls `clear_status` whenever `status_shown`, with a test for session-end-during-outage.
close_reason: Fixed with regression tests (bugs-client branch)

title: Drop keys typed during a redial instead of echoing and delivering them
description:
The client suspends raw mode before every dial (src/client.rs:576-578) so ssh can prompt. RawMode::suspend/resume (src/tty.rs:112-126) use sys::tcsetattr = TCSADRAIN (sys.rs:246-249), which never discards pending input. In cooked mode ICANON+ECHO are on: anything typed during the dial (ConnectTimeout plus auth, up to 30 s on a redial) is echoed at the cursor, corrupting a screen a lossless resume will not repaint, and sits in the canonical line buffer; when RawMode::resume() runs on WELCOME that line becomes readable and queue_input sends it to the program. reconnect::offline drops keys during the wait, but the dial phase does not. ISIG is also on, so Ctrl-C during the dial kills the client via tty::on_fatal, restoring termios but not popping the title stack or blanking the status row.

Contradicts DESIGN §5.2 "keys typed while the client knows the link is down are dropped".

Done when a redial only leaves raw mode when ssh really needs the tty (or resumes with TCSAFLUSH and discards typed-ahead), Ctrl-C during a dial cleans up the status line, and a test feeds input during a redial and asserts none reaches the pty.
close_reason: Implemented in #70 (abf94e8)

title: List the timer knobs somewhere, and stop the netwatch tests reading the environment
description:
Two small pieces of hygiene from acs-0n8 (PR #199, 491c637).

**1. There are now six undocumented timer knobs and no list of them.**
`ACS_BACKOFF_MS`, `ACS_PING_MS`, `ACS_DEAD_MS`, `ACS_NETCHECK_MS`,
`ACS_DIAL_TIMEOUT_MS` and now `ACS_EARLY_MS`. None is in the README environment
table — deliberately, since they are internal — but there is also no single
place that names them together, so the only way to find them is to grep for
`env_ms`. Each new bead adds one and nobody can see the set.

A short table in DESIGN §5.3 would do it: name, default, what it bounds. That
also makes the interactions visible, which matter — acs-p46 records that
`ACS_DIAL_TIMEOUT_MS` sets two deadlines that differ 4:1 by default, and that is
exactly the kind of thing a table surfaces and prose hides.

**2. The netwatch unit tests set process-wide environment variables.**
`ACS_NETWATCH_NETS` is read from the environment by a function called deep
inside the library, so two tests in the same binary can race each other. acs-0n8
added a `STANDIN` mutex and a `Standin` helper so its own two tests cannot, but
the hazard stays armed for the next test anyone adds to that binary — and a
mutex is a reminder, not a fix.

Taking the network source as a field on the watcher, rather than reading it from
the environment at the point of use, removes the class. The env var stays as the
way to set it; only the reading moves to construction.

Done when the timer knobs are listed in one place with their defaults and what
each bounds, and a netwatch test can set its network source without a mutex
because the source is no longer process-wide state.
notes:
Two more surfaces for the same problem, from acs-mq0 (PR #203, 33e6fdc).

**1. `acs --help` understates what is configurable.** `src/cli.rs`'s help text
lists four environment variables — `ACS_DEFAULT_SESSION`, `ACS_IDENTITY`,
`ACS_ESCAPE_KEY`, `ACS_ESCAPE_TIMEOUT_MS` — while the README documents about
twenty and several more exist only in tests. This is a distinct surface from
the timer-knob list this bead is about: the docs being incomplete is one
problem, the *program's own help* being incomplete is another, and the help is
what someone reads first. Worth deciding whether help should list everything,
list a category, or point at the README.

**2. `PENDING_MS` (100 ms) in `src/keys.rs`** — how long an incomplete escape
sequence is held before being released as typed — is another bare constant of
the same shape. Noted for completeness only: it is local-stdin only, so no link
latency reaches it, and the acs-mq0 pass found nothing wrong with the value.
Include it in the table if one is written; it does not need a knob.

Note acs-mq0 deliberately did **not** add a seventh knob, on the strength of
this bead: it made one existing setting cover both halves of the gesture rather
than introducing `ACS_COMMAND_TIMEOUT_MS`. That is the precedent worth keeping
— the table this bead asks for is partly so the next person can see the cost of
adding one.
close_reason: Completed in PR #299 (bc75d88): timer-knob table in DESIGN 5.3 with tests/knobs.rs guarding it; netwatch reads its stand-ins once in new() and tests pass them in. The notes' acs --help point (cli.rs) is not addressed.

title: Restore the terminal title after a reconnect succeeds
description:
User report: when the connection is lost, acs changes the terminal title to "acs - <alias> - connection lost - reconnecting..." — but once the connection is recovered it never restores the title to what it was (if possible), or at least removes the "connection lost - reconnecting" part.

What the code does today: `show_status` (src/reconnect.rs ~L437) pushes the title on the xterm title stack (`CSI 22;0 t`) once, then sets `OSC 2 "acs: <host> — <msg>"`; `clear_status` (~L456), called from `on_welcome` after a resume, pops it with `CSI 23;0 t` (DESIGN §5.4). So restoration relies entirely on the terminal supporting XTWINOPS title push/pop. Terminals that ignore 22/23 (e.g. macOS Terminal.app, among others) keep acs's "connection lost" title forever — the likely cause. Worth confirming on the user's terminal first, and checking that the WELCOME path really reaches `clear_status` in every resume/re-attach variant (fresh attach after `instance` is lost, persist mode, network-changed redial).

Suggested fix: have the output observer (src/modes.rs, which already parses OSC strings) remember the last OSC 0/2 title the remote program set; on recovery, after the pop, re-emit that title explicitly — or, if none was ever seen, set a neutral one (e.g. "acs: <host>") rather than leaving the outage text. The pop stays for terminals that honour the stack.

Done when: after a successful reconnect the title is either the program's last title or at least no longer says "connection lost", on terminals without title-stack support; a test drives drop → reconnect and asserts the bytes written include the restored title after `CSI 23;0 t`; DESIGN §5.4 updated to describe the fallback.
close_reason: Fixed in #227 (ff95723): title restored explicitly after the pop on reconnect

title: Cap remote-driven buffers so a hostile host cannot exhaust client memory
description:
Security, denial of service. Three client buffers grow on remote data with no ceiling. proto.rs MarkerScanner::push bounds noise at 64 KiB but only drains buf when a newline was seen, so output containing NO newline grows without limit for the whole dial window (120 s on a first connection, 30 s on a redial) and re-scans the unfinished line on every read, which is also quadratic. install.rs side_call reads the remote's stdout to the end with no cap and no deadline. list.rs and pick.rs accumulate STATUS_REPLY frames in a Vec with no cap on count or total bytes, each up to the 1 MiB frame limit.

MAX_FRAME bounds one frame, not the stream. A malicious or merely broken remote can drive the client to OOM, gigabytes on a fast link.

Done when each of the three has a byte cap that ends the operation with a clear error, and tests drive each past its cap.
close_reason: Implemented in #119: scanner line cap, install reply cap, listing session cap

title: Do not print 'the session keeps running' when no session ever existed
description: Found in review. reconnect.rs:155-165: a first (non-persisting, non-picked) connection that passes the marker and then gets EOF before WELCOME (client.rs:1675) reaches the branch with state.instance.is_none() && !persist and prints 'connection lost - the session keeps running; reattach with: acs host <name>' (name is empty for --new) and exits 255. The picked path dodges this via :149-152, the dial-failure path via client.rs:1136-1142. Cosmetic but misleading. Done when the wording branches on state.instance (and the reattach hint has one home, see the client duplicates task).
close_reason: Fixed in #315 (ad7d534): a link lost before WELCOME says 'connection to <host> lost before the session started', exit 255; regression test a_link_lost_before_the_welcome_claims_no_session

title: Only prune version directories under $HOME/.local/share/acs
description:
`versions_root()` (src/prune.rs ~L31-38) is `parent(parent(current_exe))` whenever the parent dir is named after the version, with no check that it lies under `$HOME`. A binary exec'd from the prelude's second candidate, `/usr/local/lib/acs/<v>/acs` (src/ssh.rs ~L107), therefore touches `/usr/local/lib/acs/<v>`, writes `/usr/local/lib/acs/.pruned`, and `remove_dir_all`s other users' system-wide versions older than 30 days that are not in *this user's* live set. Silent for a non-root user (errors ignored) but effective for root or wherever `/usr/local/lib` is user-writable (Homebrew on Intel macOS). DESIGN §8 says acs never writes there.

Done when pruning only runs with `root == $HOME/.local/share/acs`, with a test that a system-path binary prunes nothing.
close_reason: Fixed with regression tests (bugs-install branch)

title: Three wall-clock windows remain inside reconnect tests, and they go red under contention
description:
acs-o6x (#158), acs-o8h (#164) and acs-7wu (#174) removed the wall-clock gating
*around* assertions in `tests/reconnect.rs`. Three windows remain *inside*
tests, and the acs-iyq pass (PR #178) hit them: one run of
`cargo test --test reconnect --test shared --test timing --test persist` went
red on four tests at once when the machine was ~3.5x contended (the reconnect
binary took 34.8 s against its usual 10 s). The identical command was green
immediately after, and six further rounds were green.

The windows, each a stimulus that must complete inside a configured timeout:

- **The 4 KiB ring must be overwritten inside the 700 ms backoff** —
  `output_lost_to_a_small_ring_is_a_gap_and_redraw` and
  `modes_of_a_restarted_session_are_reset`.
- **The second client must be up inside 3 s** —
  `modes_of_a_restarted_session_are_reset`.
- **`d` must follow the BEL inside the 2 s command-mode expiry** —
  `the_bell_rings_while_the_link_is_down_too` and
  `the_escape_window_is_the_same_offline`.

These are not the same shape as what acs-7wu fixed. There the test waited a
fixed time and then asserted; here the *client* is given a deadline and the
test must get the machine to do something inside it. The fix is correspondingly
different: either drive the deadline from the test (as acs-o6x did with
ACS_DEAD_MS) so contention cannot eat it, or make the stimulus event-driven so
the deadline only starts once the test knows the client is ready.

Note acs-iyq's `refuse_one_dial()` restores each of these to the window it had
on main — the change did not widen them. And the failures were not captured
before the re-run, so the messages above are reconstructed from which tests
failed and what their windows are.

Context worth knowing: this machine was also carrying six orphaned
`acs 0.13.0 _master` processes from older test runs, ~6 h old, which is part of
why contention was reachable at all. Clean environment first before concluding
a run is telling you something.

Done when none of the three windows can be lost to host contention, each test
still goes red for the regression it covers (show it), and the suite survives
the cold full-parallel `cargo test --workspace` that produced the red runs.
notes:
A sixth test of this class, from acs-6w9 (PR #190, ae86191):
`reconnect::a_network_change_ends_a_frozen_link_without_the_dead_timeout`
failed once with `tests/common/mod.rs:674: only 1 connections`, inside a
verify.sh run that was simultaneously running clippy. It passed alone
immediately after and in every later run.

Note this test is new — it arrived with acs-ft1 (#182) — so it was written
after this bead was filed and is not one of the three in the description.
Its shape is the same family: it SIGSTOPs the transport with ACS_DEAD_MS at
60000 so that only the netcheck can end the link, then waits for a second
connection. Under contention the question is whether the wait is a condition
or a fixed duration; `wait_connections` is the absolute-count API this bead
already flags.

Worth checking together with the wait_connections rework, since that is the
same call site.
close_reason: Fixed in PRs #194 (50fc179) and #195 (3ce7f21): wait_connections(n) removed in favour of connections()/wait_more_connections(base,extra) so the class cannot be rewritten; six tests moved from windows to events; 15 -v waits anchored on the session announcement. Under load: main 8 failures in 72 runs, after 2 in 72 then 0 in 48

title: Pick a detached session from a menu on a plain acs <host>
description:
Wanted, in the user's words: change the behaviour of a plain `acs [<user>@]<alias | hostname>`. Instead of always starting a new session, check for detached sessions on the host. If there are none, create a new one. If there are, present a list of the detached sessions, like --list, and allow selecting one with a single press of its number, or by moving a cursor with up/down (and the vim equivalents j/k). Enter connects to the selection. '.' expands the list to include attached sessions too, which can then be connected to with extra confirmation. 'x' on a session exits that session on the target, and the menu is updated. At the bottom of the list, an 'Exit' option leaves the menu and returns to the command line; Esc does the same at any point.

Verified: today a plain `acs <host>` attaches to `main` (or `$ACS_DEFAULT_SESSION`), creating it if absent (DESIGN §4.4). §4.4 says outright that "the default never depends on what else happens to exist", and Decision 3 (§12) rests on it, so this reverses a recorded decision: update §4.4, §12 and the README's Use section with it. `acs <host> <name>`, `--new` and `--list` stay as they are. The session list already exists: `_proxy --list` sends each master STATUS (src/list.rs `query`, `render`), which gives name, attached/detached, who, idle time and command. Killing a session from outside it does not exist: today only Ctrl-] Ctrl-] `x` inside the session sends KILL. 'x' in the menu needs a new side call, for example `_proxy --kill <name>`, and probably a confirmation.

Open points: what "create a new one" names (`main` if absent, else the lowest free number as `--new` does); behaviour when stdin/stdout is not a tty (keep the old attach-or-create of `main`); the takeover confirmation for an attached session (reuse the BUSY/`--force` path, §4.5); an alias with several hosts resolves to one machine first (§7.3); Esc must be told apart from arrow-key escape sequences; the menu runs in raw mode and restores the terminal on every exit path; with more than nine sessions a single digit cannot address all of them.

Done when a plain `acs <host>` creates with no detached sessions and otherwise shows the menu with number/arrow/j/k selection, Enter, '.', 'x', Exit and Esc working; tests cover the menu's key handling and the create/menu decision; and the docs describe the new default. Filed as one feature, not decomposed; the remote kill side call could be split out as its own bead.
close_reason: Implemented with tests: plain acs <host> creates when nothing is detached, else a menu (digits, arrows/j/k, Enter, '.', 'x' via _proxy --kill, n, Esc); no tty keeps attach-or-create (PR #33)

title: One env-knob parser: reconnect::env_ms exists but is re-rolled in seven places, env-non-empty in seven more
description: Found in review. Numeric knobs: master.rs:25-31 (rebind_every), :136-139 (ACS_RING), prune.rs:11-28, mux.rs:95-102 (fallback_window), :86-91 (persist_from), client.rs:322-327 (ACS_ESCAPE_TIMEOUT_MS), :636-640 (ACS_DIAL_TIMEOUT_MS) each parse an env var by hand while reconnect::env_ms exists. The 'env var, non-empty' filter is repeated at config.rs:242, :710, config_cmd.rs:447, ssh.rs:99, alias.rs:348, :358, prune.rs:33, and pretty() (config_cmd.rs:446) and expand_home() (config.rs:709) are inverses that read HOME two different ways. acs-r1k is about listing the knobs; this is about one parser. Done when a generic sys::env_or::<T: FromStr>(name, default) and sys::env_nonempty(name) replace them.
close_reason: Landed in #383 (25aabf7): sys::env_or / env_ms / env_nonempty replace the hand-rolled knob parsers

title: Check offset + bytes.len() on a wire DATA frame in the client, as acs-hpf did on the master
description: Found in review. client.rs:1490: `state.offset = offset + bytes.len() as u64` with offset from the DATA frame. A frame with offset near u64::MAX panics a debug build (overflow check) and wraps in release. The mirror case on the master got checked_add in acs-hpf (resume.rs:191-199); the client side did not. Done when a non-fitting frame is treated like any other undecodable frame (LinkEnd::Channel) or the add saturates, with a unit test feeding such a frame.
close_reason: Fixed in #260

title: Choose an alias's host by the networks this machine is on (IPv4, IPv6)
description:
Wanted, in the user's words: "add functionality that overrides the selection of alternates process based on the network(s) the current host is on. Determine the 'network' based on its current IP address and check it against the IP the target host resolves to. Keep in mind to support both IPv4 and IPv6".

Verified (v0.8.1): an alias's host is chosen only by pinging (src/alias.rs `pick`, DESIGN §7.3): the first entry in configured order that answers within `reachability_timeout`. Nothing looks at the client's own addresses: there is no interface enumeration in the code (src/netwatch.rs only watches for route changes, to trigger an early redial), and entries' host names are never resolved by acs (ssh resolves them).

Change: before (or alongside) the pings, list this machine's interface addresses with their prefixes (`getifaddrs` via the `libc` crate, no new dependency: IPv4 address + netmask, IPv6 address + prefix length), resolve each entry's `host` to all its addresses (A and AAAA, `getaddrinfo`), and prefer an entry one of whose addresses lies in one of the client's directly connected networks. Such an entry overrides the order-based choice; entries on no local network keep today's rule. Example: at home the laptop is on 192.168.1.0/24 and devbox.lan resolves to 192.168.1.20, so devbox.lan is used even if it is listed after devbox.example.com.

Open points:
1. Opt-in or always on: a setting (e.g. `network_match: true`, global and per alias like `persist`) or the default behaviour.
2. Still ping the matched entry (reachable and on the local network) or dial it without a ping.
3. Which addresses count: skip loopback; IPv6 link-local (fe80::/10) needs a scope and is probably skipped; several matching entries (configured order, or longest prefix).
4. Cost and failure of resolution: resolve in parallel with the pings and bound it by `reachability_timeout`, so a slow or failing DNS costs no more than today; a name that does not resolve simply does not match.
5. How it combines with the bead that marks a host entry as preferred (`prefer: true`): the user's words say the network match "overrides" selection, so network match first, then `prefer`, then order.
6. A redial after a network change (netwatch, DESIGN §5.3) re-evaluates the match, since the client's networks changed.

Done when an entry on one of the client's networks is chosen over the configured order for IPv4 and IPv6, with unit tests on the matching (addresses and prefixes as injected data, both families, loopback and link-local excluded) and on the selection with injected interface and resolver results, `-v` says an entry was chosen because it is on a local network (naming the network), and DESIGN §7.3 and the README describe it.
close_reason: Implemented in PR #58 (f550587): prefer_local_network ranks hosts on this machine's networks first, IPv4 and IPv6

title: A config edit parses the file four or five times, and emit_block deep-clones per item
description: Found in review. config_cmd.rs:358-405: HostSet prechecks with Config::load_files(&files) (both files, :382), read_doc(target) (:389), together() re-reads the other file (:418), write() re-parses the emitted text (:1102), and defined_in reads the other file again on error (:685). yaml.rs:849 emit_block clones entries[1..].to_vec() for every `- key:` item on every emit; the parser clones each line (yaml.rs:269, :309, :353) and Parser::peek rescans from pos per call (:241). apply() allocates a PathBuf per Origin (config.rs:305-308); alias::pick clones every HostEntry up front and the winner again (alias.rs:109-120, :244). Done when both docs are loaded once and passed down, and emit takes slices.
close_reason: Landed in #387 (99f4da1): each file parsed once per edit (host set 5->3 parses), emit_map takes slices, no per-item clone; binary 1046472->1046184 bytes. Parser per-line clones, Parser::peek rescans, Origin PathBuf per value and alias::pick clones were not done (parser moves grew the binary ~490 bytes).

title: A terminal stall during an outstanding netcheck now costs a redial where stale bytes used to cover it
description:
The trade-off acs-br2 (PR #208, 28ee038) made, named here so it is not a
surprise to whoever meets it.

Before, *any* byte arriving after the netcheck PING cleared the probe. That was
the bug — bytes written before the network moved were answering for a link that
had gone. Now only the PONG for that PING answers.

The case that rule was incidentally protecting: if the terminal stalls for
longer than `ACS_NETCHECK_MS` **while a netcheck is outstanding**, the PONG sits
unread in the pipe, the deadline expires, and the link is declared dead where
stale bytes used to cover it. Cost is one redial, bounded by the change's own
deadline — not a stranding.

It is narrow by construction: the stall has to begin **after** the probe was
armed. A terminal already stalled when the network moves is the case acs-br2
fixed, and a link that is genuinely fine answers its PONG within the deadline
like any other frame.

This is the same tension acs-7k7 settled the other way for `ACS_DEAD_MS` (a
stalled terminal must not look like a dead link), so it is worth deciding
deliberately rather than leaving the two rules quietly inconsistent.

Two ways to close it, both from the acs-br2 pass:

- **decode what was just read before the tick**, so a PONG already in the buffer
  is credited rather than being one poll iteration too late;
- **do not count time the client spent blocked in `write_output`** against the
  netcheck deadline, which is the honest measure — the link was not slow, the
  terminal was.

The second is closer to what the deadline is actually asking.

Done when a terminal stall that begins after a netcheck is armed does not cost a
redial, the acs-br2 regression test
(`bytes_in_flight_when_the_network_moved_do_not_answer_the_netcheck`) still
fails without its fix, and DESIGN §5.3 and §5.4 agree about when a stalled
terminal is and is not a dead link.
close_reason: Landed in #329 (e078760): time blocked writing to the terminal is not counted against an outstanding netcheck

title: Release-side duplicates: version compare, SHA256SUMS parsing, sh_quote, install layout, file digest, tokens
