description: Found in review. Version parsing/ordering exists three times: release::parse_version/compare, xtask/src/bump.rs:60-108 (Version::parse/Ord), scripts/update-tap.sh (sort -t. -k1,1n). SHA256SUMS is parsed three ways with different whitespace rules: release::find_asset (split_once(' ')), xtask/src/formula.rs:34-41 (split_once(char::is_whitespace)), install.sh grep. xtask/src/package.rs:103 re-implements the pub ssh::sh_quote. The install layout (~/.local/share/acs/<v>/acs, /usr/local/lib/acs/<v>, ~/.local/bin/acs, /usr/local/bin/acs) is spelled in ssh.rs remote_candidates, install.rs:130-131, upgrade.rs:193-196 and install.sh:209-215. Whole-file digest `sha256::hex(&sha256::digest(&fs::read(p)?))` at upgrade.rs:357, install.rs:334, :360, xtask/src/package.rs:256 (a streaming sha256::file(path) would serve all four and drop the 1.2 MB read on the remote). Random tokens: sys::random_token vs install.rs:128 (byte-identical) vs xtask/src/bump.rs:518-534 (its own /dev/urandom reader though xtask links acs). release::archive_target(OWN_TARGET) repeated at upgrade.rs:272 and update_check.rs:214. Done when xtask uses acs::release and ssh::sh_quote, the layout and digest have one home each, and the parsers agree.
close_reason: Landed in #345 (1482e25): one implementation each for SHA256SUMS parsing, version parsing, shell single-quoting, the install layout (src/layout.rs), streaming file digests, random tokens and the own archive target; tests pin install.sh and update-tap.sh to the Rust; slim size unchanged

title: scripts/test_install.sh has been dark since release signing landed and cannot pass
description:
`scripts/test_install.sh` — one of the five checks CLAUDE.md lists, and **the
only thing that exercises the one-line installer against real releases** — has
been unable to pass since acs-o9v added release signing. Found during acs-x57
(PR #214, 1d00169), and reproduced byte-for-byte against `origin/main`'s scripts
in a temp checkout, so it is not that change's doing.

Two stale spots, both fatal:

1. **`ACS_TEST_OLD` defaults to `0.1.0`, which predates signing.**
   `v0.1.0/SHA256SUMS.sig` is a 404, so the pinned-version case dies.
2. **The local checksum-mismatch mirror it builds has no `SHA256SUMS.sig`.** The
   installer refuses at the signature check before ever reaching the checksum
   check that case exists to test.

With `ACS_TEST_OLD=0.15.0` the three reachable cases pass — latest into the
default layout, pinned then upgraded in place, and `ACS_INSTALL_DIR` — and then
it stops at (2) and **never reaches the Alpine and Ubuntu containers at all**.
So the container coverage has been dark the whole time too.

This is the same shape as acs-cu8, where `scripts/test_linux.sh` was red long
enough to stop being read, and it deserves the same priority for the same
reason: a check nobody can run is a check nobody consults, and this one guards
the path a new user's very first contact with acs takes — `curl … | sh`, often
as root.

A third thing that will bite the moment (1) and (2) are fixed, found by running
the containers by hand: **`alpine:3` in that suite has no `ssh-keygen`.** Its
setup is `adduser -D tester` only, so the installer dies on "need ssh-keygen".
Ubuntu will want `openssh-client` for the same reason. (By hand, with those
installed, both the repository script and the substituted packaged one installed
the real 0.16.0 release in `alpine:3` with busybox wget and ash, and in
`ubuntu:24.04`, as root and as a normal user — so the installer itself is fine;
it is the harness that is stale.)

For (2) there are three ways out, worth choosing between: sign the mirror with a
throwaway key and substitute that key into the installer under test (acs-x57
made that easy); test the checksum path against a signed real release with a
corrupted archive; or have the mirror carry a real `SHA256SUMS.sig` copied from
upstream, which tests less.

Done when `scripts/test_install.sh` passes end to end on a clean machine
including both containers, the checksum-mismatch case actually reaches the
checksum check, and VERIFICATION.md's installer rows say what ran rather than
what was assumed.
close_reason: Fixed in PR #234 (3223aff): scripts/test_install.sh passes end to end incl. alpine:3 and ubuntu:24.04

title: Quote flow-list scalars containing ] } , # so an IPv6 local_forward survives acs config set
description: Found in review and reproduced: `acs config set local_forwards '8080:[::1]:80'` fails with "acs: internal error: line 1: unexpected text after the value: :80]" (exit 1), likewise `host set`. The spec is valid ssh (-L to the remote's IPv6 loopback), passes ssh::check_local_forward, and works on the command line and in block form in a file. Root cause: yaml::plain_ok (yaml.rs:694-707) only guards block hazards (first char, ': ', ' #', leading/trailing space); forwards_node builds a flow Seq, flow_text/scalar_text emit [8080:[::1]:80], and the flow reader's plain-scalar scan (yaml.rs:664-676) stops at any of ,]}#, so the re-parse in write() (config_cmd.rs:1102) errors. Worse, a value 'a,b' in a flow seq silently becomes two items; 'a}b' and 'a#b' are parse errors. Done when plain_ok takes a flow flag (or a flow_plain_ok) that also refuses any of ,[]{}# anywhere, used by flow_text; Node::string("8080:[::1]:80") in a flow Seq round-trips; and the config set command succeeds and get returns it.
close_reason: Fixed in #237 (152b7b8): flow-collection items holding , [ ] { } # are double-quoted

title: Stop link_bin clobbering or downgrading ~/.local/bin/acs
description:
`link_bin` (src/install.rs ~L279) creates a symlink to the version just installed and renames it over `~/.local/bin/acs` unconditionally. Consequences: a hand-installed regular file there (what the release notes tell users to `install -m 755`) is replaced by a symlink into `~/.local/share/acs/<v>/`; an older client connecting to a host with a newer version installed silently downgrades the host's link (DESIGN §8 says it points at the *newest* installed version); a later prune of that version leaves the link dangling.

Done when the link is only replaced if absent or a symlink into `~/.local/share/acs/`, and only when the target version is >= the one it currently points at, with a test for a pre-existing file and a pre-existing newer symlink.
close_reason: Fixed with regression tests (bugs-install branch)

title: Send HELLO as soon as ssh is spawned, not after ACS-READY
description:
serve() only builds and writes HELLO after dial() has seen the ACS-READY marker (client.rs), so every dial and redial pays one extra round trip. The proxy reads stdin only after printing the marker, so the client can write HELLO into ssh's stdin right after spawning it; marker and WELCOME then come back together. Saves 1 RTT on every connection, more through a jump host.
On ACS-NEED the link is closed anyway, so a HELLO sitting unread there is harmless; check the install path and a remote startup file that reads stdin (rare) do not break. Done when HELLO is written before the marker is awaited, with a test that the handshake still works when the marker arrives after noise.
close_reason: Implemented in PR #176 (2579994): HELLO is written into the transport's stdin immediately after spawn, non-blocking, with Link::pending for the remainder. Measured ACS-READY to first output byte ~172ms to ~57ms over a 100ms-RTT relay

title: Keep retrying a lost host, dialling when it answers a ping every 5 s
description:
Wanted, in the user's words: "add functionality that an acs instance will keep trying to reconnect after a session has been disconnected. It will use the same icmp echo infra to detect if a host is reachable again. Add a command line option to enable this, e.g. --reconnect. Also add a configuration option per alias and individual host that enables this. Run the pings once every 5 seconds. Make this configurable as well."

What exists (v0.6.0), so the implementation adds to it rather than duplicating it:
- A client that has attached already redials forever after a drop (src/reconnect.rs `run`, DESIGN §5.3): backoff 1 s → 30 s by ssh dial (ConnectTimeout 10 s, 30 s handshake deadline), an early retry on a network change (netwatch.rs), and for an alias `redial_alias` re-pings its hosts before each dial (`alias::resolve`, parallel pings with `reachability_timeout`, default 500 ms). `--no-reconnect` turns it off; `-r` is accepted and ignored because reconnecting is the default.
- Where the client gives up today, exiting with the unreachable code 255 and "reattach with: acs <host> <session>": the first connection fails to dial or gets no WELCOME within 120 s (client.rs `connect_and_serve`, `Outcome::Exit(code::UNREACHABLE)`); no host of an alias answers a ping at start (client.rs `resolve_alias`); or the link is lost before the session was ever attached (`state.instance.is_none()` in reconnect.rs `run`).

New behaviour:
- **Ping-gated waiting**: while the host is unreachable, ping it once every interval (default 5 s, configurable) with the existing ping code (`alias::ping` / the parallel resolve and `reachability_timeout`), and only dial ssh once it answers. This applies to a plain hostname as well as an alias. A host with `reachability_check: false` cannot be pinged, so it keeps the ssh-dial backoff.
- **Don't give up**: when enabled, the cases above that exit 255 today wait and retry instead, showing the offline status line (§5.4). The command keys keep working (Ctrl-] Ctrl-] d leaves), as in the redial wait.
- **Switches**: a command-line flag, and a setting on an alias and on an individual host entry (the same levels as `identity_file` and `redraw_on_reconnect`; the entry beats the alias, and the flag beats both). A global default and an `ACS_*` override would fit the other settings. The interval, e.g. `reachability_interval: 5s`, is a duration like `reachability_timeout`, global and per alias. `acs config` / `acs config host set` edit both.

Open points:
1. **The flag's name.** Reconnecting is already the default and `-r`/`--reconnect`-style names read as that, so either give `--reconnect` this new meaning explicitly (and say how it relates to `--no-reconnect`) or pick a distinct name (`--wait`, `--persist`).
2. Whether the enabled mode should also replace the 1 s → 30 s ssh-dial backoff for an attached session's redials with the ping gate, or only cover the cases that give up today.
3. A network change (netwatch) should still trigger an immediate ping.

Done when, with the option enabled, an unreachable host (plain or alias) is pinged every interval and dialled as soon as it answers, both at first connect and after a drop; the flag, alias and host settings follow that precedence and validate; tests cover the gating, the interval, the precedence and the `reachability_check: false` fallback (ACS_PING as the test hook); and DESIGN §5.3/§7.2/§7.3 and the README describe it.
close_reason: Implemented in PR #49 (8088046): --persist / persist setting, ping-gated waiting every reachability_interval

title: The YAML reader ignores content on a --- marker line and does not take --- followed by a tab as a marker
description: Follow-up from acs-5mmu (PR #308), which made column-0 document markers survive an edit. Two gaps remain in src/yaml.rs: (1) a '--- <content>' line (content on the marker line, legal YAML for a top-level scalar or flow node) is kept as written but its content is ignored rather than parsed or refused; (2) '---' followed by a tab is not recognised as a marker. Done when '--- x' is either parsed or refused with a clear error naming the line, '---<TAB>' is treated as '--- ', and both have tests.
close_reason: Fixed in #322 (a379a39): content on a --- line is refused with its line; a tab ends a marker

title: Fix master dropping the child's final output at exit (stale revents)
description:
The "pty drained" check (src/master.rs ~L453-458) decides from the revents of the poll that just returned: if the child has been reaped, POLLIN was requested and the pty did not report POLLIN, `pty_open = false` and the next iteration goes to `finish()` without reading the pty again. But `sys::poll` maps EINTR to `Ok(0)` with all revents zero, and SIGCHLD is installed without SA_RESTART, so the child's own exit interrupts the poll; `reap()` then sets `status` and the same iteration closes the pty. On Linux a slave write reaches the master's read queue asynchronously (flip buffer → workqueue), so `echo done; exit` can lose its last line. The same happens when poll returned for another fd and the child wrote and exited before `reap()` ran.

Done when the drained decision requires a subsequent quiet poll of the pty *after* the status was observed (e.g. the full 50 ms timeout genuinely expiring), and a regression test exercises output-then-exit repeatedly.
close_reason: Fixed with regression tests (bugs-master branch)

title: dist and package can be run in different environments, yielding fork binaries beside an upstream installer
description:
Found during acs-x57 (PR #214, 1d00169), which made the packaged installer,
formula and notes carry the build's own releases URL and key.

xtask reads those values at **its** compile time. So `cargo xtask dist` with the
variables set, followed by `cargo xtask package` without them, produces a fork's
binaries sitting beside an **upstream** installer, upstream notes and an
upstream formula — silently, with nothing in the output saying the two halves
disagree.

The user-visible shape: a fork publishes a release; the archives contain its
binaries, and the `curl | sh` line beside them installs acs's. Or the reverse,
which fails closed but confusingly.

`scripts/release-binaries.sh` runs both in one environment, so the supported
path cannot hit it, and `package` now prints what it substituted — but neither
is a check. Anyone who runs the two steps by hand, or who caches a built xtask
across environments, can reach it.

The fix the acs-x57 pass suggested: have `dist` record the channel it built into
`dist/`, and `package` refuse a mismatch. Note **acs-gb4 already established
exactly this pattern** — `dist/source.stamp` records what the tree was, and
`scripts/e2e_ssh.sh --no-build` refuses when it does not match. Extending that
stamp to carry the releases URL and key fingerprint is the same idea and
probably the same few lines.

A second, smaller thing from the same pass, related because it is the other end
of the publish path: **`update-tap.sh` parses the release version back out of
the formula's URLs** by matching `…/releases/download/vX.Y.Z/…`. A fork whose
releases base is not GitHub-shaped renders a perfectly valid formula that the
tap script then rejects as "names no release". It is documented as a caveat
rather than fixed. Decide whether the version should be passed rather than
re-derived — it is already known at the call site.

Done when a `package` whose channel differs from the `dist/` it is packaging
refuses rather than publishing a mismatched pair, a test covers the mismatch,
and the tap script's version comes from something more reliable than a regex
over URLs it did not choose the shape of.
notes:
A second unvalidated input to `dist`, from acs-0pr (PR #220, d1aa5ac), filed
here because it is the same question: what does `dist` check about what it was
asked to build?

**`cargo xtask dist --targets …` does not validate that the names are real
target triples.** A typo builds nothing for that target and produces a `dist/`
that is silently short. acs-0pr now catches it — but only by accident and only
sometimes: its new client-binary check fires if the typo happened to be *the
host's* target, and says nothing if it was one of the others. So a release
built with a mistyped `--targets` can still ship missing a platform.

Cheap to fix at the point of parsing: `rustc --print target-list` is
authoritative, or the same fixed list `dist` already iterates when `--targets`
is absent, which is the smaller answer and matches what the project actually
supports.

Note acs-0pr deliberately declined to put the target list into
`dist/source.stamp` — reasonable, since that would make two dists of the same
tree compare unequal for no gain, and the missing-binary case is better caught
by naming the missing file. Validating the argument up front is the other half
of that decision, and is where it belongs.
close_reason: Fixed in #244 (4f9e5e8): dist writes dist/channel.stamp and package refuses a mismatched or missing one; the formula carries an '# acs-version:' line that update-tap.sh reads instead of regexing URLs; dist --targets accepts only the four released targets.

title: Resolve host aliases on connect with ping check and fallback hosts
description:
Resolve `acs <name>` through the configured host aliases, checking reachability and falling back to alternate hosts.

User's ask: "whenever connecting to a host, use the name as an alias if it is defined in the configuration. When it is, connect to the 'hostname', with user 'user' if defined (otherwise SSH will use its config). If reachability_check is true, use icmp ping once to check if the host is up. If it is, use it; if it is not, check the alternate 'host' if available. If not, display an error message and exit."

- Lookup: if the destination given to acs (without a `user@` part) is a key in `hosts`, try its entries in order.
- An entry with `reachability_check: true` is pinged once: `ping -c 1` with a short timeout. The timeout flag differs between macOS (`-t`) and Linux (`-W`). The first entry that answers is used. An entry with `reachability_check: false` is taken without a check.
- The chosen entry becomes the ssh destination: `user@host` if `user` is set, otherwise just `host`, so ~/.ssh/config decides the user.
- None reachable: print which hosts were tried and exit with the unreachable code (255, src/client.rs `code::UNREACHABLE`).
- Applies to every ssh call: session, `--list`, install. On a redial (src/reconnect.rs) the alias should be resolved again, so a fallback host is picked up after a network change. The master session stays the same only if the fallback is the same machine; say so in the docs.
- A name that is not an alias keeps today's behaviour exactly.
- `-v` should show which entry was chosen and why.

Done when: tests cover alias hit and miss, fallback to the second entry, `reachability_check: false`, all-unreachable → error/255, and `user` handling (ping is injected so tests don't need ICMP); README documents it.
close_reason: Implemented: acs <alias> resolves through hosts with ping check (ACS_PING), fallback, user handling, exit 255 when none answers, re-resolved on redial

title: net.pinged() is read as a positive assertion, but the fake logs when a ping is scheduled
description:
Four tests assert "host X was pinged" by reading `net.pinged()`:
`an_unchecked_host_is_used_without_a_ping`,
`an_alias_connects_to_its_first_reachable_host`,
`an_ipv6_host_is_pinged_with_ping6`, and the `user_at_alias_…` case.

The fake ping writes its line **when the ping is scheduled**, not when it has
run, so under load the line may not be there yet when the test looks. Measured
during acs-2dc (PR #205, 661e1dc): 4-6 failures per 60 runs in every load run.

The author of that pass hit it directly — a first draft of the alias test made
the same mistake and failed **56 of 60** until it was rewritten to assert only
the negative.

The asymmetry is the point: **`pinged()` is sound as a negative** ("this host
was never pinged" — nothing appears because nothing was scheduled) and unsound
as a positive ("this host was pinged" — the line may be pending). acs-2dc used
it negative-only for exactly this reason and left the four positive uses alone
as out of scope.

Two ways out, to choose between: make the fake log when the ping **completes**
so the positive claim is true when observed, or give the harness a
`wait_pinged(host)` that waits for the line rather than sampling once. The
second keeps the fake simple and matches how the rest of the suite waits for
events; the first makes every existing call site correct without changing them.

Done when "host X was pinged" cannot pass or fail on timing, the four tests use
whichever form is chosen, and a load run shows the rate at zero — acs-2dc's
recipe (parallel copies plus `dd` and fork/exec pressure) is the one that
surfaces it.
close_reason: Net::wait_pinged replaces the four positive pinged() samples; Net::set_lagging makes the race happen every run. PR #249 (5237a18).

title: Add acs upgrade: self-upgrade from GitHub releases
description:
Add `acs upgrade`: replace the running acs with the latest (or a given) GitHub release.

User's ask: "add ability to do a self upgrade (from github)".

Proposed design:

- `acs upgrade [--version X.Y.Z] [--check]`. `upgrade` becomes a reserved first argument, like `config` in acs-iff.
- It finds the latest release (or the given one), downloads `acs-<version>-<own target>.tar.gz` and `SHA256SUMS` via `curl` (acs has no HTTP/TLS client; DESIGN §9 size budget), and verifies the checksum.
- It replaces the binary behind `current_exe()` atomically: write a temp file next to it, then rename it into place, keeping the mode. If that directory is not writable (e.g. `/usr/local/bin`), it says to re-run with sudo.
- It refuses a downgrade unless `--version` asks for it, and does nothing when already current. `--check` only reports.
- Remote hosts need nothing: the next connection finds no binary for the new version and installs it (versioned install, DESIGN §8).
- On macOS, a curl download carries no quarantine attribute; the ad-hoc signature must still verify after the rename.
- The download-and-verify logic should match the one-line installer (same asset names), so the two agree.

Done when: tests cover upgrading from a fake release server or injected curl (success, checksum mismatch, already current, unwritable directory), a real upgrade from v0.1.0 → latest is exercised once, and README documents `acs upgrade`.
close_reason: Implemented: acs upgrade [--version X.Y.Z] [--check] via SHA256SUMS + curl/wget, checksum and --version sanity check, atomic replace (plain or versioned layout with links), sudo hint; real 0.1.0->0.2.0 upgrade verified on macOS (codesign valid) and Linux

title: Pick a session from a menu across every configured host
description:
Wanted, in the user's words: "just like the session menu that is presented if sessions exist on a host through `acs <alias|host>`, it should be possible to list all the sessions across all the hosts."

Verified (v0.7.0): the session menu (src/menu.rs, driven by src/pick.rs, DESIGN §4.4) serves one host. `Menu::render` takes a single `host` for its title, and since #40 the whole menu runs over one `_proxy --pick` connection to that host, which also carries 'x' (end a session): `_proxy --kill` no longer exists (src/proxy.rs rejects it). The all-host listing exists as a table only (`acs --list`, src/list.rs `run_all`: every alias resolved and asked in parallel with `_proxy --list`, BatchMode + ConnectTimeout=10 so no prompts, and a HOST column).

Wanted behaviour: the same menu (number / ↑↓ jk / Enter / '.' to include attached sessions / 'x' to end / Esc and Exit to leave) over every alias's sessions, with a HOST column, rows grouped in configuration order, and the hosts that could not be asked (unreachable, not installed, no sessions) shown as lines as `--list` shows them. Enter attaches to that session on that host (the normal session dial, which may prompt, so resolve that alias again and use its key and user as `acs <alias> <session>` does).

Open points:
- **Entry point**: `acs list` in a terminal (with the table when stdout is not a tty), a bare `acs` with no host, or a flag. This touches the bead "Replace acs --list without a host by an acs list subcommand"; decide there first if the menu lives on `acs list`.
- **'x' on another host**: either a short `_proxy --pick` connection to that host, or bring back a kill side call; either way refresh only that host's rows.
- '.' and "new session": whether "new" applies (it needs a host: the cursor row's) or is left out of the all-host menu.
- Latency: the parallel query takes as long as the slowest host (up to the 30 s answer limit); draw hosts as they answer rather than waiting for all.

Done when the all-host menu works with the per-host menu's keys, attaches and ends sessions on the right host, tests cover the menu's multi-host state and rendering (menu.rs unit tests) and an end-to-end pick across two hosts, and DESIGN §4.4/§7.3 and the README describe it.
close_reason: Implemented in PR #47 (34a29db): acs list in a terminal is the session menu over every host alias

title: Ring the terminal bell when Ctrl-] Ctrl-] arms command mode
description:
Ring the terminal bell when Ctrl-] Ctrl-] arms command mode, so the user knows the next key (d, x) is a command. Configurable, on by default.

User's ask: "if it is not breaking our concept of a transparent stream, trigger the bell in the terminal when the command mode sequence has been typed: ctrl-] ctrl-]. Make it possible to configure this behavior, defaulting to on".

Does it break the transparent stream? No, if done right. The bell is written by the client to the local terminal (like the reconnect status line, DESIGN §5.4). Nothing is added to the program's input, and the pty output bytes are unchanged. The one hazard is interleaving: BEL (0x07) also terminates OSC sequences, so writing it while the remote output is in the middle of an unterminated OSC/DCS would end that sequence early. The client already parses output to track terminal modes (src/modes.rs; src/keys.rs lexes escapes too); the bell should only be written at a ground-state boundary, deferred otherwise.

Proposed design:

- Ring when the detector (src/keys.rs `Detector`) arms: the second Ctrl-] within the window, online and in the offline wait (src/reconnect.rs).
- `command_bell: true|false` in the configuration (DESIGN §7.2; src/config.rs BOOLS, so `acs config set command_bell false` works), plus `ACS_COMMAND_BELL=0` in the environment.
- Never ring inside a bracketed paste (the detector already ignores the key there).

Done when tests show the BEL on the client's terminal after Ctrl-] Ctrl-], none with the setting off, and none written in the middle of an OSC sequence the program is emitting; DESIGN §6 and the README document it.
close_reason: Implemented with tests: bell on command-mode arm, deferred past OSC/DCS, command_bell / ACS_COMMAND_BELL (PR #22)

title: Accept non-UTF-8 login noise while reading the remote installer reply
description:
install::side_call (src/install.rs:164-175) reads the whole remote stdout with read_to_string and then looks for the finisher's `ok` line. read_to_string returns InvalidData and leaves the buffer empty if any byte is invalid UTF-8 (confirmed with a scratch program: b"Welcome \xe9\n\nok\n" gives out == ""). The result is ignored, so expect_ok fails with `unexpected reply while installing: ""` although `_install --finish` completed and printed ok.

Scenario: a remote .bashrc or motd prints a Latin-1 or CP437 banner on stdout (bash sources .bashrc for ssh commands). The binary is installed and ~/.local/bin/acs linked, but the client exits INSTALL_FAILED; the next `acs host` works because the prelude then finds the binary. dial()'s MarkerScanner tolerates non-UTF-8 noise line by line, so the two paths are inconsistent.

Done when side_call reads bytes and scans lines with from_utf8_lossy or byte comparison, with a test whose fake finisher emits an invalid byte before ok.
close_reason: Implemented in #77 (649d386)

title: Consider a shorter or RTT-adaptive dead-link timeout
description:
Optional. A link is declared dead after 10 s of silence (pings after 3 s). Resume is lossless, so a false alarm only costs a redial; a shorter or RTT-adaptive timeout (a few times the measured PING/PONG RTT, with a floor) would catch drops sooner where netwatch sees no change. Decide once per-phase timings exist; ACS_DEAD_MS already overrides it.
Touches reconnect.rs Liveness, DESIGN §5.3.
close_reason: Decided: keep fixed 10 s dead interval, not RTT-adaptive (#397, DESIGN §5.3, decision 12)

title: Ping a lost host every second at first when persisting
description:
With --persist, the ping gate pings a lost host every reachability_interval (5 s default), so the dial can start up to 5 s after the host is back. Pings are cheap: ping every 1 s for the first ~30 s after a loss, then back off to reachability_interval.
Touches reconnect.rs wait_for_answer and client.rs wait_for_host, DESIGN §5.3. Done when the interval ramps, with a test using ACS_PING.
close_reason: Landed in #335: a lost host is pinged every second for the first 30 s, then every reachability_interval

title: A refused acs config edit says 'fix the file by hand' when the bad value came from the edit itself
description: Follow-up from acs-5mmu (PR #308). write() now validates the edited tree and cites a line of the file on disk, or no line for a value the edit added. But the refusal hint still ends '(not saved; fix the file by hand)', which is wrong advice when the value at fault is the one the user just typed on the command line: the file is fine and nothing needs fixing by hand. Done when the hint distinguishes the two (a value from the edit -> 'not saved' and nothing about the file; a pre-existing bad value in the file -> the current hint), with a test for each.
close_reason: Fixed in #317: the by-hand hint only when the file on disk is itself refused

title: Filter control characters out of remote text before it reaches the terminal
description:
Security, escape-sequence injection. Nothing in the client filters remote-supplied text before printing it: a grep for is_control over src/ hits only config.rs (local alias names) and yaml.rs (emit). StatusInfo.name, .identity, .command, .version, Welcome.session and the ERROR frame's message all reach the terminal verbatim through list::cells and list::render (which does not clip at all), Menu::render, Menu's note, client::note and reconnect::ask_takeover. menu::clip truncates by display width and char_width gives ESC width 1, so clipping neutralises nothing and can also cut a sequence in half.

Why it matters. `acs list` with no host contacts every alias in parallel and prints every reply, so one compromised or untrusted host in the config can redraw rows in a list the user is acting on: the row read as "trusted-host main detached" need not be the row the cursor is on, and Enter attaches to, or x ends, something else. The same primitive rewrites the takeover question, which is a security decision, and the ERROR note printed mid-session while the terminal is in raw mode. On terminals that answer queries (title report, OSC 52) the reply lands on the client's stdin and can be delivered as INPUT to a different, trusted host. Session names are validated on the remote (session::validate_name) but the client never re-validates what it receives, and identity and command are validated nowhere.

Honest scope: an attached session's stream is deliberately unfiltered (DESIGN's unfiltered guarantee) and dial() inherits stderr, so a hostile login banner already reaches the terminal. What is new here is acs's own UI, the listing and the menu.

Done when one helper replaces C0/C1 controls with a visible placeholder and caps length, applied at every point remote text enters a terminal-bound string (list::cells, menu note and render, client::note, reconnect::ask_takeover), Welcome.session and each StatusReply.name are re-validated client-side, and tests cover a hostile name, identity and ERROR message rendering inert.
close_reason: Implemented in #109: safe::display at every terminal sink, inbound session-name validation

title: Clamp the offline poll timeout in reconnect.rs: ACS_BACKOFF_MS >= 2^31 blocks poll forever
description: Found in review. reconnect.rs:386-395 converts a Duration to a poll timeout with `as_millis() as i32` and no .min(i32::MAX), so a value >= 2^31 ms wraps negative and poll blocks with no timeout. reachability_interval is bounded by config, so only the ACS_BACKOFF_MS env knob reaches it. The other three sites (client.rs:1538-1553, pick.rs:296-299, and the `left.as_millis().min(i32::MAX as u128) as i32` idiom at client.rs:749, list.rs:207, pick.rs:249) clamp. Done when it clamps, preferably via the shared poll-timeout helper (see the poll-timeout/wait-readable task), with a unit test for a Duration above i32::MAX ms.
close_reason: Fixed in #255: offline poll timeout clamped via poll_timeout() with a unit test

title: A command key whose window expires during the handshake is sent as INPUT before WELCOME
description: Found in review. In offline() the detector's forwarded bytes are discarded by design (acs-qty). The detector is shared across the dial (acs-e80), so a Ctrl-] whose 400 ms window expires after the backoff ran into the dial, during the handshake before WELCOME, hits the `deadline passed -> tick -> queue_input` branch at client.rs:1629-1638, which runs regardless of welcomed; the 0x1d goes out as INPUT ahead of WELCOME. Dedupe makes the seq harmless but the byte reaches the program. Same press, two outcomes depending on a few ms. Done when queue_input is gated on welcomed (drop before it), matching offline(), with a test.
close_reason: Fixed in #320 (e6631fc): serve() drops a command key whose window runs out before WELCOME

title: Answer END_SESSION on a session someone else holds with the BUSY identity, not a 10 s timeout
description: Found in review. master.rs:691-708 answers a non-forced KILL from another identity with Msg::Busy and leaves the connection Pending ('the asker may agree and retry'); it never closes it. proxy.rs:496-525 end_session only matches Msg::Error and otherwise keeps reading, so EOF never comes, the KILL_WAIT (10 s) read timeout fires and it returns INTERNAL "session 'x' did not end within 10 s". pick::end draws 'ending session...' and blocks, so the user watches a frozen menu for 10 s and then reads a timeout, when the truth was 'attached from alice@laptop' and the menu already has the take-over question (Ask::Kill). Trigger: the menu sends force: s.attached, so it bites when the listing is stale (someone attached between the list and the x) or any client sends EndSession{force:false}. Done when end_session matches Msg::Busy and returns at once with the identity (an ERROR carrying it, or a code the menu turns into the take-over prompt), and a tests/proxy.rs test attaches as alice, sends EndSession as bob with force:false, and asserts the answer arrives well under KILL_WAIT.
close_reason: Fixed in #230 (772b8f6): end_session answers BUSY at once with the holder's identity

title: Honour ACS_ESCAPE_TIMEOUT_MS in the offline command-key detector
description:
`client_escape()` (src/reconnect.rs ~L194-203) copies only ACS_ESCAPE_KEY into the detector config used while the link is down; `escape_config()` (src/client.rs ~L74-89) reads both ACS_ESCAPE_KEY and ACS_ESCAPE_TIMEOUT_MS. A user with a custom escape window who double-taps Ctrl-] d during an outage gets the hard-coded 400 ms window instead, so the timing silently differs while disconnected.

Done when both sites share one config constructor and a test asserts the offline detector uses the configured window.
close_reason: Fixed with regression tests (bugs-client branch)

title: Fix proxy busy-spin after client EOF while input is backpressured
description:
In `relay()` (src/proxy.rs ~L217-225) once stdin hits EOF `stdin_open = false` and its pollfd gets `events = 0`, but poll reports POLLHUP on a closed pipe regardless of `events`. Every iteration then returns immediately from poll, reads 0, and loops, for as long as `to_master` cannot drain — which is exactly when the master has stopped reading (PTY_IN_HIGH_WATER, child not consuming input). Trigger: paste a lot into a program not reading stdin, then the ssh connection drops → the proxy spins at 100 % CPU until the child reads or the session ends.

Done when the stdin pollfd uses `fd = -1` once closed (poll ignores negative fds), with a backpressure test in tests/proxy.rs.
close_reason: Fixed with regression tests (bugs-master branch)

title: Run the downloaded binary from its destination directory in acs upgrade, not from /tmp
description:
Scratch::new (src/upgrade.rs:238-247) puts the archive and the extracted acs-<v>-<target>/acs under std::env::temp_dir(), and download() (upgrade.rs:375-378) runs it with --version as the "it works here" proof. On hosts with /tmp mounted noexec (common Linux hardening, some CI images) Command::new(&new) fails with EACCES: "the downloaded acs does not run here: Permission denied", and the upgrade is impossible with no hint. scripts/install.sh does not have this problem, it only runs the binary from its final location.

Done when the binary is copied to the destination directory under a temporary name first (already probed writable by check_writable) and --version is run from there before the rename, with a test or at least an error hint naming noexec.
close_reason: Implemented in #85 (b063216)

title: Remove dsh references from the README and help
description:
Remove the dsh references from the README; the general public does not know what dsh is.

User's ask: "remove 'It replaces the dsh shell function (ssh + dtach).' in the README.md file. In general we don't have to talk too much about dsh. The general public doesn't know what it is".

Found in README.md today:

- line 10: "It replaces the `dsh` shell function (`ssh` + `dtach`). The design is in [docs/DESIGN.md](docs/DESIGN.md)." Drop the dsh sentence and keep the pointer to the design.
- line 113: "`-l` is `--list` (as in `dsh`)". Keep the fact (`-l` means `--list`, not ssh's login option) without naming dsh.

Also check the other public surfaces for dsh: `acs --help` (src/cli.rs USAGE) and the release notes (xtask/src/package.rs). docs/DESIGN.md keeps its dsh history: that is design rationale (§1, §10), not user documentation.

Done when README, --help and the release notes no longer mention dsh, and markdownlint passes.
close_reason: Done: README no longer mentions dsh; --help and release notes had none (PR #24, docs: drop the dsh references from the README)

title: Substitute the build's releases URL and key into the packaged installer and formula, finishing the fork knobs
description:
acs-5em (#153, be220ed) and acs-ktm (#160, df58317) made the two knobs that
matter settable at build time: the default releases URL and the release signing
key. The Forking table in docs/VERSIONING.md now has two build-time knobs and
three remaining **source edits**, all of the same shape — a fork still has to
patch files it will then re-conflict on at every upstream sync, which is the
exact problem those two beads removed.

What is left, and why each is the same problem:

1. **`scripts/install.sh`** carries its own `releases=` default and its own
   hardcoded `release_key=`. `cargo xtask package` copies the script into each
   release **verbatim**, which is why a build-time value cannot reach it today.
   If package substituted the build's URL and key into the packaged copy, a
   fork would need no source edit for the installer at all. The drift guard
   `tests/scripts.rs::the_installer_carries_the_same_release_key_and_checks_before_reading`
   is the test that would have to move with it.
2. **`xtask/src/formula.rs`'s `REPO`** — the Homebrew formula's URLs.
   `scripts/update-tap.sh` already takes `ACS_TAP_REPO`, so the tap half is
   done and only the formula contents are not.
3. **`xtask/src/package.rs`** — the install instructions written into NOTES.md
   point at upstream, so a fork's own release notes send its users to acs.

Related asymmetry worth deciding on at the same time: `scripts/install.sh`
honours `ACS_RELEASES_URL` at runtime (https-only, ignored under sudo) but has
**no `ACS_RELEASE_KEY` equivalent** — its key cannot be overridden the way the
binary's can via `signature::key_for`. That is not a hole, because it fails
closed: a release signed by another key is simply refused. But it means the
installer and the binary disagree about what is configurable, and if the
packaged copy starts carrying the build's key the question is whether the
runtime override should exist too, or whether the build-time value is the whole
answer. Decide explicitly rather than by omission.

Done when a fork can build and publish a complete release — binary, packaged
installer, Homebrew formula and notes — without editing a tracked source file,
the drift guard still catches an installer that disagrees with the binary, the
Forking table lists no remaining source edits (or says plainly which are
deliberate), and the runtime-override question above is answered in the doc.
close_reason: Implemented in PR #214 (1d00169): a fork edits no tracked file — three env vars reach the binary, the packaged installer, the formula and the notes. Values are single-quoted POSIX shell words so injection is impossible. Found and fixed a fourth source edit in update-tap.sh

title: Apply local_forwards and the shared-master decision to a session picked from the every-host menu
description: Found in review. client.rs:82 returns into pick::every_host before apply_local_forwards (client.rs:94) and mux::configure (client.rs:95); every_host (pick.rs:418-432) clones args, resolves the alias and calls client::run directly. So `acs list` in a terminal, pick a session on alias db whose config has local_forwards: 5432:db.internal:5432, binds no forward, while `acs db <session>` does. The comment at pick.rs:420 claims it behaves 'As `acs <alias> <session>`'. Skipping the master decision for the listing is deliberate (client.rs:86-89); skipping it for the picked session is not. Done when every_host applies the configured forwards and then mux::configure on the picked args (forwards first, see client.rs:141-144), and a test like the_configured_forwards_merge_with_the_command_lines runs through the every-host path.
close_reason: Fixed in #240 (d2176de): the every-host picked session goes through client::prepare_session

title: Stop the proxy relay draining quadratically under backlog
description: Found in review. proxy.rs:356 and :367 extend_from_slice into the queue, and :394 buf.drain(..n) on each partial write. With limit = 1 MiB and a stalled peer, every partial write memmoves up to 1 MiB: O(n^2) per backlog. Done when the relay writes through from buf when the queue is empty, queues only the remainder, and consumes with a cursor; the backpressure tests (acs-wza) stay green.
close_reason: Landed in #341 (dd9baf8): relay writes through and queues the remainder in the shared cursor OutQueue (src/outq.rs)

title: Add a YAML config file (/etc/acs, ~/.config/acs) with install_on_remote
description:
Add a YAML configuration file for the acs client.

User's ask: "add support for a configuration file, stored as YAML, using the latest unix directory standard, so local in ~/.config/acs/config.yaml as well as a global /etc/acs/config.yaml equivalent. If the global one exists, it is read first, overridden by the local one. Individual parameters override global, dictionaries and arrays are additive."

- Locations (XDG Base Directory): global `/etc/acs/config.yaml`, then local `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/acs/config.yaml` (default `~/.config/acs/config.yaml`). Either may be missing.
- Merge: the local file wins for scalars; dictionaries merge key by key (recursively); arrays concatenate (global entries first).
- First option: `install_on_remote` (bool, default `true`). When false, the ACS-NEED path (src/install.rs) does not install; it exits with a message saying acs is missing on the host and how to install it.
- `hosts`: a map of alias → list of entries `{host: string, user: string (optional), reachability_check: bool (default true)}`. This bead only parses and validates it; using it is the alias-resolution bead.
- A malformed file is an error that names the file and line, not a silent default.
- Nothing exists yet: no config code in src/, and today the only knobs are env vars (README "Environment").
- Binary size matters (budget 1 MB slim, DESIGN §9; deps today are only libc and lexopt). Choose between a small YAML crate and a hand-written parser for the subset used, and record the size cost.

Done when: both files are read and merged with those rules; `install_on_remote: false` stops a remote install; unit tests cover the merge rules, the defaults and error reporting; README and DESIGN document the file.
close_reason: Implemented: YAML config (/etc/acs, XDG local) with merge rules, install_on_remote, hosts parsing; hand-written YAML subset (+17 KB)

title: Write the mode resets before clearing the observer on a gap or fresh resume
description:
On AttachKind::Fresh and AttachKind::Gap the client writes ESC[H ESC[J and then state.observer.clear() (src/client.rs:765-774) without first writing observer.reset_sequence(). The modes the remote program had on before the drop (alt screen ?1049, mouse ?1000/?1006, kitty keyboard stack, bracketed paste) are forgotten, so leave() emits no resets for them.

Scenario: htop runs; the link is dead long enough for its output to overrun the 1 MiB ring; the resume comes back as Gap (or Fresh after "session was restarted"). On a later Ctrl-] Ctrl-] d, or when the session ends, the local terminal stays on the alternate screen with mouse reporting on - the dtach failure DESIGN §6.4 says acs fixes. tests/reconnect.rs::output_lost_to_a_small_ring_is_a_gap_and_redraw only checks the clear sequence.

Done when the resets are written before the clear on Fresh/Gap (or Gap keeps its modes) and a regression test asserts the reset bytes after a gap resume followed by detach.
close_reason: Implemented in #66 (148f35c)

title: A network change during the handshake is drained and ignored, so a doomed dial runs its full timeout
description:
acs-ft1 (PR #182, ecd5d5e) made a network change act on a *connected* session:
a PING at once, and the link is declared dead in ~2s rather than ~10s if the
host does not answer. acs-6p8 (#180) made it act on an *offline* one. Between
the two sits the handshake, where a hint is drained and nothing else.

So between the dial and the WELCOME, a network change is the one moment it is
ignored — and it is the moment it is most likely to be decisive. A dial in
flight when the machine's addresses move is very probably doomed: the ssh
connect is bound to an address that no longer exists. Today it waits out
ACS_DIAL_TIMEOUT_MS — **30s on a redial, 120s on the first connection** —
before anything happens, while the evidence that it will fail arrived
immediately.

The user-visible shape: close the laptop on the train, open it on a different
network while acs was mid-connect, and wait two minutes for a connection that
was dead the moment the lid opened.

Deliberately out of scope in acs-ft1 because it is a structurally different
change: `dial()` **blocks** before `serve()` is entered, so there is no poll
loop to add a fifth fd to. Acting on the hint means either making the dial
interruptible or giving it its own watcher — which is also why it carries more
risk than acs-ft1 did, and deserves its own pass.

Points to settle when taking it:

- **Abandon or shorten?** Killing the ssh child on a change is decisive but
  loses a connect that might have survived (a second interface appearing while
  the first still routes). Bringing the deadline forward to something small,
  the way acs-ft1 brings the dead-link deadline forward rather than replacing
  it, is the more conservative shape and matches the precedent.
- **The first connection is the 120s case** and the one a user actually feels;
  a redial's 30s is already tolerable. Consider whether they want the same
  treatment.
- Interaction with acs-trw (#176): the HELLO is already written into the
  transport's stdin before the marker, so abandoning a dial has to not leave
  a half-sent greeting behind.
- The prelude and the remote-install path (ACS-NEED) both run inside this
  window.

Done when a network change during a dial brings that dial's deadline forward
instead of being ignored, the ACS-NEED/install path still completes across one,
a test drives it with ACS_NETWATCH_FIFO + ACS_NETWATCH_NETS the way acs-ft1's
do, and DESIGN §5.3 says what happens in each of the three phases — offline,
handshake, connected.
close_reason: Landed in #352 (e671d2f): a network change that removed an address abandons the handshake and dials again at once, except while ssh is asking the user something

title: Attach straight from _proxy --pick when nothing is detached
description:
Plain acs <host> already shares one connection between the menu and the attach (decision 8), but with nothing detached it still costs two round trips: the list, then HELLO -> WELCOME. The client could send a HELLO template up front on the pick call, and the proxy, finding nothing detached, would attach at once and answer with the list and WELCOME together. Saves 1 RTT on the most common plain acs <host>.
Touches proxy.rs pick(), pick.rs choose(), DESIGN §4.3/§4.4. With a menu, reading time dominates, so that path is unchanged.
close_reason: Completed in PR #265 (4df9394)

title: Clear the force flag after the attach it was granted for
description:
Security, stale consent. pick.rs does `args.force |= force;` and client.rs passes args.force to hello() on every dial, including automatic redials. Verified by reading both. So a takeover confirmed once sticks to the process for its whole life.

Scenario: you answer y to take the session from alice at 09:00. At 14:00 your link drops and bob has attached meanwhile. The redial carries force, so bob is kicked out with no question, hours later and about a different person. A command-line --force behaves the same way. This is exactly the accident the confirmed-takeover design is meant to prevent.

Done when force applies to the attach it was granted for and is cleared afterwards, a redial that finds a different identity attached asks again, and a test covers drop, new attacher, redial.
close_reason: Implemented in #117: force is a one-shot, spent at the WELCOME it was given for

title: One poll-timeout-from-deadline helper and one wait-readable helper
description: Found in review. Four hand-rolled 'poll timeout from a deadline' computations: client.rs:1538-1553 (consider closure, i64, clamped), reconnect.rs:386-395 (unclamped, its own bug bead), pick.rs:296-299 (clamped), and the `left.as_millis().min(i32::MAX as u128) as i32` idiom at client.rs:749, list.rs:207, pick.rs:249. Three copies of 'wait until readable or the deadline, re-polling after EINTR': client.rs:746-764 (marker loop in dial_once), list.rs:201-224 (query), pick.rs:242-256 (wait_readable). pick::wait_readable already is the helper. Done when a sys::poll_timeout(deadline) (or a Deadline type) and sys::wait_readable live next to poll_retry and the sites use them.
close_reason: Landed in #310 (0bd18d2): sys::poll_timeout, sys::poll_timeout_ms and sys::wait_readable; release -96 bytes

title: Nothing enforces that a note raised outside the frame loop knows the terminal's state
description:
Two loose ends from acs-p4u (PR #210, ad04421), both small.

**1. The invariant is held by accident, not by construction.**

acs-z22 holds `-v` notes to a boundary, but only inside `serve`'s frame loop.
acs-p4u fixed `leave`'s parting note by ending the open sequence first. Every
other note raised **outside** the frame loop — the dial, the offline wait,
alias resolution, the exit notes — is written with no knowledge of terminal
state at all.

Today none of them is broken, and the reason is circumstantial: they all happen
either before raw mode is entered, or after `leave` has written its `ST`. So
the terminal is never inside a program's sequence when they run. Nothing in the
code says so, nothing tests it, and a note added mid-outage by the next person
would land in whatever the last frame left open — which acs-p4u showed is not a
hypothetical: `leave`'s own note was being eaten by an unfinished CSI.

The cheap version is a debug assertion or a single documented entry point, so
the constraint is stated where a new note would be written rather than inferred
from where the existing ones happen to sit.

**2. `show_status` redraws unconditionally on every backoff step.**

Each one now writes `ST` + the line + the reopened sequence. Harmless, and the
reopen is what makes it correct — but the text often has not changed, so a long
outage sends the whole span repeatedly for nothing. A "only when the text
differs" check would cut terminal traffic during exactly the period when the
link is worst.

Worth knowing while in there, from the same pass: after a `Resumed` attach the
observer's lexer state and the terminal's are now in sync where they used to
diverge, and that divergence was what could make `notes::at_boundary` hold a
note for up to `ACS_NOTE_HOLD_MS`. Relevant if anyone tunes that hold.

Done when a note written outside the frame loop cannot land inside a program's
sequence — by construction or by an assertion that would fire if one did — and
the status line does not redraw a message that has not changed.
close_reason: Done in #379 (56997f8): out-of-loop notes step over an open sequence via one entry point, debug-asserted against the observer; show_status skips an unchanged redraw

title: A -v note can land inside a program's output, splitting an escape sequence
description:
`client::note` writes to **fd 2** while the session's bytes go to **fd 1**, and
under `-v` both land on the same terminal. Nothing synchronises them, so a note
can be written in the middle of a frame the remote program is emitting —
splitting an escape sequence, a UTF-8 character, or a line the program is
drawing.

Found during acs-4i2 (PR #192, 9bc0b5c), which deliberately kept
`assert_consecutive` out of its new `-v` tests for exactly this reason. It is
**pre-existing and `-v`-only**, not caused by the notes that pass added — but
that pass added three more notes on a path that fires while a session is live
(a network hint arriving mid-session), so the window is wider than it was.

Why it is worth fixing rather than accepting: `-v` is what someone uses when
something is already wrong. A `-v` that corrupts the screen it is explaining
costs exactly when it is most needed, and the corruption looks like the bug
being investigated.

Not trivial, which is why it is P3 rather than P2: acs owns the frame boundary
on the way *in* (it decodes frames from the link), so queueing a note until the
current frame has been flushed to the tty is possible — but notes are also
emitted from paths that are not inside the frame loop at all (the dial, the
offline wait, alias resolution), where there is no frame in flight and no
reason to wait. The answer is probably "queue only while a frame is being
written", which needs the writer to say when it is between frames.

Worth checking what the status line already does here — it writes to the same
terminal from `reconnect::offline` and has the same hazard, and may already
have a convention worth reusing.

Done when a `-v` note cannot split a frame the program is emitting, notes from
outside the frame loop are not delayed, a test asserts an interleaved note
leaves the program's bytes consecutive (the assertion acs-4i2 had to leave
out), and DESIGN says what the ordering guarantee is.
close_reason: Fixed in PR #201 (da1368c): notes are held to a ModeObserver boundary of the program's stream, the same convention as the command-mode bell, spliced inside the next frame rather than waiting for one to end. Bounded by ACS_NOTE_HOLD_MS and flushed on every serve exit

title: Fetch tags before snapshotting them in version-bump.sh so stale tags are not re-released
description:
scripts/version-bump.sh (lines 15-29) takes `before` from `git tag --list` on the local checkout; `cargo xtask bump` then runs `git fetch --tags origin` (xtask/src/bump.rs:356). Every tag that existed on origin but not locally shows up in `comm -13 before after` and is passed to scripts/release-binaries.sh, which rebuilds it and `gh release upload --clobber`s its assets, writing a new SHA256SUMS for an already-published release. update-tap.sh guards the tap against going backwards, but the release assets are still replaced and CI time spent.

Trigger: running the bump from a checkout whose tags are stale.

Done when the script runs `git fetch --tags origin` before taking the before snapshot (or diffs against the tag the bump reports), and tests/scripts.rs covers a pre-existing remote tag not being released again.
close_reason: Implemented in #81 (335d0f9)

title: install::install holds three copies of the client binary and hashes it twice
description: Found in review. install.rs:119-121 fs::read(self_exe), plan's own_file.to_vec() (:56-58) and side_call's input.to_vec() (:224) hold up to three copies of the ~1.2 MB complete binary; the Payload branch also copies gz and the 600 KB blob (:66-67) and Payloads::from_self re-reads the trailer from disk (payload.rs:137-156) though own already holds it; the whole file is read in the Payload case where it is never sent. The remote shell checks the upload (check_upload) and then _install --finish re-hashes the same file into memory (install.rs:334-338, :360-365), documented as belt-and-braces after acs-4km. Done when plan takes/returns borrowed slices or Cow, side_call writes a borrowed slice from a scoped thread, and the second digest streams if kept.
close_reason: Landed in #325 (b570004): plan borrows, side_call writes a borrowed slice from a scoped thread, Payloads holds a Cow blob, the finisher's second digest streams. Slim x86_64 musl 1,023,504 -> 1,023,480 bytes.

title: Bound dial and the HELLO→WELCOME handshake with a deadline
description:
`dial()` (src/client.rs ~L124-170) reads the ssh pipe with a plain blocking `read` — no poll, no deadline, the signal fd is not watched — and `serve()` uses `timeout = -1` and only starts `Liveness` after the first WELCOME (~L551, L639). ssh's own keepalive is disabled by design (ServerAliveInterval=0) and ConnectTimeout=10 only covers TCP connect. A redial whose connect succeeds but then stalls (half-alive host, firewall that accepts and blackholes, a wedged remote before WELCOME) hangs the client until Ctrl-C. The 10 s dead-link guarantee of DESIGN §5.3 has a hole exactly in the reconnect path. A login file with `printf` and no trailing newline (see the marker bead) triggers the same hang deterministically.

Done when the marker wait and the handshake are covered by a deadline (poll-based, with the signal fd), a timed-out redial returns to backoff, and a test with a silent remote proves it.
close_reason: Fixed with regression tests (bugs-client branch)

title: Dial the last winning alias entry at once while pings confirm
description:
Alias resolution waits up to reachability_timeout (500 ms default) whenever a higher-ranked entry is down, e.g. a preferred devbox.lan while away from home, and pays it on every connect. Remember the last entry chosen per set of local networks (state under XDG_STATE_HOME) and, on the same networks, dial it immediately while the pings confirm in parallel.
Also consider probing the ssh port with a TCP connect instead of ICMP: a truer signal and it works for hosts that drop pings, at the cost of resolving the port (ssh -G, ProxyJump). Touches alias.rs, client.rs resolve_alias, DESIGN §7.3.
close_reason: Landed in #301 (1cb92df): remembered entry per alias and set of local networks, taken as soon as its own ping answers; TCP probe split to acs-fbes
